title: Oeufs en Meurette
summary: Burgundy's brunch: eggs poached in red wine, set on garlic toast and coated in a glossy sauce made from that same wine, with lardons, glazed onions and mushrooms. It is in the course because it joins three disciplines at the top of the trade: a wine reduction that must lose its harshness without turning inky, a starch-thickened sauce finished with butter, and eggs poached in an acidic, coloured liquid where you cannot see the yolk.
skills: a meurette sauce reduced from the poaching wine and stock, mounted with butter
equipment: Wide heavy frying pan or sauté pan, 10 to 11 inches (25 to 28 cm)
Small deep saucepan for poaching, about 7 inches (18 cm) across
Small bowl and fork for the beurre manié
Kitchen scissors for trimming the eggs
Bread knife and an overhead grill (broiler) or toaster

ingredients.item: Young red Burgundy or other light Pinot Noir
ingredients.note: drinkable but not precious; the sauce tastes of it
homemade or a good low-salt bought stock

ingredients.item: Smoked lardons or thick bacon cut in batons

ingredients.note: peeled; blanch 1 minute to loosen the skins

ingredients.item: Unsalted butter, for the garnish pan
Unsalted butter, softened, for the beurre manié

ingredients.note: crushed, plus 1 halved clove for the toast
two per person; the freshest whites hold together best

mise: Peel the onions: drop them into boiling water for 1 minute, drain, trim the root end and squeeze them out of their skins.
Quarter the mushrooms, cut the lardons, slice the shallot and crush the 2 garlic cloves.
Mash the 3 tbsp (40 g) softened butter and 1/4 cup (30 g) flour together with a fork to a smooth paste, the beurre manié, and chill it.
Dice the 2 tbsp (30 g) cold butter and keep it in the fridge.
Crack each egg into its own small cup or ramekin.
Measure the wine and stock; tie the bay and thyme.
Cut the bread, halve the extra garlic clove and warm the bowls by standing them in a sink of hot tap water, drying them just before plating, so the grill is free for the toast.

timeline.do: Peel onions, cut garnish, make the beurre manié.
Cook the lardons, glaze the onions and fry the mushrooms.
Start the wine reduction with shallot, garlic and herbs.
Add the stock and reduce; transfer some wine to the poaching pan.
Poach the eggs in the wine, two at a time, and hold them in warm water.
Thicken and strain the sauce; toast the bread.
Warm the garnish in the sauce, mount with cold butter, plate.

steps.do: Put the lardons in the cold wide pan with 1 tbsp (15 g) of the garnish butter and set over medium heat. Cook 6 to 8 minutes, stirring now and then, until the fat has run and the lardons are golden. Lift them out with the slotted spoon onto a plate, leaving the fat behind.
steps.look: The fat turns clear and the lardons sizzle steadily rather than spit; they are golden at the edges and smell of smoky bacon, not burnt sugar.
steps.mistake: Starting in a hot pan, so the outside burns before the fat renders.
steps.fix: Start cold and keep the heat moderate. If edges catch, lower the heat and add a splash of water to lift the dark bits before they turn bitter.

steps.do: Add another 1 tbsp (15 g) butter, the onions and the 2 tsp (10 g) sugar to the pan with 3 tbsp (45 ml) water. Cook over medium heat, shaking the pan, for 10 to 12 minutes until the water has gone and the onions are glazed and burnished. Lift them onto the lardon plate.
steps.look: The water evaporates, the syrup thickens and the onions roll in a shiny brown glaze; a knife slides into one with slight resistance. It smells of caramel.
steps.mistake: High heat, so the sugar burns before the onions are tender.
steps.fix: If the glaze darkens before the onions soften, add 2 tbsp (30 ml) water, lower the heat and keep shaking until tender.

steps.do: Add the last 1 tbsp (15 g) butter and the mushrooms. Fry over medium-high heat, without stirring for the first 2 minutes, then tossing, for 5 to 6 minutes until browned. Season lightly and add them to the plate. This is the garnish.
steps.look: First the mushrooms release liquid and the pan goes quiet, then the liquid boils away, they begin to squeak against the pan and brown. Nutty smell.
steps.mistake: Crowding the pan or stirring constantly, so they steam grey.
steps.fix: Use the widest pan you have, or cook in two batches. If they are swimming in liquid, keep cooking until it evaporates; they will still brown.

steps.do: In the saucepan sweat the shallot and crushed garlic in 1 tsp (5 ml) of the lardon fat over low heat for 3 minutes until soft. Add all but 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) of the wine, plus the herb bundle, and boil hard over high heat for 12 to 15 minutes to reduce by half.
steps.look: Large rolling bubbles, the kitchen smells first of alcohol and then, as it reduces, of warm red fruit. The level drops to half its starting mark.
steps.mistake: Simmering timidly, so the alcohol lingers and the sauce tastes raw and sharp.
steps.fix: Keep a proper boil and check the level with a spoon handle dipped in at the start as a gauge. If the sauce still smells boozy at half volume, boil 2 minutes more before adding stock.

steps.do: Add the 1 cup (240 ml) stock and keep boiling until you have about 1 2/3 cups (400 ml) of liquid, 8 to 10 minutes more. Keep it at a bare simmer while you poach.
steps.look: The colour deepens to garnet, the liquid coats the spoon thinly and tastes savoury as well as fruity.
steps.mistake: Reducing until thick and dark, which concentrates tannin into an inky, astringent sauce.
steps.fix: Stop at 400 ml; the beurre manié gives body. If it has gone too far, add 1/4 cup (60 ml) stock or water to soften it.

steps.do: Pour the reserved 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) wine into the small deep pan with 1/2 cup (120 ml) water and heat to 180°F (82°C), trembling but not bubbling. Do not add vinegar; the wine is acidic enough.
steps.look: Tiny bubbles cling to the base but the surface barely moves. The thermometer reads 180°F (82°C).
steps.mistake: Boiling poaching liquid, which shreds the whites.
steps.fix: Lower the heat and add a splash of cold water to bring it down quickly.

steps.do: Stir the wine to make a gentle whirlpool and slip in one egg, then a second at the edge. Poach 3 minutes, basting the tops with a spoon. Lift each out, press the base lightly to feel the yolk, and slide into a bowl of hand-hot water at about 140°F (60°C). Repeat until all 8 are done, keeping the liquid at 180°F (82°C).
steps.look: The whites set quickly and stain purple; a lifted egg feels firm outside and trembles like a full water balloon in the middle.
steps.mistake: Poaching too many at once, so the temperature collapses and the eggs stick together.
steps.fix: Two at a time in a small pan. If the white drifts into rags, trim them off with scissors before serving; the yolk is what matters.

steps.do: Pour the poaching wine through the sieve into the sauce. Bring the sauce to a simmer and whisk in the beurre manié a small knob at a time. Simmer 2 minutes, then strain into a clean pan.
steps.look: Each knob dissolves and the sauce thickens to coat the back of a spoon; a finger drawn across leaves a clean line. The floury smell disappears after 2 minutes.
steps.mistake: Adding all the beurre manié at once, which makes lumps, or not simmering long enough, which leaves a raw flour taste.
steps.fix: Add it gradually and whisk. If lumps form, strain them out. Always give the sauce its full 2 minutes at a simmer.

steps.do: Toast the bread in the toaster or under the overhead grill until golden on both sides, then rub one side with the cut garlic clove.
steps.look: Golden, crisp edges; the garlic catches on the rough surface and you smell it at once.
steps.mistake: Pale, soft toast that turns to mush under the sauce.
steps.fix: Toast it darker and drier than for butter; it has to stand up to the sauce.

steps.do: Return the garnish to the sauce and heat through for 1 minute. Off the heat, swirl in the 2 tbsp (30 g) cold butter a few cubes at a time. Taste and season with salt and pepper.
steps.look: The sauce turns glossy and clings to the garnish; it tastes rounded, with no sharp edge of wine.
steps.mistake: Boiling after the butter goes in, which splits it and makes the sauce greasy.
steps.fix: Keep it off the heat once the butter is in. If it breaks, whisk in 1 tbsp (15 ml) hot stock.

steps.do: Lift the eggs from the warm water and blot them on kitchen paper. Set a toast in each warm bowl, two eggs on top, and spoon the sauce and garnish around and over so it pools rather than soaks the bread. Scatter parsley.
steps.look: Purple-stained eggs glistening under the sauce, the toast edges still crisp, and lardons, onions and mushrooms around them.
steps.mistake: Wet eggs that dilute the sauce.
steps.fix: Always blot the eggs. Serve at once; the toast softens within a few minutes.

science: Wine is mostly water, acid, alcohol and tannin with almost no body. Boiling drives off alcohol, which boils at a lower temperature than water, and concentrates the fruit. Push it too far and tannin, a group of polyphenols that bind to proteins in your saliva, becomes harsh and drying, which is why brown stock is added: its gelatin binds some tannin and softens it. The beurre manié works because each flour granule is coated in fat, so it disperses without clumping, then swells and thickens as its starch gelatinises above about 150°F (66°C). Cold butter whisked in at the end forms a fragile emulsion that adds gloss. In the poaching pan, the wine's acidity lowers the pH, helping egg white proteins set faster and tighter, so no vinegar is needed.
plating: Use warm, wide, shallow bowls. Place the toast slightly off centre, the two eggs leaning against each other on it, and spoon the sauce so it pools in a dark ring around the bread. Arrange three onions, a few lardons and mushrooms in the sauce, not piled on the eggs, so each element is visible. A pinch of parsley over the eggs only, and a twist of pepper. Wipe the rim.

pairing.drink: A young red Burgundy or other light Pinot Noir: the same family as the sauce, with red fruit and gentle tannin that sit with the eggs instead of fighting the yolk.
pairing.brennans: Damien Martin Bourgogne Pinot Noir 2023: a red Burgundy on the Brennan's list, the very wine this sauce is built from, so tasting it beside the dish lets you describe the match to a guest from experience.

variations: Beaujolais meurette: use a Gamay for a lighter, fruitier sauce and skip the mushrooms.
Meurette with marrow: lay a slice of poached bone marrow on each toast under the egg.
Vegetarian: replace the stock with a dark mushroom stock and the lardons with smoked mushrooms.
safety: The yolks stay runny. For pregnant guests, young children, the elderly or anyone with a weakened immune system, use pasteurised eggs or poach 5 minutes until the yolk sets.
Not all the alcohol cooks out of a wine sauce; mention it to anyone avoiding alcohol.

title: Eggs Hussarde
summary: Holland rusks topped with grilled ham, a dark marchand de vin sauce, soft poached eggs and hollandaise: a breakfast signature of Brennan's in New Orleans. It is here because it asks you to cook two opposite sauces for one plate, a reduced brown wine sauce and a warm butter emulsion, and to time them with poached eggs so everything arrives hot together.
skills: a marchand de vin sauce of red wine and veal stock
Holland rusks, Canadian bacon and poached eggs plated to order
equipment: Heatproof bowl that sits over one saucepan for the hollandaise
Frying pan or griddle for the ham
Thermos flask for holding the hollandaise

ingredients.item: Unsalted butter, for the marchand de vin

ingredients.note: finely sliced, white and green kept separate
bought, or 8 rounds of brioche dried in the oven

mise: Chop the ham, shallots, spring onions, garlic and mushrooms for the sauce; keep the spring onion greens apart.
Measure the wine, stock and Worcestershire.
Separate 3 yolks into the hollandaise bowl with the 1 tbsp (15 ml) lemon juice and 1 tbsp (15 ml) water.
Melt the 12 tbsp (170 g) butter and keep it warm at about 140°F (60°C).
Fill the poaching pan 3 inches (8 cm) deep, add the vinegar and heat to 185°F (85°C).
Crack the 8 eggs into separate cups; set up the iced water and a tray lined with kitchen paper.
If making rusks, cut 3 inch (8 cm) rounds of brioche 1/2 inch (1 cm) thick and dry them at 300°F (150°C) for 25 minutes until crisp through.
Warm the thermos with hot water and the plates in a low oven.

timeline.do: Prepare all chopped sauce ingredients; dry the rusks if homemade.
Build the marchand de vin and leave it simmering to reduce.
Poach the eggs in two batches and chill them in iced water.
Make the hollandaise and hold it in the thermos.
Finish the brown sauce; warm the ham.
Reheat the eggs in hot water.
Build the plates and serve.

steps.do: Melt the 4 tbsp (55 g) butter in a saucepan over medium heat. Add the chopped ham and cook 2 minutes, then the shallots, spring onion whites and garlic and cook 3 minutes until soft. Add the mushrooms and cook 4 minutes until their liquid has evaporated.
steps.look: The pan sizzles gently, the shallots turn translucent and the mushrooms darken and smell nutty; the base of the pan is dry, not wet.
steps.mistake: Adding the flour while the mushrooms are still wet, which makes a paste rather than a roux.
steps.fix: Keep cooking until the pan is almost dry and you hear the butter frying again before you add flour.

steps.do: Sprinkle in the 2 tbsp (16 g) flour and stir for 3 to 4 minutes over medium heat to a light brown roux.
steps.look: The flour coats everything, turns the colour of peanut butter and smells toasty, like biscuits.
steps.mistake: Raising the heat to hurry the colour, so it scorches in specks.
steps.fix: Keep it at medium and stir the bottom constantly. If you see black specks and smell burning, start the roux again; the bitterness will not cook out.

steps.do: Pour in the 3/4 cup (180 ml) red wine, whisking, and boil 3 minutes until reduced by half. Add the 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) stock, the Worcestershire, thyme and bay. Simmer gently, stirring now and then, for 25 to 30 minutes.
steps.look: It thickens smoothly with no lumps, the alcohol smell fades and the sauce reduces to a rich brown that coats a spoon like single cream.
steps.mistake: Adding the stock all at once to a hot roux and not whisking, which leaves lumps.
steps.fix: Whisk steadily as the liquid goes in. If lumps remain, blend briefly with a stick blender or press through a sieve; the chopped garnish can be returned after.

steps.do: Poach the eggs in two batches of four. Drain each egg in the sieve for 20 seconds to lose the watery white, lower it into the 185°F (85°C) water and poach 3 minutes. Lift out and slide into the iced water.
steps.look: Neat ovals with the white wrapped round the yolk; the yolk wobbles when pressed. In the iced water they firm and stop cooking.
steps.mistake: Boiling water, which tears the whites.
steps.fix: Keep only a few bubbles rising. Trim any ragged tails after chilling.

steps.do: Make the hollandaise: whisk the yolks, lemon and water over a pan of barely simmering water, the bowl not touching it, for 3 to 5 minutes until pale, tripled and thick, 145 to 155°F (63 to 68°C).
steps.look: The whisk leaves trails and a ribbon sits on the surface for 2 seconds; it smells faintly of warm custard.
steps.mistake: Overheating, so the yolks scramble at the edges.
steps.fix: Lift the bowl off the heat every 20 seconds. At the first speck of scrambling, whisk in 1 tsp (5 ml) cold water off the heat and strain.

steps.do: Off the heat, on a damp cloth to steady the bowl, whisk in the warm butter drop by drop, then in a thin stream. Season with salt, cayenne and lemon. Thin with warm water if thicker than double cream, and pour into the warm thermos.
steps.look: Thick, glossy and pale yellow, falling from the whisk in a soft ribbon.
steps.mistake: Pouring butter too fast at the start, so it never emulsifies.
steps.fix: Stop and whisk hard. If it splits completely, whisk the broken sauce a spoonful at a time into 1 tbsp (15 ml) warm water in a clean bowl.

steps.do: Finish the marchand de vin: remove the thyme and bay, stir in the spring onion greens, and season with salt and pepper. Keep it warm over the lowest heat.
steps.look: Dark, glossy, tasting of wine, beef and mushroom, with a little bite from the spring onion.
steps.mistake: Letting it reduce too far while you work on the hollandaise, so it turns pasty.
steps.fix: Add stock or water 1 tbsp (15 ml) at a time until it flows again.

steps.do: Warm the ham slices in a dry frying pan over medium heat for 1 minute a side. Bring the poaching water down to 150 to 160°F (65 to 71°C), slip in the chilled eggs and reheat 60 to 90 seconds. Drain well on kitchen paper.
steps.look: The ham is hot and lightly coloured, still juicy; the eggs are warm outside and still soft in the middle.
steps.mistake: Reheating eggs in simmering water, which sets the yolks.
steps.fix: Keep the water hot but well below a simmer and test one egg first.

steps.do: Build each plate: two rusks, a slice of ham on each, about 2 tbsp (30 ml) of marchand de vin over the ham, a drained egg on top, then 2 tbsp (30 ml) of hollandaise over each egg. Dust with paprika and scatter parsley.
steps.look: Two clear layers of sauce: dark brown under the egg, pale yellow over it, the rusk edges still crisp.
steps.mistake: Spooning the brown sauce over the egg so the two sauces muddy together.
steps.fix: Brown sauce goes on the ham, never on the egg; hollandaise goes on last.

science: The two sauces are thickened in completely different ways. Marchand de vin relies on starch: flour cooked in butter to a light brown roux develops toasted flavour, and when liquid is added the starch granules absorb water and swell, thickening the sauce as it simmers. Browning the flour weakens its thickening power a little, so a brown roux needs a longer simmer to reach body. Hollandaise relies on an emulsion: yolk lecithin and proteins coat tiny butterfat droplets and stop them merging. It must stay between about 120°F (49°C), where the butter firms and goes grainy, and 160°F (71°C), where yolk proteins tighten and squeeze the fat out. That is why the brown sauce can sit on a low flame but the hollandaise must be held warm, never hot.
plating: Warm plates, rusks set side by side in the middle with a small gap so the sauces fall outward. Keep the dark sauce tidy on the ham, just visible beneath the egg. Coat each egg fully with hollandaise and dust paprika in a fine line across the two. A few parsley leaves on the rim only.

pairing.drink: A Brandy Milk Punch or a Brut Champagne: the punch's cream and nutmeg echo the hollandaise, while Champagne's bubbles cut both sauces.
pairing.brennans: Eggs Hussarde: this is the Brennan's dish itself, so cook it at home first and you can tell a guest exactly what each layer is and why it works.

variations: Eggs Sardou: creamed spinach and artichoke bottoms in place of the ham and marchand de vin.
Eggs Owen style: short rib braised in red wine until it falls apart, over a Creole-spiced potato with a soft-boiled egg, under the same two sauces.
Make the marchand de vin a day ahead; it reheats well and tastes deeper.
safety: Hollandaise yolks are only lightly cooked: use pasteurised eggs for pregnant guests, young children, the elderly or anyone with a weakened immune system.
Hold hollandaise at about 145°F (63°C) and use it within an hour; never keep or reheat it.
Chilled poached eggs keep 2 days in water in the fridge below 40°F (4°C).

title: Lobster Benedict
summary: Warm butter-poached lobster on toasted English muffins with soft poached eggs and a bright lemon hollandaise. It is in the course because breaking down a live lobster humanely, extracting every piece of meat cleanly and then holding that meat at a precise temperature is a professional's skill, and building a Benedict around it tests timing at speed.
skills: dispatching and cooking a live lobster humanely
equipment: Large stockpot, at least 8 quarts (7.5 litres), with lid
Lobster crackers or the back of a heavy knife
Small saucepan for the beurre monté
Heatproof bowl and saucepan for the hollandaise
Wide deep pan for poaching eggs
Kitchen towels and a board with a groove

ingredients.note: lively, heavy for their size; cook the day you buy them

ingredients.item: Coarse salt, for the lobster water
Unsalted butter, for the beurre monté

mise: Bring 6 quarts (5.7 litres) of water and the 1/4 cup (70 g) salt to a rolling boil in the stockpot.
Put the lobsters in the freezer for 20 minutes to sedate them; they become still and calm.
Set up a large bowl of iced water and a board on a towel to catch juices.
Dice the beurre monté butter and keep it cold; melt the hollandaise butter and keep it warm.
Separate 3 yolks with the lemon juice and 1 tbsp (15 ml) water; zest the lemon.
Heat the egg poaching water 3 inches (8 cm) deep with the vinegar to 185°F (85°C); crack the eggs into cups.
Chop the herbs; split the muffins; warm the thermos and plates.

timeline.do: Boil the lobster water; sedate the lobsters in the freezer.
Dispatch, cook and ice the lobsters.
Shell the lobsters and portion the meat.
Poach the eggs and chill them.
Make the hollandaise and hold it.
Make the beurre monté and warm the lobster in it; toast the muffins.
Reheat the eggs; assemble and serve.

steps.do: Dispatch each lobster humanely. Lay it flat on the board, belly down, head towards you, a towel over the tail. Find the cross-shaped mark behind the eyes. Place the tip of the heavy knife on that mark, blade facing the eyes, and push down firmly in one quick stroke through the head to the board.
steps.look: One decisive motion; the legs may twitch for a moment afterwards, which is a reflex of the nerves, not awareness.
steps.mistake: Hesitating or using a light knife, which prolongs the process.
steps.fix: Commit to one firm stroke with a heavy, sharp knife. If unsure, plunge the sedated lobster head first straight into the rolling boil instead and cover at once.

steps.do: Twist off the claws with their knuckles and the tail from the body. Drop the claws into the boiling water for 5 minutes, adding the tails after 2 minutes so they get 3 minutes. Lift everything into the iced water for 5 minutes.
steps.look: The shells turn bright red within a minute; the water returns to the boil. The meat is just set at the edges and still translucent in the very centre, which is right because it finishes in butter.
steps.mistake: Boiling the lobster through fully at this stage, which leaves it tough after the butter poach.
steps.fix: Undercook here on purpose. If you overshoot, skip the butter poach and simply warm the meat gently for 1 minute.

steps.do: Remove the tail meat: squeeze the sides of the tail shell until it cracks, then pull it open and ease the meat out in one piece. Cut along the back with the knife and lift out the dark intestinal vein. Halve each tail lengthways.
steps.look: A single curved piece of tail meat, white with red streaks, the vein removed cleanly.
steps.mistake: Tearing the tail into shreds by pulling from one end.
steps.fix: Crack the shell on both sides first with the shears, cutting down the soft underside, then peel it open like a book.

steps.do: Remove the claw meat: wiggle the small pincer back and forth and pull it straight out, taking the cartilage with it. Crack the large claw with the back of the knife near the joint and slide out the meat whole. Crack the knuckles and pick out the meat with a skewer.
steps.look: Whole claws shaped like the shell, the thin flat cartilage drawn out with the small pincer; knuckle meat in chunks.
steps.mistake: Smashing the claw so bits of shell lodge in the meat.
steps.fix: Tap firmly once at the base rather than smashing. Run fingers over every piece to feel for shell fragments.

steps.do: Poach the 8 eggs in batches of four in the 185°F (85°C) water for 3 minutes each, draining each in the sieve first. Transfer them to iced water.
steps.look: Neat whites wrapped round wobbling yolks; they firm in the cold water.
steps.mistake: Too hot water ripping the white apart.
steps.fix: Keep a bare shiver on the surface; trim tails after chilling.

steps.do: Make the lemon hollandaise: whisk the yolks, lemon juice and water over barely simmering water to a thick ribbon at 145 to 155°F (63 to 68°C), then whisk in the warm butter off the heat, drops first then a stream. Season with salt, cayenne and the zest, and hold it in the warm thermos.
steps.look: Glossy and pale, thick enough to ribbon, smelling clearly of lemon.
steps.mistake: Adding the zest early, which can make tiny bitter specks if the sauce overheats.
steps.fix: Add zest at the end; if the sauce splits, whisk it a spoonful at a time into 1 tbsp (15 ml) warm water.

steps.do: Make the beurre monté: bring the 2 tbsp (30 ml) water to a boil in the small pan, then over low heat whisk in the 8 tbsp (115 g) cold butter a cube at a time until creamy and emulsified. Hold it at 160 to 180°F (71 to 82°C).
steps.look: An opaque, creamy liquid butter, never clear and oily; the thermometer stays in range.
steps.mistake: Letting it boil, which breaks the emulsion into clear fat and milky water.
steps.fix: Keep the heat low. If it splits, whisk in 1 tbsp (15 ml) cold water off the heat.

steps.do: Slip the lobster meat into the beurre monté and poach gently for 4 to 5 minutes, spooning butter over it, until opaque throughout and the thickest part of a tail reads 145°F (63°C).
steps.look: The translucent centre turns fully opaque white; the meat is springy, not rubbery. It smells sweet, like hot buttered shellfish.
steps.mistake: Butter too hot, so the meat seizes and toughens.
steps.fix: Hold below 180°F (82°C). Rubbery lobster cannot be undone, so pull it the moment it reads 145°F (63°C).

steps.do: Toast the muffins until deeply golden. Reheat the eggs in 150 to 160°F (65 to 71°C) water for 60 to 90 seconds and drain on kitchen paper.
steps.look: Crisp, craggy muffins; warm eggs with soft yolks.
steps.mistake: Pale muffins that go soggy, wet eggs that water down the sauce.
steps.fix: Toast darker than you think, and always blot eggs before plating.

steps.do: Assemble: two muffin halves per plate, a portion of lobster on each (half a tail and a claw between two halves), an egg on top, 2 tbsp (30 ml) hollandaise over each egg. Finish with chives, tarragon and a few grains of cayenne.
steps.look: Coral-red lobster visible under the egg, glossy sauce draping down one side, herbs bright green.
steps.mistake: Burying the lobster completely so the guest cannot see what they paid for.
steps.fix: Let a claw tip or the red edge of the tail show at the side of each muffin.

science: Lobster muscle is made of short fibres and very little connective tissue, so it toughens quickly when proteins overcook: above about 150°F (66°C) the fibres contract hard and squeeze out moisture. Par-boiling sets the outside and loosens the meat from the shell, and finishing in beurre monté gives slow, even heat. Beurre monté is butter emulsified with a little water, held as a fluid emulsion between about 160 and 190°F (71 and 88°C), so it can poach delicate food without the fierce heat of simmering water. Chilling the lobster first slows its metabolism, and a single cut through the head destroys the main nerve centre quickly. Lemon in the hollandaise adds acid that keeps the yolk proteins flexible and cuts the richness of two butters.
plating: Warm white plates. Muffins set slightly apart, the claw placed so its curved tip points outward over the edge of the muffin. Sauce only on the egg, herbs over the sauce, a dusting of cayenne in a single stroke. Add a small heap of dressed watercress at the top of the plate for colour and a pepper note.

pairing.drink: A Brut Champagne or a rich Chardonnay: the bubbles or the creamy oak meet the butter and lobster sweetness while the acidity keeps the plate from feeling heavy.
pairing.brennans: Brennan’s Essential by Piper-Heidsieck Extra Brut NV: the house Champagne, very dry, which is exactly what two butter sauces and sweet lobster want.

variations: Crab Benedict: warm jumbo lump crab in the beurre monté in place of lobster, 2 minutes only.
Lobster Benedict with béarnaise: tarragon, shallot and vinegar reduction in place of the lemon.
Use the lobster shells to make a quick stock for another dish; roast them first for depth.
safety: Cook lobsters the day you buy them and only while alive; discard any that have died before cooking.
Cook lobster until opaque throughout and 145°F (63°C) at the thickest part.
Hollandaise yolks are only lightly cooked: use pasteurised eggs for pregnant guests, the very young, the elderly or anyone with a weakened immune system.
Keep fingers clear of the knife's path and use a towel to hold the tail; lobster shell edges are sharp.

title: Devilled Kidneys on Toast
summary: Lamb kidneys trimmed of fat and core, seared quickly to pink and tossed in a hot, sharp sauce of mustard, cayenne and Worcestershire, served on buttered toast. It belongs here because it teaches offal preparation, which many cooks avoid, and a pan sauce built and finished in about a minute while the meat rests.
skills: trimming lamb kidneys of fat and core
a mustard, cayenne and Worcestershire pan sauce
equipment: Large heavy frying pan, cast iron or carbon steel

ingredients.note: as fresh as possible, pale and firm, with no strong smell
use less for a milder sauce

ingredients.item: Thick slices of sourdough or white bloomer
Butter for the toast and chopped parsley

ingredients.note: for a squeeze at the end

mise: Peel off any thin membrane from each kidney with your fingers.
Halve each kidney lengthways through the core with the paring knife.
Snip out the white fatty core and tubes with scissors; you want only the brown-red meat.
Soak the trimmed halves in the milk for 20 minutes, then drain and pat very dry.
Mix the flour, mustard powder, cayenne and salt in the shallow dish.
Chop the shallot; measure the sherry, Worcestershire, mustard, stock and cream into separate cups beside the stove.
Have the bread ready to toast and the plates warming.

timeline.do: Trim the kidneys and start the milk soak.
Drain and dry the kidneys; set out the seasoned flour and sauce ingredients.
Heat the pan; toast and butter the bread.
Sear the kidneys.
Build the sauce and toss the kidneys back in.
Spoon onto toast and serve immediately.

steps.do: Look at each trimmed half: the cut face should show only firm reddish-brown flesh. Cut away any remaining white gristle with the tip of the scissors, working in small snips around the core.
steps.look: Clean, smooth halves with a neat notch where the core was; no white strands left.
steps.mistake: Leaving the core in because it looks small; it is tough and tastes of urine.
steps.fix: Be thorough. A notch the size of a fingernail is normal and correct.

steps.do: Soak the halves in the 1 cup (240 ml) milk for 20 minutes, then drain and pat completely dry with kitchen paper.
steps.look: The kidneys look slightly paler and smell mild and clean, not sharp.
steps.mistake: Leaving them wet, so they steam instead of searing.
steps.fix: Dry each piece individually; press them between two layers of paper.

steps.do: Toss the kidneys in the seasoned flour and shake off the excess in a sieve.
steps.look: A thin, even, rusty coat with no clumps.
steps.mistake: Flouring too early, so the coating turns gummy.
steps.fix: Flour them only as the pan heats, within 2 minutes of cooking.

steps.do: Heat the oil and 1 tbsp (15 g) of the butter in the heavy pan over high heat until the butter foams and the foam begins to subside. Lay the kidneys in cut side down in one layer, spaced apart.
steps.look: A loud, immediate sizzle; the butter smells nutty, not burnt.
steps.mistake: Crowding the pan, which drops the temperature and stews them.
steps.fix: Cook in two batches in a smaller pan. Wait for the fat to recover heat between batches.

steps.do: Sear 60 to 90 seconds until well browned, turn and sear another 60 seconds. Move them to a warm plate. They should be firm at the edges and pink in the middle.
steps.look: Deep brown crust; a kidney pressed with a finger feels like the fleshy base of your thumb with your hand relaxed, springy rather than hard.
steps.mistake: Cooking too long, which turns kidneys hard, grainy and strong flavoured.
steps.fix: Kidneys go from tender to rubbery in a minute. Take them off early; they keep cooking on the plate.

steps.do: Lower the heat to medium, add 1 tbsp (15 g) butter and the shallot and cook 30 seconds. Pour in the 3 tbsp (45 ml) sherry and let it bubble, scraping up the browned bits with a wooden spoon.
steps.look: The sherry hisses and almost evaporates; the brown film on the pan lifts into the liquid. Smells sweet and nutty.
steps.mistake: Pouring alcohol from the bottle near a flame.
steps.fix: Always measure into a cup first and add it with the pan briefly off the heat. If it ignites, let the flame burn out or cover with a lid.

steps.do: Add the 1 tbsp (15 ml) Worcestershire, the 2 tsp (10 g) mustard and the 1/2 cup (120 ml) stock. Boil hard for 1 minute to reduce by about half, then stir in the cream if using.
steps.look: Large bubbles, the sauce turns glossy and coats the spoon; it smells sharp, savoury and hot.
steps.mistake: Reducing too far, so the sauce becomes salty and sticky.
steps.fix: Stop when it coats a spoon. If too thick, add 1 tbsp (15 ml) stock.

steps.do: Return the kidneys and their juices to the pan and toss for 30 seconds to coat and warm through. Add the last 1 tbsp (15 g) butter, a squeeze of lemon, and taste for salt.
steps.look: The kidneys gleam in a dark, spicy sauce that clings to them; the sauce tastes hot, sharp and savoury in balance.
steps.mistake: Simmering the kidneys in the sauce, which overcooks them.
steps.fix: Thirty seconds only, off the heat if needed.

steps.do: Pile the kidneys and sauce on hot buttered toast and scatter parsley. Serve at once.
steps.look: The sauce soaks into the edges of the toast while the centre stays crisp.
steps.mistake: Letting it sit, so the toast goes soggy and the kidneys cool.
steps.fix: Plate and send immediately; this dish will not wait.

science: A kidney is a working filter, so its core holds the tubes that carry waste, and these carry strong flavours; removing them is the main step in taming offal. Soaking in milk draws out some of the soluble compounds and blood near the surface, softening the taste. Kidney muscle is lean and finely structured, so like liver it turns from tender to grainy once its proteins pass about 160°F (71°C) and squeeze out water. The thin flour coat browns fast and later helps thicken the sauce. Mustard and Worcestershire bring acid, salt and pungency that cut through the iron-rich meat. The sauce is reduced over high heat because rapid evaporation concentrates flavour in a minute, so the resting kidneys never sit long enough to overcook.
plating: Warm plates, one thick slice of toast cut on the diagonal and overlapped. Spoon the kidneys over the toast so they tumble onto the plate, and pour every drop of sauce over the top. A pinch of parsley and a lemon wedge at the side.

pairing.drink: A dry Amontillado sherry or a Bloody Mary: both carry savoury depth and spice that match the mustard and Worcestershire.
pairing.brennans: Brennan’s Bloody Mary: the same flavours of Worcestershire, heat and lemon run through this sauce, so it is a natural partner at a Brennan's breakfast.

variations: Devilled chicken livers: same method and sauce, seared 2 minutes a side.
Add 4 oz (115 g) sliced mushrooms, fried first, to the sauce.
Serve on a fried slice of bread instead of toast for a richer, old-fashioned version.
safety: Kidneys are traditionally served pink; official guidance for offal is 160°F (71°C). Cook them through for pregnant guests, young children, the elderly or anyone with a weakened immune system.
Use kidneys within a day of buying and keep them below 40°F (4°C).
Add alcohol to a hot pan only from a measured cup, away from your face.

title: Home-Smoked Salmon with Scrambled Eggs and Brown Bread
summary: A whole side of salmon cured with salt and sugar, dried to a tacky pellicle, cold smoked below 80°F (27°C) and sliced long and thin, served with soft scrambled eggs and Irish brown soda bread. It is the most exacting cure in the course: temperature, time and hygiene each decide whether you make something beautiful or something unsafe.
equipment: Cold smoke generator (a maze-style smoke box) with oak or alder dust
A kettle barbecue, smoker cabinet or clean cardboard smoking box
Probe thermometer that reads the air inside the smoker
Wire rack that fits the tray
Long thin slicing knife, very sharp
Frozen ice packs or a tray of ice
Non-stick frying pan and silicone spatula for the eggs
Mixing bowl and baking tray for the bread

ingredients.note: previously frozen or frozen at home first; see safety

ingredients.us: about 3 tbsp, weighed at 3% of the fish
about 2 tbsp, weighed at 2% of the fish

ingredients.item: Fine oak or alder smoking dust

ingredients.note: plus a little more if needed

mise: Make sure the fish has been frozen to -4°F (-20°C) for 7 days, or buy fish sold as previously frozen for raw eating.
Run your fingers along the flesh and pull every pin bone with tweezers, pulling in the direction the bone points.
Weigh the fish, then weigh salt at 3 percent and sugar at 2 percent of that weight; mix with the pepper.
Clean the tray, rack and every surface with hot soapy water; the fish will not be cooked.
Check the weather forecast: smoke on a cool, dry day or night with air below 60°F (16°C).
Fill the smoke generator with dust, level it, and have a tea light ready to light it.

timeline.do: Pin bone, weigh and cure the salmon in the fridge.
Rinse, dry and leave uncovered on a rack in the fridge overnight for the pellicle.
Cold smoke 6 to 8 hours, keeping the air below 80°F (27°C).
Wrap and rest in the fridge for at least 24 hours.
Bake the soda bread.
Slice the salmon; make the scrambled eggs last.

steps.do: Lay the side skin down in the clean tray. Scatter the cure evenly over the flesh, a little thicker on the thick shoulder and thinner on the tail. Cover with cling film and refrigerate at 34 to 38°F (1 to 3°C) for 24 hours for a thin side or 36 hours for a thick one.
steps.look: Within a few hours the salt draws liquid that pools in the tray; the flesh darkens and starts to feel firmer.
steps.mistake: Piling cure on the thin tail, which turns it hard and salty.
steps.fix: Graduate the cure by thickness. If the tail feels firm long before the shoulder, scrape its cure off early.

steps.do: Check the fish: press the thickest part. It should feel firm throughout, like a cold steak, not soft in the middle. Rinse off all the cure under cold running water for 30 seconds and pat completely dry.
steps.look: Glossy, deep orange flesh, uniformly firm; no grains of salt left on the surface.
steps.mistake: Rinsing too long or soaking, which washes out the cure.
steps.fix: Rinse briefly and dry thoroughly. If it tastes too salty on a fried test sliver, soak 15 minutes in cold water and dry again.

steps.do: Set the fish skin down on the rack over the tray and leave it uncovered in the coldest part of the fridge for 12 hours, ideally with a small fan in the room to move the air near the open fridge, or simply overnight.
steps.look: The surface becomes tacky and faintly shiny, like dried varnish; a fingertip comes away dry and slightly sticky. This is the pellicle.
steps.mistake: Skipping the pellicle, so the smoke washes off a wet surface and colours unevenly.
steps.fix: Give it more time; it cannot be rushed. A damp surface after 12 hours needs another 4 to 6.

steps.do: Set up the cold smoke: put the generator in the bottom of the kettle barbecue or smoker, with no other heat source, and a tray of ice beside it. Light one end of the dust with a tea light, let it catch for 10 minutes, then blow out the flame so the dust smoulders.
steps.look: A thin, steady wisp of pale blue-white smoke and a glowing red line creeping along the maze; it smells sweet, like a distant bonfire.
steps.mistake: Thick yellow-grey smoke from damp dust or a flame, which tastes acrid.
steps.fix: Use dry dust and make sure no flame remains. If the smoke turns thick, open the vents a little more.

steps.do: Place the salmon on the top grate, as far from the generator as possible. Put the probe thermometer at fish height. Close the lid with the vents slightly open.
steps.look: The air reading stays below 80°F (27°C), ideally 60 to 70°F (16 to 21°C).
steps.mistake: Smoking on a warm day, so the air climbs and the fish starts to cook and soften.
steps.fix: If the reading passes 80°F (27°C), remove the fish to the fridge and finish smoking at night; add more ice in the meantime.

steps.do: Smoke for 6 to 8 hours in total, checking the air temperature every hour and refilling or relighting the generator as needed. Smoke in two sessions with the fish back in the fridge between them if you need to.
steps.look: The surface turns a deeper copper, like old brass, and smells of wood; the fish stays cool and firm.
steps.mistake: Leaving the fish out at room temperature between sessions.
steps.fix: Return it to the fridge whenever it is not in active smoke.

steps.do: Wrap the smoked side in clean cling film and rest it in the fridge for at least 24 and up to 48 hours.
steps.look: After a day the raw bonfire smell has softened and spread evenly; the colour looks the same inside and out at the edges.
steps.mistake: Slicing straight from the smoker, when the smoke tastes harsh on the surface and absent inside.
steps.fix: Patience: the rest lets the smoke compounds move inward.

steps.do: Make the brown soda bread on serving day. Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C) with a tray inside. Mix the 2 cups (250 g) wholemeal flour, 1 cup (125 g) plain flour, 1 tsp (5 g) bicarbonate and 1 tsp (6 g) salt, then pour in the 1 3/4 cups (400 ml) buttermilk and mix quickly to a soft, sticky dough.
steps.look: A wet, shaggy dough that just holds together; small bubbles appear as the soda meets the acid.
steps.mistake: Kneading it like yeast bread, which develops gluten and makes it tough and heavy.
steps.fix: Mix only until no dry flour remains, about 20 strokes. A slightly wet dough is correct.

steps.do: Tip it onto the floured hot tray, shape into a round about 2 inches (5 cm) deep, cut a deep cross across the top and bake 40 to 45 minutes until it sounds hollow when tapped underneath. Cool on a rack wrapped in a clean tea towel.
steps.look: Dark brown, cracked crust; a hollow knock from the base; the kitchen smells nutty and malty.
steps.mistake: Underbaking, which leaves a gummy centre.
steps.fix: If unsure, give it 5 more minutes upside down on the oven rack. An internal reading of 200°F (93°C) means done.

steps.do: Slice the salmon: lay it skin down, start about 4 inches (10 cm) from the tail, and with the long knife almost flat, draw it in long smooth strokes towards the tail to cut slices thin enough to see the blade through. Leave the dark brown flesh next to the skin behind.
steps.look: Long, translucent, unbroken slices that drape; the knife makes almost no sound.
steps.mistake: Sawing back and forth with a short knife, which tears the slices.
steps.fix: Use the full length of a very sharp blade in one long pull per slice. Chill the fish well before slicing if it feels soft.

steps.do: Make the eggs last. Whisk the 8 eggs with a pinch of salt. Melt the 2 tbsp (30 g) butter in the non-stick pan over low heat, add the eggs and stir constantly with the spatula, lifting the pan off the heat every 20 seconds, for 4 to 5 minutes until barely set. Stir in the crème fraîche off the heat.
steps.look: Small, soft, glossy curds that look slightly wet; they hold together on a spoon but slump gently.
steps.mistake: High heat, which makes dry, rubbery lumps that weep water.
steps.fix: Low and slow, and take them off while still a little loose; they finish on the plate.

steps.do: Serve the eggs on warm plates with the salmon laid in loose folds beside them, chives over the eggs, slices of buttered brown bread and a lemon wedge.
steps.look: Bright orange folds of salmon, pale yellow eggs, dark bread: three clean colours.
steps.mistake: Laying cold salmon on top of hot eggs so it warms and turns opaque.
steps.fix: Keep the salmon beside, not on, the eggs.

science: Salt draws water out of the fish by osmosis and moves inward, unwinding the muscle proteins so the flesh firms and turns translucent; sugar softens the harshness and holds moisture. Removing water lowers what microbiologists call water activity, which slows bacterial growth. The pellicle forms as dissolved proteins on the surface dry into a sticky film; smoke particles, which carry phenols and other compounds, stick to it far better than to a wet surface, and those phenols both flavour the fish and slow the oxidation of its fats. Cold smoking stays below about 80°F (27°C) because above that the muscle proteins start to set and the texture turns flaky and cooked. Resting lets the smoke compounds spread evenly through the flesh.
plating: Warm plates for the eggs, but serve the salmon on a chilled side if you can. Spoon a soft mound of eggs to one side, fold three or four slices of salmon in loose ribbons beside them so their edges catch the light, scatter chives over the eggs, and lean two slices of brown bread against the plate's edge.

pairing.drink: A crisp Chablis or a Brut Blanc de Blancs Champagne: high acidity and chalky freshness cut the oily salmon and lift the soft eggs.
pairing.brennans: Domaine Louis Michel ‘Montmains’ Chablis Premier Cru 2023 (375 ml): a steely, unoaked Chablis on the Brennan's list, the classic white for smoked salmon.

variations: Gravlax-style: skip the smoke and add dill and a splash of aquavit to the cure for a Nordic version.
Beetroot cure: add 1 grated raw beetroot to the cure for a vivid magenta edge.
Hot-smoked salmon: a different technique; smoke at about 180°F (82°C) until the fish reaches 145°F (63°C) and flakes.
safety: Cold-smoked salmon is not cooked. Freeze the fish to -4°F (-20°C) for 7 days first, or buy fish sold as previously frozen, to kill parasites.
Keep the smoker air below 80°F (27°C) and the fish in the fridge at 40°F (4°C) or below whenever it is not being smoked.
Listeria can grow at fridge temperature: eat home-smoked salmon within 7 days, and do not serve it to pregnant guests, young children, the elderly or anyone with a weakened immune system.
Smoke outdoors only; smouldering wood produces carbon monoxide.

title: Kaisendon (Market Seafood Rice Bowl)
summary: A bowl of seasoned sushi rice crowned with raw fish you have broken down yourself, raw scallop, sweet poached prawns and glistening salmon roe, the breakfast of Japan's fish markets. It is in the course because it is pure judgement: choosing fish fit to eat raw, filleting a whole fish cleanly, cutting every slice to the same thickness and keeping everything cold and safe from market to bowl.
skills: breaking down a whole fish to sashimi blocks
equipment: Fish scaler or the back of a knife
Long thin slicing knife (yanagiba) or the sharpest long knife you own
Large board kept only for fish, with a damp cloth under it
Heavy saucepan with a tight lid for the rice
Wide wooden or glass bowl for seasoning the rice
Rice paddle and a fan or a piece of card
Small saucepan and a bowl of iced water for the prawns
Clean tea towels and kitchen paper
Tray of ice to hold the sliced fish

ingredients.item: Whole sea bream or sea bass, sold for raw eating
ingredients.note: bright eyes, red gills, firm flesh, sea smell only; farmed fish sold for raw eating, or wild fish filleted a day or more ahead and frozen at -4°F (-20°C) for 7 days
previously frozen, sold for raw eating
previously frozen, sold for raw eating
cut into thin strips with scissors

ingredients.item: Wasabi, freshly grated or from a tube

mise: Keep all the seafood in the coldest part of the fridge until the moment you work on it.
Rinse the rice in a bowl of cold water, swirling and draining, 5 or 6 times until the water runs almost clear; drain 15 minutes.
Heat the vinegar, sugar and salt in a small pan until dissolved, then cool: this is the sushi vinegar.
Set up the fish station: board on a damp cloth, knives sharpened, tweezers, kitchen paper, a bowl of iced water to rinse hands and a tray of ice with cling film over it.
Bring a small pan of salted water to the boil for the prawns and have iced water ready.
Slice the cucumber, cut the nori, wash and dry the shiso.

timeline.do: Rinse and drain the rice; make the sushi vinegar and let it cool.
Cook the rice, then rest it.
Scale, gut and fillet the whole fish.
Season and cool the rice; poach and peel the prawns.
Trim the fillets, pull pin bones, skin them and chill.
Slice all the fish and scallops onto the ice tray.
Fill bowls with rice and arrange the toppings.

steps.do: Put the drained rice, the 2 cups plus 2 tbsp (510 ml) water and the kombu in the heavy pan. Bring to the boil over medium-high heat with the lid on, about 5 minutes, then lower to the gentlest heat for 13 minutes. Turn off the heat and leave covered for 10 minutes. Remove the kombu.
steps.look: You hear the boil rattle the lid, then quiet; when you open it the surface shows small steam holes and the grains stand up glossy and separate. It smells sweet, not scorched.
steps.mistake: Lifting the lid during cooking, which lets out the steam the grains need.
steps.fix: Keep it shut. If the base catches lightly, do not scrape it into the rice; leave the crust behind.

steps.do: Tip the hot rice into the wide bowl. Pour the sushi vinegar over a paddle onto the rice and cut and fold with the paddle in slicing strokes, never mashing, while fanning it with card for 2 minutes until glossy and body temperature. Cover with a damp cloth.
steps.look: Each grain shines and stays whole; the rice smells sharp and sweet and steam stops rising.
steps.mistake: Stirring hard, which crushes the grains to paste.
steps.fix: Use slicing motions only. If the rice is gluey, it was rinsed too little or over watered; it still tastes right, so press on.

steps.do: Scale the whole fish over the sink or inside a large plastic bag, scraping from tail to head on both sides. Cut off the head behind the gill plate on both sides. Slit the belly from vent to head, pull out the guts and rinse the cavity under cold running water for 30 seconds, scraping away the dark bloodline along the spine with a spoon. Pat completely dry.
steps.look: Smooth skin with no scales catching your fingertip; a clean, pale cavity with no red streak along the backbone; a fresh sea smell.
steps.mistake: Leaving the bloodline, which tastes bitter and spoils faster.
steps.fix: Scrape it out with a teaspoon under running water, then dry well; water left on fish breaks down its texture.

steps.do: Fillet the fish in three pieces: cut along the backbone from the head end to the tail with the filleting knife, keeping the blade angled against the bone, and lift the first fillet away in four or five long smooth strokes, about 2 minutes a side. Turn the fish and repeat. Keep the knife tip on the bones and listen.
steps.look: You hear and feel the knife ticking over the bones; two clean fillets come away with very little flesh left on the frame.
steps.mistake: Sawing, which shreds the flesh, or cutting too high so meat stays on the frame.
steps.fix: Long strokes, the knife flat against the bones. Scrape any meat left on the frame with a spoon and use it for a tartare.

steps.do: Lay each fillet skin down. Cut away the thin belly bones in one slice about 1/2 inch (1 cm) wide, then run your fingertips down the centre to find the pin bones and pull each with tweezers towards the head. Skin the fillet: hold the tail end with a cloth, angle the knife almost flat against the skin and push it forward while pulling the skin back.
steps.look: No bones when you stroke the flesh in either direction; a smooth, skinless fillet with the silver layer left on.
steps.mistake: Pulling pin bones against their angle, tearing the flesh.
steps.fix: Grip each bone and pull gently in the direction it points. A torn fillet can still be sliced; cut around the tear.

steps.do: Poach the prawns: drop them in boiling salted water for 2 minutes until pink and curled into a loose C, then plunge into iced water. Peel, leave the tail on, and slit down the back to remove the dark vein. Butterfly them lightly so they lie flat.
steps.look: Shells turn bright coral, flesh turns opaque white with no grey translucence; a loose C shape, not a tight O, which would mean overcooked.
steps.mistake: Cooking until tightly curled, which makes them rubbery.
steps.fix: Two minutes is enough for large prawns; ice stops the cooking at once.

steps.do: Slice all the fish: with the long knife, place the heel of the blade on the far edge of the fillet and draw the whole length of the blade towards you in one pull, cutting across the grain into slices about 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick. Lay each slice on the ice tray. Slice the scallops horizontally into 2 or 3 discs.
steps.look: Glossy, clean-faced slices with sharp edges; the knife glides with no sawing sound.
steps.mistake: Pressing down or sawing, which crushes the flesh and makes it look dull.
steps.fix: One pull per slice, using the full length of the blade, and wipe the blade with a damp cloth between cuts.

steps.do: Wet your hands lightly and fill each bowl two thirds full with rice, about 1 cup (180 g) each, levelling the top without packing it.
steps.look: Loose, glossy rice at body temperature; not cold from the fridge.
steps.mistake: Refrigerated rice, which turns hard and loses its flavour.
steps.fix: Keep sushi rice covered at room temperature and use within 4 hours of cooking.

steps.do: Lay shiso leaves and a little cucumber on the rice, then arrange the fish in overlapping fans of 3 slices by colour: red tuna, orange salmon, white bream, scallop discs, prawns, finishing with a spoonful of roe in the centre. Add a mound of wasabi and pickled ginger and scatter nori strips.
steps.look: A bowl where each fish sits in its own group, no rice showing between them, colours alternating; everything looks wet and fresh.
steps.mistake: Piling everything in a heap, which hides the cutting.
steps.fix: Overlap slices like fallen dominoes in groups of three, rotating around the bowl.

steps.do: Serve within 10 minutes of assembling, with soy sauce in small dishes. Guests dab wasabi on the fish, not into the soy, and drizzle soy over the bowl.
steps.look: Cold fish, room-temperature rice and a clean sea smell at the table.
steps.mistake: Assembling long before serving, so the fish warms and dulls.
steps.fix: Assemble within 10 minutes of eating; keep the sliced fish on ice until then.

science: Raw fish relies on freshness and cold rather than heat for safety. Freezing at -4°F (-20°C) for seven days kills parasites such as anisakis, which is why sashimi-grade tuna and salmon are usually sold previously frozen. Fish muscle is built in short flakes held together by thin sheets of connective tissue; cutting across those sheets with one long pull gives slices with a clean, glossy face, while sawing tears them and lets water escape. Sushi rice works because short-grain rice is rich in amylopectin, a branched starch that makes grains sticky but still distinct. Vinegar seasoning adds acid that sharpens flavour and slows bacterial growth on the rice, while fanning drives off excess moisture so each grain turns glossy rather than soggy.
plating: Use deep bowls with a wide mouth. Fill rice two thirds high, then build the fish above the rim in fans by colour around the bowl like a clock face, the prawns curled at one side and the roe at the centre. A shiso leaf tucked under each group frames it. Wasabi and ginger sit at the front edge so the guest can reach them without disturbing the arrangement.

pairing.drink: A chilled junmai ginjo sake or a dry Albariño: clean, gently fruity and saline, they echo the sea without covering the delicate fish.
pairing.brennans: Pazo das Bruxas Albariño 2025: a crisp Galician white on the Brennan's list with a saline edge that suits raw fish and shellfish.

variations: Chirashi style: scatter the fish in small cubes over the rice with sliced omelette and pickles.
Zuke-don: marinate the sliced tuna in soy, mirin and sake for 10 minutes before topping.
Cooked-seafood bowl for anyone who will not eat raw fish: seared scallops, poached prawns and lightly torched salmon.
safety: Use only fish sold as fit for raw eating. Wild fish should be frozen to -4°F (-20°C) for 7 days before serving raw.
Keep raw seafood at 40°F (4°C) or below and assemble only minutes before eating; discard leftovers.
Raw fish and shellfish are not advised for pregnant guests, young children, the elderly or anyone with a weakened immune system.
Use a fish-only board and wash knives, board and hands in hot soapy water after filleting.
Work with the knife edge moving away from your hand and keep the board steady on a damp cloth.

title: Korean Breakfast Table with Doenjang Jjigae and Banchan
summary: A traditional Korean breakfast table: rice cooked in a pot, a bubbling doenjang stew built on anchovy and kelp stock, a salted grilled mackerel and five small side dishes, each made by a different technique. It is in the course because cooking many dishes for one table teaches planning, sequence and balance: the hot dishes must land together while the cold ones wait patiently.
skills: a doenjang stew from anchovy stock
equipment: Heavy saucepan with a tight lid, or a Korean stone pot, for the rice
Earthenware pot (ttukbaegi) or small heavy saucepan for the stew
Small non-stick frying pan, ideally rectangular, for the rolled omelette
Small saucepan with lid for the potatoes
Ten or so small serving dishes

ingredients.note: 1/2 inch (1 cm) cubes, for the stew
half in the stew, half for a side dish

mise: Rinse the rice until the water runs clear and soak it in its measured water for 30 minutes.
Remove anchovy heads and the black innards; put them in the stock pan with the kelp and 5 cups (1.2 litres) water.
Cube the potato, tofu and half the courgette; dice the onion; slice mushrooms, chilli and spring onions.
Cut the other half of the courgette into half moons; finely dice the carrot and one spring onion for the omelette.
Salt the cucumber rounds with 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt in a bowl.
Salt the mackerel on both sides with the 1 tsp (6 g) coarse salt and leave it in the fridge on a rack.
Bring a large pan of salted water to the boil for the spinach and set up iced water.
Line up the small serving dishes.

timeline.do: Soak the rice; start the anchovy stock; salt the mackerel and cucumbers.
Strain the stock; braise the potatoes.
Blanch and dress the spinach; dress the cucumbers.
Stir-fry the courgette; make the rolled omelette.
Start the rice.
Build the doenjang stew.
Grill the mackerel.
Rice into bowls, stew bubbling to the table, everything served at once.

steps.do: Make the stock: bring the anchovies, kelp and 5 cups (1.2 litres) water to a simmer over medium heat. Remove the kelp after 10 minutes, simmer the anchovies 5 minutes more, then strain.
steps.look: Pale gold stock that smells of the sea, savoury and clean, not fishy. The kelp feels slippery and soft when lifted out.
steps.mistake: Boiling the kelp hard or too long, which makes the stock slimy and bitter.
steps.fix: Keep a gentle simmer and remove the kelp on time. If it tastes strong, dilute with a little water.

steps.do: Braised potatoes (gamja jorim): put the halved baby potatoes, 2 tbsp (30 ml) soy sauce, 1 tbsp (20 g) rice syrup, 1 garlic clove and 1 cup (240 ml) water in the small pan. Simmer covered 10 minutes, then uncovered 8 to 10 minutes, stirring, until the liquid reduces to a sticky glaze. Finish with 1 tsp (5 ml) sesame oil and sesame seeds.
steps.look: Potatoes tender to a knife and lacquered dark brown; the bubbling syrup becomes thick and sticky and smells sweet and savoury.
steps.mistake: Walking away at the end so the glaze burns.
steps.fix: Stay with the pan once the liquid is low. If it catches, add 2 tbsp (30 ml) water and stir.

steps.do: Blanched spinach (sigeumchi namul): plunge the spinach into the boiling salted water for 30 seconds, then into iced water. Squeeze out the water firmly in your fists, cut into 2 inch (5 cm) lengths and toss with 1 tbsp (15 ml) sesame oil, 1 garlic clove, a pinch of salt, 1 tsp (5 ml) soy and 1 tsp (3 g) sesame seeds.
steps.look: Vivid green leaves still with a little bite; a compact, dry ball after squeezing; it smells nutty from the sesame.
steps.mistake: Leaving water in the spinach, which dilutes the seasoning and pools in the dish.
steps.fix: Squeeze hard, twice. Taste and adjust salt only after dressing.

steps.do: Cucumber salad (oi muchim): squeeze the salted cucumber rounds to remove their liquid, then toss with 1 tsp (2 g) gochugaru, 1 tbsp (15 ml) rice vinegar, 1 tsp (4 g) sugar, 1 tsp (5 ml) sesame oil and a few sesame seeds.
steps.look: Crisp, slightly translucent rounds coated in red flakes; they snap when bitten and taste bright and sharp.
steps.mistake: Skipping the salting, so the salad goes watery within minutes.
steps.fix: Always salt and squeeze first; it seasons and firms the cucumber.

steps.do: Stir-fried courgette (hobak bokkeum): heat 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil in the large frying pan over medium-high heat, add the courgette half moons and a garlic clove and toss for 2 to 3 minutes. Season with a pinch of salt and finish with 1 tsp (5 ml) sesame oil and seeds.
steps.look: Bright green edges just turning translucent; it sizzles and smells of garlic.
steps.mistake: Cooking until limp and grey.
steps.fix: Keep the heat high and the time short; it carries on softening off the heat.

steps.do: Rolled omelette (gyeran mari): beat the 4 eggs with the diced carrot, diced spring onion and a pinch of salt. Heat the small non-stick pan over medium-low with 1 tsp (5 ml) oil, pour in a third of the egg, and when it is almost set at the edges roll it from one side to the other with a spatula. Add another third, lift the roll so it runs underneath, set and roll again. Repeat. Rest 5 minutes and slice into 1 inch (2.5 cm) pieces.
steps.look: A smooth yellow log with no brown spots, layered like a spiral when sliced; it smells gently of egg and spring onion.
steps.mistake: High heat, which browns and blisters the egg so the roll cracks.
steps.fix: Keep the heat low and roll while the top is still slightly wet so the layers stick.

steps.do: Cook the rice: bring the soaked rice and its water to the boil over medium-high heat with the lid on, then lower to the gentlest heat for 13 minutes. Turn off the heat and rest covered 10 minutes.
steps.look: The lid rattles, then the pan goes quiet; inside, glossy grains with small steam holes on the surface. A faint toasty smell means a little crust at the base, which is welcome.
steps.mistake: Opening the lid during cooking.
steps.fix: Keep it closed and trust the time.

steps.do: Build the stew: in the ttukbaegi over medium heat, fry the pork belly 2 minutes if using. Add 2 1/2 cups (600 ml) of the stock, then press the 3 tbsp (55 g) doenjang through a sieve into it so it dissolves without lumps. Add the potato and simmer 5 minutes.
steps.look: The stock turns cloudy tan and smells deeply savoury and fermented; the potato begins to soften at the edges.
steps.mistake: Dropping the paste in whole, so lumps of salty paste remain.
steps.fix: Press it through a sieve or dissolve it in a ladle of stock first.

steps.do: Add the onion, courgette cubes, mushrooms and 1 tsp (2 g) gochugaru and simmer 8 minutes. Add the tofu, chilli and spring onions and simmer 3 minutes more. Taste; add more stock if salty or a little doenjang if thin.
steps.look: A rolling, lively bubble in the pot; vegetables tender, tofu trembling and heated through. It smells rich and earthy with a little heat.
steps.mistake: Stirring hard after the tofu goes in, so it breaks up.
steps.fix: Push the tofu under with a spoon rather than stirring.

steps.do: Grill the mackerel: pat the fillets dry. Heat 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil in the large frying pan over medium-high heat and lay the fillets skin side down. Press gently for 10 seconds, cook 4 to 5 minutes until the skin is crisp, then turn and cook 1 to 2 minutes until the flesh flakes and reads 145°F (63°C).
steps.look: Loud sizzle, crackling golden skin, opaque flesh that flakes at the thickest part; it smells rich and savoury.
steps.mistake: Turning too early, so the skin tears and sticks.
steps.fix: Wait until the fillet releases on its own when you nudge it.

steps.do: Serve everything at once: rice in individual bowls, the stew bubbling in the centre on a trivet, the mackerel on a shared plate, and the five side dishes plus kimchi in small dishes around them.
steps.look: A full table of contrasting colours and textures, steam rising from the rice and stew.
steps.mistake: Serving the hot dishes as each is ready, so the stew and fish go cold.
steps.fix: Time the stew and fish to finish together; the side dishes are designed to wait at room temperature.

science: Dried anchovies and kelp build stock in minutes because both are packed with free glutamate and nucleotides such as inosinate; together they amplify each other, so the savoury taste is far stronger than either alone. Doenjang is soybeans fermented by moulds and bacteria that break proteins into amino acids, giving deep savoury flavour; unlike delicate miso it can be boiled, which is why the stew bubbles at the table. The side dishes each use a different technique: blanching sets the green colour of spinach by driving air from its cells, salting draws water from cucumber by osmosis so it stays crisp, and braising with soy and syrup lets the sauce reduce into a glaze as the water evaporates and sugars concentrate.
plating: Set the table, not the plate. Each person gets a bowl of rice front left and a soup spoon and chopsticks to the right. The stew sits in the centre, still bubbling, with the mackerel beside it. Arrange the six small dishes in a ring around them so that no two dishes of the same colour sit next to each other: green spinach, red cucumber, yellow omelette, brown potatoes, pale courgette, red kimchi.

pairing.drink: Roasted barley tea (boricha), hot or cold: its toasty, gentle flavour cleanses the palate between salty and spicy bites and is the everyday drink at a Korean table.

variations: Replace the pork belly with 8 oz (225 g) small clams, scrubbed and purged, added with the tofu.
Swap the mackerel for salted yellow croaker or salmon, grilled the same way.
Add a sixth side dish of blanched soybean sprouts dressed with sesame oil and garlic.
safety: Cook the mackerel to 145°F (63°C) at the thickest part.
Refrigerate leftover side dishes within 2 hours; most keep 3 days in the fridge.
Keep the hot earthenware pot on a heatproof trivet and warn diners: it stays dangerously hot for a long time.

title: Turkish Breakfast Spread with Simit and Menemen
summary: The Turkish serpme kahvaltı: sesame-crusted simit dipped in grape molasses, a pan of soft menemen, homemade kaymak with honey, and a generous arrangement of olives, cheeses, tomatoes and cucumbers. It is here because one table asks for three separate skills done well, a shaped and glazed bread, egg cookery judged to the second, and a slow-set dairy cream, plus the art of laying out a generous table.
skills: simit dipped in pekmez and sesame
olives, cheeses and tomatoes arranged as a spread
equipment: Wide, shallow ovenproof dish for the kaymak, about 10 inches (25 cm)
Large mixing bowl or stand mixer with dough hook
Two baking trays and baking paper
Two wide shallow dishes for dipping
Dry frying pan for toasting sesame
Shallow frying pan or a sahan (two-handled pan), about 9 inches (23 cm)

ingredients.item: Green Turkish peppers (çarliston) or 1 small green pepper and 1 mild chilli
Kaşar or another mild semi-hard cheese
Cucumbers and tomatoes for the platter

mise: The night before: make the kaymak so it can set and chill overnight.
Toast the sesame seeds in a dry pan over medium heat, stirring, for 4 minutes until golden; tip onto a plate to cool.
Whisk the molasses and its water in one shallow dish; spread the sesame in the other.
Line two baking trays with baking paper.
Halve the menemen tomatoes and grate them on the coarse side of a box grater, discarding the skins.
Slice the peppers; slice the platter cheese, cucumbers and tomatoes; pick the herbs.
Put the honey, olives and white cheese into small bowls.

timeline.do: Heat the cream and milk and set the kaymak in a 180°F (82°C) oven for 8 hours.
Lift out the kaymak and chill; mix and knead the simit dough.
Toast sesame; set out dipping dishes; prepare the platter.
Shape, dip, coat and proof the simit.
Bake the simit.
Cook the menemen.
Serve everything together, the menemen in its pan.

steps.do: Make the kaymak: pour the 2 cups (480 ml) cream and 1/2 cup (120 ml) milk into the wide ovenproof dish so the liquid is about 1 inch (2.5 cm) deep. Set it in a 180°F (82°C) oven, uncovered, for 8 hours or overnight.
steps.look: A thick, wrinkled, pale golden skin forms on top; the cream underneath stays liquid. It smells like warm butter.
steps.mistake: Using ultra-pasteurised cream, which refuses to form a proper skin.
steps.fix: Buy cream that is pasteurised only. If the skin is thin after 8 hours, give it 2 hours more.

steps.do: Cool the dish at room temperature for 1 hour, then refrigerate uncovered at least 8 hours. Lift the thick top layer off with a slotted spatula, leaving the thin liquid behind, and roll or fold it onto a plate.
steps.look: A firm, thick, clotted layer that holds its shape, with a yellow crust on top; it tastes sweet and nutty.
steps.mistake: Disturbing it while warm, so it collapses.
steps.fix: Let it chill fully before lifting. Save the liquid underneath for baking or porridge.

steps.do: Make the simit dough: mix the 3 1/4 cups (400 g) flour, yeast, sugar and salt, then add the 1 cup (240 ml) warm water and 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil. Knead 10 minutes by hand or 6 minutes in a mixer until smooth and elastic. Cover and rest 45 minutes.
steps.look: A smooth, slightly firm dough that springs back slowly when poked; it smells yeasty.
steps.mistake: Adding extra flour because the dough sticks at first.
steps.fix: Keep kneading; it tightens up. A firm dough is right for simit, but it should not tear.

steps.do: Divide the dough into 12 equal pieces of about 2 1/2 oz (55 g). Roll each piece under your palms into a rope 20 inches (50 cm) long. Lay two ropes side by side, pinch the ends together and twist them around each other along the whole length.
steps.look: Even, smooth ropes without lumps; a tight, regular twist like a cord.
steps.mistake: Ropes that shrink back as you roll them.
steps.fix: Let them rest 5 minutes under a cloth and roll again; the gluten relaxes.

steps.do: Bring the two ends of each twisted rope together to form a ring about 6 inches (15 cm) across, overlap them by 1 inch (2.5 cm) and pinch and roll the joint to seal. You will have 6 rings.
steps.look: Round, even rings about 6 inches (15 cm) across, with a seamless join you can barely see.
steps.mistake: A weak join that opens in the oven.
steps.fix: Wet the ends slightly before pressing them together.

steps.do: Heat the oven to 450°F (230°C). Dip each ring into the molasses water on both sides, let excess drip off, then press it into the sesame on both sides so it is thickly coated. Place on the lined trays and stretch each ring gently to 7 inches (18 cm). Proof 20 minutes.
steps.look: Rings glossy brown from the molasses and completely covered in golden seeds; they puff a little as they proof.
steps.mistake: Too little molasses, so the seeds fall off and the crust stays pale.
steps.fix: Dip generously and let it drip for just a second. Press the seeds on firmly.

steps.do: Bake 15 to 18 minutes until deep reddish brown. Cool on a rack for 10 minutes.
steps.look: Dark mahogany crust, toasted sesame smell filling the kitchen, a hollow tap underneath.
steps.mistake: Pulling them out pale, when they lack crunch and flavour.
steps.fix: Bake until clearly dark; the molasses colours fast but the crumb needs the time.

steps.do: Lay out the platter: cheeses, olives, sliced tomatoes and cucumbers, herbs, the kaymak with honey poured over, and small bowls of jam if you like. Put it on the table before the eggs.
steps.look: A generous, colourful spread with no empty gaps.
steps.mistake: Laying everything in rows like a buffet.
steps.fix: Group by colour and cluster small bowls; overlap slices for abundance.

steps.do: Cook the menemen: heat the 2 tbsp (30 g) butter and 1 tbsp (15 ml) olive oil in the shallow pan over medium heat. Add the peppers and soften 4 minutes.
steps.look: Peppers soften and brighten; the butter foams and smells sweet.
steps.mistake: Browning the peppers hard.
steps.fix: Medium heat only; you want them soft, not charred.

steps.do: Add the grated tomato and a pinch of salt and cook 6 to 8 minutes, stirring, until the liquid has mostly evaporated and the sauce is thick and glossy.
steps.look: The sauce stops looking watery, the spoon leaves a trail across the pan and the fat begins to glisten at the edges.
steps.mistake: Adding eggs to a watery sauce, which makes a soupy, pink scramble.
steps.fix: Keep reducing until a spoon drawn through leaves a clear path.

steps.do: Crack in the 6 eggs, wait 30 seconds, then stir lazily with a wooden spoon, folding large curds through the sauce every 15 seconds, for 2 to 3 minutes. Take it off the heat while still glossy and slightly loose. Sprinkle with pul biber.
steps.look: Big, soft curds streaked red and yellow, still wet and shining; it keeps cooking in the pan on its way to the table.
steps.mistake: Stirring constantly or cooking until dry.
steps.fix: Stop one minute before you think it is ready. Serve in the pan, with the simit to scoop it up.

science: Simit gets its deep colour and chewy crust from the molasses dip. Grape molasses is mostly sugar, which caramelises in a hot oven and also feeds the Maillard reaction between sugars and the flour's proteins, so the crust browns far faster than plain dough. The sticky coating also glues on the sesame. Kaymak relies on heat and time: held at about 180°F (82°C), milk fat rises and the proteins at the surface set into a thick skin while water slowly evaporates, concentrating the fat; chilling then firms it into a clotted layer. Menemen works because grated tomato is reduced first, removing water, so the eggs set in a thick sauce instead of a watery one, and stirring gently creates large soft curds.
plating: Bring the menemen to the table in its own pan on a board. Arrange the simit in a basket, stacked on their sides. On the platter, set the kaymak in the centre with honey pooled over it, then fan the cheeses beside it, mound the olives, and alternate tomato and cucumber slices in an arc, finishing with sprigs of parsley and mint.

pairing.drink: Strong black Turkish tea (çay), brewed in a double teapot and served in tulip glasses: it cuts the salty cheese and rich kaymak, and is drunk glass after glass through the meal.

variations: Add sucuk: slice a spiced beef sausage and fry it in the pan before the peppers.
Onion menemen: add 1 small onion, finely chopped, with the peppers.
Açma: shape the same dough into soft buttered rolls without sesame.
safety: Hold the kaymak at 180°F (82°C) in the oven and chill it within 2 hours of removing it; eat within 4 days.
Runny menemen eggs are not fully set: cook them firmer for pregnant guests, young children, the elderly or anyone with a weakened immune system.
