title: Persian Breakfast with Barbari Bread
summary: Nan-e barbari, the long ridged Persian flatbread, made from a dough fermented slowly overnight and glazed with a cooked flour paste called roomal, served warm with feta, fresh herbs, walnuts, butter, soft eggs and cardamom tea. It is in the course because it moves bread craft forward: a cold, slow fermentation, a glaze cooked to a set thickness and a loaf ridged by hand before it meets a very hot stone.
skills: feta, herbs, walnuts and soft eggs
equipment: Large mixing bowl with a lid or cling film
Small saucepan and whisk for the roomal
Baking stone or steel, or a heavy upturned baking tray
Baking paper and a pizza peel or rimless tray

ingredients.note: less yeast for a long, cold rise

ingredients.item: Fresh herbs: basil, mint, tarragon, chives or spring onions
Loose black tea and cardamom pods

mise: The evening before: mix, fold and refrigerate the dough.
Make the roomal early so it cools completely.
Place the stone on the middle shelf and heat the oven to its highest setting, at least 500°F (260°C), for 45 minutes.
Cut two sheets of baking paper about 16 by 8 inches (40 by 20 cm).
Toast the walnuts at 350°F (175°C) for 8 minutes before the oven goes up.
Wash and dry the herbs and radishes; arrange on a platter with the cheese.
Bring a pan of water to a gentle boil for the eggs; set out iced water.

timeline.do: Mix the dough, give it three folds, refrigerate overnight.
Take the dough out; make and cool the roomal.
Heat the oven and stone; divide and pre-shape the dough.
Shape the loaves; prepare the herb platter.
Glaze, ridge and bake the first loaf, then the second.
Soft-boil the eggs; brew the tea.
Serve the bread warm with everything else.

steps.do: Mix the 4 cups (500 g) bread flour, 1 1/2 cups (350 ml) warm water, yeast, salt and oil in the bowl to a shaggy mass with no dry flour. Cover and rest 20 minutes.
steps.look: A rough, sticky dough; after resting it looks smoother and has relaxed.
steps.mistake: Adding more flour because it feels wet.
steps.fix: This is a wet dough on purpose. Wet your hands rather than flouring them.

steps.do: Stretch and fold: with a wet hand, lift one side of the dough, stretch it up until it resists and fold it over the top. Turn the bowl a quarter and repeat four times. Rest 20 minutes and repeat the set twice more, then cover and refrigerate 10 to 14 hours.
steps.look: Each set the dough feels stronger, holds its shape longer and peels from the bowl in one smooth sheet.
steps.mistake: Tearing the dough by stretching too far.
steps.fix: Stretch only until you feel resistance; strength builds over the sets.

steps.do: Make the roomal: whisk the 2 tbsp (15 g) plain flour, 3/4 cup plus 1 tbsp (200 ml) water, the bicarbonate and sugar in the small pan until smooth. Bring to a simmer over medium heat, whisking, and cook 1 to 2 minutes until it thickens to the consistency of single cream. Cool completely.
steps.look: It turns from milky to slightly translucent and coats a spoon thinly; it smells faintly of cooked flour.
steps.mistake: Cooking it too thick, like custard, so it sits in lumps on the dough.
steps.fix: Whisk in water 1 tbsp (15 ml) at a time until it pours like single cream.

steps.do: Tip the cold dough onto a lightly floured surface and divide in two. Fold each piece into a loose rectangle, seam down, and rest under a cloth for 45 minutes until it is no longer cold and has puffed by about half.
steps.look: The dough feels soft and airy, slightly domed, and a fingertip dent springs back slowly.
steps.mistake: Shaping it straight from the fridge, so it bakes tight and dense.
steps.fix: Let it warm and rise; time depends on your kitchen, so watch the dough, not the clock.

steps.do: Lay one piece on a sheet of baking paper and gently press and stretch it with oiled fingers into an oval about 14 by 6 inches (35 by 15 cm) and 1/2 inch (1 cm) thick, keeping air in the edges.
steps.look: An even oval with bubbles visible under the surface.
steps.mistake: Pressing it flat everywhere and knocking out all the gas.
steps.fix: Press from the centre outwards and leave a puffy rim.

steps.do: Brush a thick coat of the cooled roomal over the whole surface. Then hold four fingers together and press them firmly down to the paper, drawing them along the length of the loaf to make 5 or 6 deep parallel furrows, leaving a 1 inch (2.5 cm) border all round.
steps.look: Deep, wet, glossy grooves that hold their shape; the roomal pools in them.
steps.mistake: Shallow furrows that close up in the oven.
steps.fix: Press all the way to the paper. The roomal helps the grooves hold.

steps.do: Sprinkle with half the sesame and nigella seeds. Slide the loaf on its paper onto the peel, then onto the hot stone. Bake 12 to 14 minutes until deep golden with dark amber ridges.
steps.look: The bread puffs within 2 minutes, the ridges turn glossy amber and the kitchen smells of toasted sesame.
steps.mistake: Opening the oven repeatedly, which drops the temperature.
steps.fix: Check once at 10 minutes. If the base browns before the top, move the bread to a higher shelf for the last 2 minutes.

steps.do: Lift the bread onto a rack and wrap in a clean tea towel for 5 minutes to keep the crust supple. Bake the second loaf the same way, letting the stone reheat for 10 minutes first.
steps.look: A glossy, flexible crust, crisp at the edges, soft and chewy inside.
steps.mistake: Leaving it uncovered, so the crust turns hard.
steps.fix: Wrap while warm; serve within the hour, or reheat briefly.

steps.do: Soft-boil the eggs: lower them into gently boiling water for 6 1/2 minutes, then into iced water for 1 minute. Peel or serve in cups.
steps.look: Whites fully set, yolks thick and runny like honey.
steps.mistake: Boiling too hard, which cracks the shells.
steps.fix: Lower the eggs on a spoon and keep a gentle boil.

steps.do: Brew the tea: warm the pot, add the tea and crushed cardamom, pour on 4 cups (950 ml) water just off the boil and steep 5 minutes. Serve the bread torn by hand with butter, feta, walnuts, herbs, radishes, honey, eggs and tea.
steps.look: Deep amber tea scented with cardamom; a table where everyone builds their own mouthful.
steps.mistake: Cutting the bread with a knife, which crushes it.
steps.fix: Tear it along the ridges.

science: A small amount of yeast and a long, cold fermentation slow gas production while enzymes in the flour keep working, breaking starch into sugars and proteins into flavour compounds; the bread tastes deeper and browns better than a fast dough. Stretching and folding align gluten strands into a strong network without heavy kneading. The roomal is the key: cooking flour and water gelatinises the starch into a gel that seals the surface, keeping the crust glossy and supple rather than dry. Bicarbonate of soda raises the surface pH, and the Maillard browning reaction runs much faster in alkaline conditions, so the ridges darken quickly in the few minutes the bread spends in a very hot oven.
plating: Lay one whole loaf on a long board and tear the second in pieces into a basket. Build a large platter of herbs in loose bunches with radishes tucked between them, a block of feta drizzled with a little olive oil and walnuts scattered around. Butter and honey in small bowls, eggs in cups, tea in glasses.

pairing.drink: Persian black tea brewed with cardamom, served strong in clear glasses; sip it through a sugar cube or with dates, which balances the salty cheese.

variations: Za'atar barbari: brush with oil mixed with za'atar instead of nigella after the roomal.
Smaller loaves: divide into four and bake 9 to 10 minutes for individual breads.
Same-day version: use 2 tsp (7 g) yeast and ferment at room temperature for about 90 minutes.
safety: Use oven gloves and a peel at 500°F (260°C); the stone stays hot for an hour after the oven is off.
Soft-boiled yolks are runny: boil 9 minutes for pregnant guests, young children, the elderly or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Barbacoa de Borrego with Consomé
summary: Lamb wrapped in leaves and steamed for hours over a pot of chickpeas, rice and chillies that catches every drop of juice, then served in warm tortillas with a cup of the rich consomé on the side. It is the Sunday breakfast of central Mexico, and it is in the course because it teaches pit cooking adapted to a home oven: slow, sealed, moist heat, and a broth that becomes a second dish.
skills: wrapping lamb in maguey or banana leaves
steaming over a broth for hours
serving the consomé that caught the drippings
equipment: Deep roasting tin, at least 4 inches (10 cm) deep, that fits your oven
Wire rack that sits inside the tin above the liquid, on balls of foil if needed
Comal, cast-iron pan or griddle for the leaves and tortillas
Tortilla warmer or a clean tea towel

ingredients.note: cut in 3 or 4 pieces by the butcher; yearling lamb or hogget is ideal

ingredients.item: Ground cumin and dried oregano (Mexican if possible)

ingredients.note: frozen from Latin or Asian shops; maguey leaves if you can find them
half sliced for the broth, half chopped to serve

ingredients.item: Coriander, limes and a salsa roja

mise: The night before: soak the chickpeas, rub the lamb with salt and leave it uncovered on a rack in the fridge.
Thaw the banana leaves, wipe them clean and cut off the hard central rib.

Toast the adobo chillies on a dry pan 20 seconds a side until fragrant, soak in hot water 20 minutes, then blend with garlic, cumin, oregano, vinegar and 1/4 cup (60 ml) soaking water to a smooth paste.
Drain the chickpeas; slice half the onion and dice the carrot.
Heat the oven to 300°F (150°C) and set a shelf low enough for the deep tin.

timeline.do: Soak the chickpeas; salt the lamb and chill uncovered.
Make the adobo; soften the leaves on the comal.
Build the consomé base in the tin, wrap the lamb, seal and put in the oven.
Check the lamb is falling from the bone.
Shred the lamb; skim and season the consomé.
Warm the tortillas; set out garnishes.

steps.do: Soften the banana leaves: pass each piece over a gas flame or lay it on a hot dry comal for 10 to 20 seconds a side until it turns glossy, darker green and pliable.
steps.look: The leaf shines as if oiled, smells grassy and sweet, and bends without cracking.
steps.mistake: Using leaves straight from the packet, which split when you fold them.
steps.fix: Warm every piece; work quickly and keep them under a towel.

steps.do: Rub the adobo all over the salted lamb pieces, working it into every crevice; use about 3 tbsp (45 g) per pound of meat.
steps.look: A thin, even, brick-red coat; it smells of dried chilli and garlic.
steps.mistake: A thick layer of paste that slides off.
steps.fix: Use just enough to coat; save any extra to stir into the consomé.

steps.do: Put the chickpeas, rice, sliced onion, the consomé guajillos and garlic, the mint, carrot and 6 cups (1.4 litres) water in the roasting tin with 1 tsp (6 g) salt. Set the rack over it so it sits clear of the liquid.
steps.look: Liquid about 2 inches (5 cm) deep with at least 1 inch (2.5 cm) of space below the rack.
steps.mistake: The rack touching the liquid, so the lamb boils instead of steams.
steps.fix: Raise the rack on balls of foil, or use less water and top up later.

steps.do: Line the rack with overlapping banana leaves, glossy side up, letting them hang over the sides. Lay the lamb on top with the 6 avocado leaves, then fold the leaves over to wrap the meat in a loose parcel, adding more leaves to cover any gaps.
steps.look: A neat green parcel with no meat exposed.
steps.mistake: Wrapping so tightly that leaves split, or leaving gaps that let the meat dry.
steps.fix: Patch gaps with extra pieces; it should be covered, not airtight.

steps.do: Cover the whole tin tightly with two layers of foil, crimping the edges to seal in the steam. Cook at 300°F (150°C) for 4 1/2 to 5 hours.
steps.look: After an hour the kitchen smells of lamb, chilli and grass; you may hear a gentle bubbling.
steps.mistake: Loose foil that lets steam escape, so the consomé evaporates and the base scorches.
steps.fix: Seal it well. Check once at 3 hours: lift a corner, and if the liquid is low, add 2 cups (480 ml) boiling water.

steps.do: Lift a corner of the foil and leaves and test the lamb after 4 1/2 hours: a fork should slide in with no resistance and the bone should pull away cleanly.
steps.look: The meat collapses into soft strands and the internal reading is around 200°F (93°C), far past safe, where the connective tissue has melted.
steps.mistake: Pulling it at the first sign of tenderness, when it is still chewy.
steps.fix: Give it another 30 to 45 minutes, resealed, until the bone wiggles free.

steps.do: Carefully lift the parcel onto a tray. Open it, remove the bones, gristle and leaves, and pull the meat into large shreds about 2 inches (5 cm) long with two forks. Moisten with a ladle of consomé and cover.
steps.look: Glistening, red-edged shreds of lamb; a rich, meaty smell.
steps.mistake: Shredding too finely, so it dries out.
steps.fix: Leave chunky shreds and keep them covered and moistened.

steps.do: Skim the consomé: tilt the tin and spoon off most of the clear fat from the surface. Taste and season with salt. The rice will have broken down and thickened the broth slightly; the chickpeas will be soft.
steps.look: A ruddy, slightly cloudy broth, rich but not greasy, with tender chickpeas. It smells of lamb and chilli.
steps.mistake: Leaving all the fat, so the consomé feels oily.
steps.fix: Skim well, or blot the surface with kitchen paper laid flat for a second.

steps.do: Warm the tortillas on the hot comal for 30 seconds a side until soft and lightly spotted, stacking them in a tea towel.
steps.look: Pliable tortillas with a few brown spots, puffing slightly; they smell of toasted corn.
steps.mistake: Cold or dry tortillas that crack when folded.
steps.fix: If they are stiff, splash them with a few drops of water before warming.

steps.do: Serve the lamb with the warm tortillas, chopped onion, coriander, lime wedges and salsa, and a mug of hot consomé with chickpeas for each person, garnished with onion, coriander and lime.
steps.look: Steaming mugs of red consomé beside a platter of glistening lamb; guests build their own tacos.
steps.mistake: Serving the consomé lukewarm.
steps.fix: Bring it back to a simmer in a saucepan just before serving.

science: The sealed tin turns the oven into a steamer. Moist heat transfers energy efficiently but never takes the meat surface above about 212°F (100°C), so the lamb cooks gently and evenly while collagen, the tough connective tissue in a working shoulder, slowly converts to gelatin between about 160 and 205°F (71 and 96°C). That gelatin is what makes the meat moist and the consomé rich. Everything the lamb sheds, fat, juices and dissolved gelatin, drips into the pot below, where rice starch breaks down and gives the broth body. Salting the night before lets salt diffuse into the muscle and partially dissolve its proteins, so the meat holds more moisture. Banana leaves add a faint grassy aroma and keep the surface from drying.
plating: Bring the lamb to the table on a warm platter in loose chunks with a few softened leaves underneath for colour. Stack tortillas in a cloth-lined basket. Serve the consomé in clay mugs or bowls with a few chickpeas visible, a pinch of onion and coriander on top and a lime wedge on the rim.

pairing.drink: A michelada or an ice-cold Mexican lager with lime and salt: cold, bubbly and sharp, it cuts the rich lamb and refreshes after the heat of the salsa.
pairing.brennans: Bloody Bull: the Brennan's Bloody Mary made with beef broth, the same pleasure as sipping a savoury consomé beside a rich breakfast.

variations: Goat barbacoa: use bone-in goat shoulder, which is leaner; add 30 minutes.
Beef cheek barbacoa: cheeks cooked the same way until they fall apart, about 5 hours.
Slow cooker version: lamb and adobo in the cooker with 1 cup (240 ml) consomé base, 8 hours on low; make the consomé separately.
safety: Lamb is safe from 145°F (63°C), but for barbacoa cook it until tender, around 200°F (93°C).
Cool leftovers quickly and refrigerate within 2 hours; reheat lamb and consomé to 165°F (74°C).
Open the foil away from your face; the escaping steam scalds.

title: Ewa Agoyin with Agege Bread
summary: Soft mashed honey beans under a dark, smoky pepper sauce fried slowly in palm oil, eaten with slices of soft, dense agege bread baked at home. It is Lagos street breakfast, and it is in the course because it is a two-day project that rewards patience at every stage: beans cooked until they collapse, a sauce fried for close to an hour until the oil separates, and an enriched loaf kneaded long for its tight, springy crumb.
skills: cooking beans to a soft mash
a dark pepper sauce fried slowly in palm oil
equipment: Large heavy saucepan or pressure cooker for the beans
Heavy-based frying pan or wide saucepan for the sauce, at least 10 inches (25 cm)
Stand mixer with dough hook, or a clean worktop for kneading
Loaf tin, 9 by 5 inches (23 by 13 cm)
Extractor fan on, or an open window

ingredients.item: Dried red chillies (such as ata gungun or kashmiri)
ingredients.note: seeds shaken out for less heat
one chopped for blending, one thinly sliced

mise: Day 1: soak the dried chillies in very hot water for 30 minutes, then drain.
Blend the soaked chillies, bell peppers, Scotch bonnet and the chopped onion with 1/4 cup (60 ml) water to a coarse purée.
Thinly slice the second onion.
Weigh the bread ingredients; soften the butter; oil the loaf tin.
Day 2: pick over the beans and rinse them; have the extractor fan running before you heat the palm oil.

timeline.do: Mix and knead the agege dough; first rise.
Shape, proof and bake the loaf; cool and wrap.
Fry the pepper sauce slowly for about an hour; cool and refrigerate.
Cook the beans until completely soft.
Salt and mash the beans; reheat the sauce.
Serve beans under sauce with thick slices of bread.

steps.do: Make the agege dough: mix the 4 cups (500 g) flour, sugar, yeast, salt and milk powder, add the 1 1/4 cups (300 ml) warm water and mix to a firm dough. Knead 10 minutes, then work in the 3 tbsp (40 g) butter and knead another 8 to 10 minutes.
steps.look: The dough turns from sticky to very smooth, satiny and elastic; a small piece stretches into a thin, translucent windowpane without tearing.
steps.mistake: Stopping when it is merely smooth; agege bread needs a long knead for its tight, stretchy crumb.
steps.fix: Keep going until the windowpane test passes. A mixer on medium-low makes this easier.

steps.do: Cover and let the dough rise at room temperature for about 1 hour until doubled. Press it out into a rectangle 9 inches (23 cm) wide, roll it up tightly like a carpet and pinch the seam closed. Put it seam down in the oiled tin.
steps.look: A smooth, taut log filling the tin about halfway, with no air pockets on the surface.
steps.mistake: Rolling loosely, which leaves big holes in the crumb.
steps.fix: Roll tightly, pressing each turn down with your thumbs.

steps.do: Proof about 1 hour until the dough domes 1 inch (2.5 cm) above the rim. Bake at 350°F (175°C) for 35 to 40 minutes until deep golden and 195°F (90°C) inside. Brush the top with butter, turn out and cool on a rack.
steps.look: A tall, golden loaf with a soft, thin crust; it smells sweet and milky and knocks hollow underneath.
steps.mistake: Cutting it hot, so the crumb squashes into paste.
steps.fix: Cool at least 1 hour, then wrap tightly so the crust stays soft.

steps.do: Heat the palm oil in the heavy pan over medium heat with the fan on until it shimmers and just begins to smoke at the edges, then lower the heat at once. Cool 3 minutes.
steps.look: The oil turns from deep orange to a paler, clearer amber and smells nutty; a thin wisp of smoke rises.
steps.mistake: Heating the oil until it pours smoke, which is a fire risk and fills the house.
steps.fix: Watch it constantly and pull the pan off the heat at the first smoke. If it catches fire, cover with a lid and turn off the heat; never use water.

steps.do: Return to low heat, add the sliced onion and fry 8 to 10 minutes, stirring, until deep brown and fragrant.
steps.look: The onions sizzle gently, darken to mahogany and smell sweet and slightly smoky.
steps.mistake: High heat, which burns the onions black and bitter.
steps.fix: Keep the heat low; this is a slow sauce from the start.

steps.do: Pour in the pepper purée, standing back as it spits. Stir well, then cook over low heat for 45 to 60 minutes, stirring every few minutes and scraping the bottom, using a splatter guard.
steps.look: The sauce bubbles slowly and spits, then darkens from red to rust to very dark brown; the oil separates and floats on top, and the raw pepper smell turns deep and smoky.
steps.mistake: Turning up the heat to save time, so the purée burns on the base.
steps.fix: Low heat and regular scraping. If it catches, move it to a clean pan without scraping the burnt layer.

steps.do: Season with the crayfish, stock cube and salt and cook 5 minutes more. Cool and refrigerate overnight if making ahead.
steps.look: A thick, glossy, almost black sauce with a layer of red oil; savoury, smoky and hot.
steps.mistake: Under-frying, so the sauce tastes raw and sharp.
steps.fix: Keep frying until the oil clearly separates; that is the sign it is done.

steps.do: Cook the beans: put them in the large pan with 10 cups (2.4 litres) water, bring to the boil, skim the foam and simmer 1 1/2 to 2 hours, topping up with hot water so they stay covered, until they crush to a paste between your fingers. A pressure cooker takes about 25 minutes at high pressure.
steps.look: The beans split and collapse, the liquid turns thick and creamy and smells sweet and earthy.
steps.mistake: Adding salt at the start, which can keep the skins tough.
steps.fix: Salt only once the beans are completely soft.

steps.do: Drain off any excess liquid, keeping it. Add the 1 1/2 tsp (9 g) salt and mash the beans roughly with a masher, adding back liquid until they are soft and spoonable. Taste.
steps.look: A soft, thick mash with some whole beans left, like loose porridge.
steps.mistake: Mashing to a smooth purée, which loses the character.
steps.fix: Mash lightly; some texture is right.

steps.do: Reheat the sauce in a small pan over low heat until bubbling. Spoon the beans into bowls and ladle the sauce generously over the top, oil and all. Serve with thick slices of agege bread.
steps.look: Pale beans under a dark, glossy, red-rimmed sauce; it smells smoky and hot.
steps.mistake: Stirring the sauce into the beans before serving.
steps.fix: Serve the sauce on top; each person mixes as they eat.

science: Dried beans soften as heat and water break down pectin and other cell wall materials and swell their starch. Salt in the water from the very start can slow this in some beans by strengthening the skins, which is why it goes in at the end here. The sauce depends on frying the pepper purée in fat for a long time: water evaporates, sugars caramelise and the Maillard reaction browns the peppers and onions, turning them dark and savoury. When nearly all the water has gone the oil separates out, the reliable sign of a finished sauce. Agege bread is an enriched dough; sugar, milk powder and fat soften the crumb, while long kneading builds a strong gluten network that gives its tight, stretchy texture.
plating: Use a wide bowl: a mound of beans on one side, the dark sauce spooned over the top so it runs down the side with its red oil pooling at the edge. Serve two thick slices of agege bread on a side plate, or tucked into the bowl, for scooping.

pairing.drink: Chilled zobo, a hibiscus drink sweetened lightly and spiced with ginger and cloves: tart and cold, it soothes the chilli heat and cuts the palm oil.

variations: Add fried plantain (dodo) on the side for a classic combination.
Ewa riro: cook the beans with the pepper sauce stirred through for a stewed version.
Milder sauce: replace half the dried chillies with smoked paprika and use no Scotch bonnet.
safety: Heat palm oil only with ventilation, never leave it, and keep a lid nearby; never put water on an oil fire.
Refrigerate the sauce within 2 hours; it keeps 1 week. Reheat beans to 165°F (74°C).

title: Arepas de Huevo
summary: Corn arepas fried until they puff, split to open a pocket, filled with a raw egg, sealed and fried again until the egg sets inside, as they are sold on the beaches of Colombia's Caribbean coast. It is in the course because it is pure handling skill: shaping dough thin enough to puff, opening a hot pocket without tearing it, and controlling oil temperature through two fries.
equipment: Heavy deep saucepan or Dutch oven, at least 4 inches (10 cm) deep
Two sheets of baking paper or a cut freezer bag for pressing
Lid that fits the pan, kept nearby
Small bowl for the sealing paste

ingredients.note: plus a little more if needed
small eggs fit the pocket best

ingredients.item: Spring onions and coriander, for the ají
ingredients.us: 2 spring onions and a small bunch
ingredients.metric: 2 spring onions and a small bunch

ingredients.item: Fresh hot chilli, for the ají

mise: Make the ají picante: mix vinegar, water, spring onions, coriander, chilli, a pinch of salt and a squeeze of lime; leave at least 30 minutes.
If using the beef, fry it with a little chopped onion and tomato until cooked through and dry; cool and season.
Crack each egg into its own small cup.
Mix 2 tbsp (20 g) of masarepa with a little water to a thick paste in a small bowl, for sealing.
Set a wire rack over a tray beside the stove.
Pour the oil into the pan to 2 1/2 inches (6 cm) deep, leaving at least half the pan empty.

timeline.do: Make the ají; cook the beef filling if using.
Mix and rest the dough; heat the oil.
Shape six thin discs.
First fry until puffed; drain.
Open pockets, add eggs, seal.
Second fry until the egg sets; drain and serve hot.

steps.do: Mix the 2 cups (280 g) masarepa, salt and sugar, then pour in the 2 cups (480 ml) warm water and knead for 2 minutes. Rest 5 minutes, then knead again until soft and smooth.
steps.look: A soft, smooth dough like play dough that does not crack at the edges when pressed.
steps.mistake: Dough too dry, which cracks and will not puff.
steps.fix: Knead in warm water 1 tbsp (15 ml) at a time until a pressed ball has smooth edges.

steps.do: Divide into 6 balls of about 4 1/2 oz (130 g). Put one ball between two sheets of baking paper and press with a flat plate or tortilla press into a disc 5 inches (13 cm) across and a scant 1/4 inch (5 mm) thick. Smooth any cracks at the edge with a wet finger.
steps.look: Even, round discs with smooth, uncracked edges and the same thickness everywhere.
steps.mistake: Discs too thick, which stay solid instead of puffing into a pocket.
steps.fix: Aim for the thickness of two coins. Thicker discs can be pressed again.

steps.do: Heat the oil to 350°F (175°C). Slide in 2 discs, laying them away from you. Fry 2 to 3 minutes, turning once, until they puff up like a balloon and turn pale golden. Lift onto the rack.
steps.look: The discs sink, then float, then swell as steam separates the two surfaces; a lively sizzle and a toasted corn smell.
steps.mistake: Oil too cool, so the arepas soak up oil and never puff.
steps.fix: Keep it at 350°F (175°C). If a disc does not puff, it was too thick; it still makes a good plain arepa.

steps.do: While still hot, hold each arepa with a towel and cut a slit 2 inches (5 cm) long into its edge with the paring knife, opening the pocket inside without piercing the other side.
steps.look: A clear hollow inside, with steam escaping as you cut.
steps.mistake: Cutting across the top or through the back, which leaves no way to hold the egg.
steps.fix: Cut into the edge only, the blade parallel to the faces.

steps.do: Add 1 tbsp (15 g) of the beef filling into the pocket if using, then slide one egg from its cup into the pocket. Seal the slit with a dab of the masarepa paste, pressing the edges together.
steps.look: The egg settles inside and the slit closes neatly with no egg leaking.
steps.mistake: Using a large egg that overflows.
steps.fix: Pour off some of the white before adding, or use small eggs. If it leaks, seal with more paste.

steps.do: Lower the filled arepas, sealed side up, back into the oil at 350°F (175°C), one or two at a time, and fry 2 to 3 minutes, turning once carefully, until deep golden and the egg feels set when you press gently.
steps.look: The arepas brown evenly; when pressed with tongs they feel firm, not liquid inside.
steps.mistake: Turning roughly so the seal opens and egg spills into the oil, causing spatter.
steps.fix: Turn with a spider and tongs together. If a little egg escapes, lift the arepa out, let the oil settle and skim the bits.

steps.do: Drain on the rack for 1 minute, then serve hot with the ají picante spooned in or alongside.
steps.look: A crisp, golden shell; inside, a set white and a soft or firm yolk, steaming when cut.
steps.mistake: Draining on paper, where the base steams and goes soft.
steps.fix: A rack keeps them crisp. Serve at once.

science: Masarepa is corn that has been cooked and dried before milling, so its starch is already gelatinised and it forms a dough with water alone. When a thin disc hits hot oil, water near both surfaces turns to steam faster than it can escape, the outer layers set into a crust, and the trapped steam pushes them apart, which is how the pocket forms. Oil at 350°F (175°C) sets the surface quickly, keeping oil absorption low; cooler oil lets the dough soak it up. In the second fry the dough insulates the egg, so it sets gently while the shell browns, and egg white proteins set fully between about 145 and 160°F (63 and 71°C).
plating: Serve on a board or a plate lined with paper, the arepas stacked two high, one cut open across the middle to show the egg. Put the ají picante in a small bowl with a spoon so guests can spoon it into the pocket.

pairing.drink: A fresh, cold lulo or passion fruit juice, or a Colombian tinto (small black coffee): the fruit's acidity cuts the fried corn, and the coffee is how the coast takes it.

variations: Arepa de queso: fill with grated fresh cheese instead of egg and griddle rather than fry.
Shredded chicken filling with the egg for a heartier breakfast.
Baked arepas: griddle thicker discs and bake for a lighter everyday arepa.
safety: Fill the pan no more than half full of oil, keep a lid nearby, and never leave hot oil unattended; smother a fire with the lid, never water.
Lower food in away from you; a leaking egg makes oil spatter.
Fry until the egg is set: press to check it is firm. Cook fully for pregnant guests, the very young, the elderly or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Appam with Kerala Stew
summary: Lace-edged rice and coconut hoppers, crisp at the rim and spongy in the centre, swirled in a curved pan, with a delicate chicken stew in coconut milk scented with whole spices, ginger and curry leaves. It is in the course because the batter is alive: it must ferment to the right sourness and lightness, and the stew asks for restraint, gentle heat that keeps the coconut milk from splitting.
skills: a fermented rice and coconut batter
swirling in an appachatti for lacy edges
a coconut milk stew with whole spices
equipment: Appachatti (appam pan) with lid, or a small non-stick wok with a lid
Large bowl for fermenting, with a lid
Heavy saucepan or kadai for the stew
Thermometer for the batter if your kitchen is cool
Kitchen paper for oiling the pan

ingredients.item: Raw white rice (pachari or any short-grain non-sticky rice)

ingredients.note: for the stew, plus a little for the pan
cut in half through the bone by the butcher, or boneless thighs

ingredients.item: Cinnamon stick, green cardamom, cloves, black peppercorns
Thin coconut milk (or 1 can coconut milk diluted half and half with water)
Thick coconut milk, for finishing the stew

mise: Soak the raw rice in plenty of water for 4 hours, then drain.
Dissolve the yeast and 1 tsp (4 g) sugar in the warm water and leave 10 minutes until foamy.
Slice onion, ginger and garlic; slit chillies; strip curry leaves; cube potato; slice carrot.
If using canned coconut milk, open it without shaking and spoon off the thick cream from the top; dilute the rest for thin milk.
Have a cloth-lined basket ready to keep the appam warm.

timeline.do: Soak the rice.
Grind the batter, add yeast and leave to ferment overnight.
Finish the batter with salt, sugar and thick coconut milk; rest 15 minutes.
Start the stew: spices, aromatics, chicken, potatoes in thin coconut milk.
Season the appam pan and start making appam.
Finish the stew with thick coconut milk; serve with hot appam.

steps.do: Grind the soaked rice, cooked rice and grated coconut with the 3/4 cup plus 1 tbsp (200 ml) water in the blender for 3 to 4 minutes, scraping down, until very smooth, with only the faintest grit when rubbed between finger and thumb.
steps.look: A thick, smooth, pourable batter like double cream, silky with a hint of sand.
steps.mistake: Grinding too briefly, so the batter is gritty and the appam crumbly.
steps.fix: Blend in short bursts to keep it cool and keep going until smooth. Add water 1 tbsp (15 ml) at a time if the blades stall.

steps.do: Stir the foamy yeast through the batter. Cover loosely and leave to ferment at 82 to 86°F (28 to 30°C) for 6 to 8 hours, or overnight in a warm place.
steps.look: The batter doubles, domes and fills with bubbles; it smells pleasantly sour, like bread dough and toddy.
steps.mistake: A cold kitchen, so the batter barely moves.
steps.fix: Put it in the oven with only the light on, or near a warm spot; give it more time rather than more yeast.

steps.do: Gently stir down the batter and mix in the remaining 1 tbsp (12 g) sugar, the salt and the 1 cup (250 ml) thick coconut milk. It should be thinner than before, like single cream. Rest 15 minutes.
steps.look: A pourable batter that ribbons off the ladle and still has small bubbles.
steps.mistake: Adding salt before fermenting, which slows the yeast.
steps.fix: Salt goes in only now. If it is thick, add water 1 tbsp (15 ml) at a time.

steps.do: Start the stew: heat the 3 tbsp (45 ml) coconut oil in the heavy pan over medium heat, add the whole spices and fry 30 seconds, then the onion, ginger, garlic, chillies and half the curry leaves and cook 5 minutes until soft but not coloured.
steps.look: Whole spices crackle and smell warm and sweet; onions turn translucent and soft; the curry leaves crackle and perfume the oil.
steps.mistake: Browning the onions, which darkens a stew that should be pale and delicate.
steps.fix: Medium heat and stir; add a splash of water if anything starts to colour.

steps.do: Add the chicken, potato and carrot, stir 2 minutes to coat, then pour in the 2 cups (480 ml) thin coconut milk and 1 tsp (6 g) salt. Bring to a gentle simmer, cover and cook 20 to 25 minutes until the chicken reaches 165°F (74°C) and the potatoes are tender.
steps.look: A pale, gently bubbling stew; the chicken turns opaque and the potatoes yield to a knife.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, which can split the coconut milk into oily curds.
steps.fix: Keep it at a gentle simmer with the lid on.

steps.do: Heat the appachatti over medium heat until a drop of water sizzles away in 2 seconds. Wipe it lightly with coconut oil on kitchen paper.
steps.look: A faint shimmer of oil; the pan feels evenly hot when you hold your hand above it.
steps.mistake: A pan too hot, which sets the batter before it can swirl.
steps.fix: Lower the heat and wait a minute. Test with a small ladle first; the first appam is often a practice one.

steps.do: Pour a ladle of batter, about 1/3 cup (80 ml), into the centre. Immediately lift the pan by both handles and rotate it in one full circle so the batter climbs the sides in a thin layer and the rest pools in the centre. Cover and cook 2 to 3 minutes.
steps.look: A thin film clings to the sides and turns lacy and golden at the rim; the centre puffs, sets white and spongy and looks dry on top. It smells of toasted coconut.
steps.mistake: Swirling twice, or too slowly, so the edges are thick and the lace never forms.
steps.fix: One smooth, quick rotation. If the edges are thick, thin the batter slightly.

steps.do: Ease the appam out with a spatula without flipping it, and keep warm in the cloth-lined basket. Wipe the pan with oil every two or three appam and repeat with the remaining batter.
steps.look: Bowl-shaped appam with crisp, golden, lacy edges and a soft, white, spongy centre.
steps.mistake: Flipping it, which flattens the centre.
steps.fix: Never flip; the lid steams the top.

steps.do: Finish the stew: stir in the 1 cup (240 ml) thick coconut milk and the peas and warm through over low heat for 3 to 4 minutes without boiling. Add the remaining curry leaves and check the salt.
steps.look: A creamy, ivory stew flecked with green, gently steaming but not bubbling; it smells of coconut, ginger and cardamom.
steps.mistake: Boiling after the thick milk goes in, which makes it split.
steps.fix: Keep it just below a simmer. If it splits a little, stir in a spoonful of fresh coconut milk off the heat.

steps.do: Serve two or three appam per person in a shallow bowl or plate, with the stew ladled beside or into the centre.
steps.look: Crisp edges standing up beside a pale, fragrant stew.
steps.mistake: Pouring the stew over the whole appam, so the lace goes soggy.
steps.fix: Spoon the stew into the centre only, or serve it alongside.

science: Fermentation does two jobs here. Yeast eats the sugars and produces carbon dioxide that lifts the batter, while lactic bacteria from the rice and coconut produce acids that give the gentle sourness. The cold cooked rice adds starch that is already gelatinised, giving the batter enough body to cling to the sides of the pan in a thin film; that film dries and crisps to lace while the thicker centre steams under the lid into a sponge. Salt and coconut milk go in after fermenting because salt slows yeast and coconut milk sours over many hours. Coconut milk is an emulsion of fat droplets in water stabilised by proteins; a hard boil breaks it, which is why the stew is kept below a simmer once the thick milk goes in.
plating: Use a wide, shallow bowl. Lay two appam slightly overlapping on one side, their lacy rims upright, and ladle the stew beside them so the chicken, potato and carrot are visible, finishing with a few fried curry leaves on top.

pairing.drink: A dry or off-dry Riesling: its bright acidity and stone fruit balance the coconut, and a touch of sweetness soothes the green chilli.
pairing.brennans: Trimbach Riesling Réserve 2020: a dry Alsace Riesling on the Brennan's list, bright and aromatic, which suits a coconut stew with gentle spice.

variations: Vegetable stew: potato, carrot, green beans and peas only, simmered 15 minutes.
Mutton stew: lamb shoulder simmered 1 hour in thin coconut milk before finishing.
Egg appam: crack an egg into the centre just after swirling and cover until set.
safety: Cook the chicken to 165°F (74°C) at the thickest part.
Refrigerate leftover batter and use within 1 day; discard it if it smells unpleasantly sharp or alcoholic, or shows mould.
Refrigerate the stew within 2 hours and reheat to 165°F (74°C).

title: Bánh Cuốn
summary: Paper-thin sheets of rice batter steamed on a cloth stretched over boiling water, lifted with a flat stick, rolled around minced pork and wood ear mushrooms, and served with fried shallots, herbs and nước chấm. It is Hanoi's breakfast, and it is in the course because it is the finest work with starch you will do: a batter so thin you can read through it, cooked in seconds and handled with care.
skills: a thin rice batter steamed on cloth
a pork and wood ear filling
equipment: Wide stockpot, about 10 inches (25 cm) across
Thin cotton cloth or muslin, larger than the pot opening
Domed lid that fits over the cloth
Flat bamboo stick, a long thin offset spatula or a wide chopstick

ingredients.item: Neutral oil, for frying the shallots
Mint, Vietnamese coriander, Thai basil, lettuce

mise: Whisk the rice flour, tapioca, potato starch, salt, oil and 2 1/2 cups (600 ml) water to a thin batter; rest at least 1 hour.
Soak the wood ears in hot water 20 minutes, trim hard stems and chop finely.
Make the nước chấm: dissolve sugar in warm water, add fish sauce, lime, garlic and chilli; taste for balance.
Fry the sliced shallots in the 1/2 cup (120 ml) oil over medium heat for 8 to 10 minutes until golden; drain on paper and keep the shallot oil.
Stretch the cloth tightly over the pot, tie it firmly under the rim with string, and cut a small vent at one side for adding water.
Fill the pot two thirds with water under the cloth; oil a large tray.

timeline.do: Mix the batter and rest it; soak the wood ears.
Fry shallots; make nước chấm; prepare herbs.
Cook the pork filling.
Rig the cloth steamer and bring to the boil.
Steam, fill and roll sheets one by one.
Serve with fried shallots, herbs and dipping sauce.

steps.do: Cook the filling: heat 1 tbsp (15 ml) shallot oil in the frying pan over medium heat, fry the chopped shallots 2 minutes, then add the pork and break it up finely. Cook 5 minutes until no pink remains, add the wood ears, fish sauce, sugar and pepper and cook 2 minutes more.
steps.look: Fine, crumbly pork with no pink, flecked with dark wood ear; it smells of shallot and fish sauce and reads 160°F (71°C).
steps.mistake: Leaving large clumps, which tear the sheets when rolled.
steps.fix: Break the pork up with a potato masher or the back of a fork as it cooks.

steps.do: Bring the pot to a full rolling boil so steam pushes up through the cloth. Brush the cloth lightly with oil.
steps.look: Steam rises evenly through the cloth, which feels hot and slightly damp.
steps.mistake: Too little steam, so the batter never sets.
steps.fix: Keep a strong boil, topping up with boiling water through the vent as needed.

steps.do: Stir the batter well because the starch settles. Ladle about 3 tbsp (45 ml) onto the cloth and immediately spread it into a thin circle 7 inches (18 cm) across with the back of the ladle in a spiral.
steps.look: A very thin, even, milky layer, almost see-through.
steps.mistake: Too much batter, making a thick, gummy sheet.
steps.fix: Use less batter and spread fast. Thin is the whole point.

steps.do: Cover the cloth with the domed lid straight away and steam the sheet for 30 to 45 seconds over the rolling boil.
steps.look: The sheet turns from milky white to translucent and bubbles slightly in places.
steps.mistake: Steaming too long, which makes the sheet stick and tear.
steps.fix: Lift the lid as soon as it is translucent.

steps.do: Slide the flat stick under one edge of the sheet and, in one confident motion, lift and roll the sheet off the cloth onto the oiled tray.
steps.look: The sheet peels cleanly from the cloth and drapes over the stick like silk.
steps.mistake: Hesitating, so the sheet tears on the cloth.
steps.fix: Work the stick under the full width of the sheet first. Torn sheets are still delicious; fold them together.

steps.do: Spread 1 tbsp (15 g) of filling across the near third of the sheet, fold in the sides and roll it into a loose cylinder about 1 inch (2.5 cm) across. Brush the roll with a little shallot oil.
steps.look: A soft, translucent roll with the dark filling visible through it.
steps.mistake: Overfilling, which splits the delicate sheet.
steps.fix: Use less filling; elegance is the goal.

steps.do: Repeat, stirring the batter each time, oiling the cloth every few sheets, until all the batter and filling are used, about 20 rolls.
steps.look: A tray of glossy rolls, each the same size.
steps.mistake: Letting the water run low, so steam weakens.
steps.fix: Add boiling water through the vent every 6 or 7 sheets.

steps.do: Plate the rolls and scatter generously with fried shallots. Serve with nước chấm in bowls, herbs, bean sprouts and sliced pork roll on the side.
steps.look: Glossy white rolls under a tangle of golden shallots; bright green herbs; amber sauce.
steps.mistake: Serving cold rolls that have gone stiff.
steps.fix: Serve within 20 minutes. Cover with a damp cloth if they must wait.

science: Rice has no gluten, so the sheet's structure comes entirely from starch. When the thin layer of batter meets steam at 212°F (100°C), the starch granules absorb water and swell until they gelatinise, linking into a soft, flexible film. Tapioca and potato starch add elasticity, so the sheet stretches rather than cracks when lifted. Steam heats the thin layer from below and above in seconds, much faster and more evenly than a dry pan, which is why the sheet turns translucent: gelatinised starch scatters less light. Resting the batter lets the flour hydrate fully so it does not taste chalky. Nước chấm balances four tastes, salt from fish sauce, sweet sugar, sour lime and hot chilli, so a mild dish tastes vivid.
plating: Arrange the rolls in two neat rows on a platter or plates, slightly overlapping, brushed with oil so they shine. Pile crisp shallots in a line down the centre. Serve sauce in individual bowls with slices of pork roll on the side and herbs in a basket.

pairing.drink: Hot jasmine or green tea: clean and floral, it refreshes between bites and does not cover the delicate rice sheets.

variations: Non-stick pan method: lightly oil a non-stick pan over medium heat, swirl in the batter, cover 30 seconds and slide out.
Bánh cuốn trứng: crack an egg onto the sheet as it steams for a richer roll.
Vegetarian: fill with shiitake, wood ear and shredded jicama, and serve with a soy and lime dip.
safety: Cook the pork filling to 160°F (71°C).
Keep fingers clear of the steam when lifting the lid and sheets; steam burns quickly.
Fry shallots in a pan no more than one third full of oil, and never leave it.

title: Har Gow
summary: Translucent crystal dumplings made from a wheat starch dough scalded with boiling water, pressed thin with a cleaver, folded with at least ten pleats around a snapping prawn filling and steamed for six minutes. They are the dim sum chef's test, and they are in the course because nothing hides: the wrapper shows every flaw, and guests count the pleats.
skills: a wheat starch dough scalded with boiling water
equipment: Bamboo steamer with lid over a wok or saucepan
Baking paper cut to fit the steamer, punched with holes
Chinese cleaver or a large, flat-bladed chef's knife
Small oiled board or smooth worktop

ingredients.item: Water at a full rolling boil

mise: Pat the prawns completely dry on kitchen paper.
Blanch the diced bamboo shoot in boiling water for 1 minute, drain and squeeze dry.
Cut baking paper rounds for the steamer and punch small holes; oil them lightly.
Oil the board and the flat of the cleaver.
Have the kettle ready to boil exactly when you need it.

timeline.do: Make the filling and chill it for 1 hour.
Make the dough while the water is at a rolling boil.
Press wrappers and pleat the dumplings, keeping the dough covered.
Bring the steamer water to a hard boil.
Steam the dumplings 6 minutes.
Serve straight from the steamer.

steps.do: Make the filling: cut two thirds of the prawns into pieces about 1/2 inch (1 cm). Mash the rest to a paste with the flat of the cleaver. Mix with the bamboo, pork fat, salt, sugar, pepper, sesame oil and potato starch, stirring in one direction for 2 minutes. Chill 1 hour.
steps.look: A sticky, springy mixture that holds together on a spoon; whole prawn pieces bound by a glossy paste.
steps.mistake: Mincing all the prawns, which makes a dense, rubbery filling without snap.
steps.fix: Keep chunks for texture and paste for binding. Stir hard in one direction to make it sticky.

steps.do: Make the dough: whisk the wheat starch, tapioca and salt in the metal bowl. Pour the 2/3 cup (150 ml) water on straight from a rolling boil all at once, stir hard with chopsticks for 10 seconds, then cover with a plate for 2 minutes.
steps.look: The starch turns from white powder to a translucent, lumpy mass; steam rises when you lift the plate.
steps.mistake: Water that has cooled even slightly, which leaves the dough chalky and cracking.
steps.fix: Pour the water the moment it boils. If the dough cracks badly, start again; it cannot be rescued.

steps.do: Add the lard and knead the hot dough on the lightly oiled surface for 2 to 3 minutes until smooth and satiny, like warm marzipan. Roll into a log and keep it under a damp cloth.
steps.look: A smooth, soft, slightly translucent dough that does not crack when pressed.
steps.mistake: Letting it cool uncovered, so it dries and splits.
steps.fix: Work while warm and keep everything covered except the piece in your hands.

steps.do: Cut a piece of dough weighing about 0.4 oz (12 g), roll it into a ball and set it on the oiled board. Press down firmly with the oiled flat of the cleaver, twisting it slightly as you press, to make a round wrapper about 3 inches (8 cm) across and very thin.
steps.look: A thin, even, circular wrapper you can almost see through, slightly thicker in the centre.
steps.mistake: Uneven pressure, making a lopsided wrapper.
steps.fix: Press with your palm flat on the blade, twisting in one smooth motion. Trim with a round cutter if needed.

steps.do: Hold the wrapper in one hand and place 1/2 oz (15 g) of filling in the centre. Fold it in half without sealing. With your thumb and index finger, make a small pleat on the near side, press it onto the flat far side, and keep pleating along the near edge only, making at least ten pleats from one end to the other.
steps.look: A crescent with a fan of fine pleats on one side and a smooth curve on the other, sealed firmly along the top.
steps.mistake: Pleating both sides, or too few, wide pleats.
steps.fix: Small pleats close together; practise on spare dough first. The far side stays flat.

steps.do: Pinch the whole edge firmly to seal and set each dumpling on the punched baking paper in the steamer, 1 inch (2.5 cm) apart. Keep made dumplings covered with a damp cloth.
steps.look: Neat crescents in rows, with no gaps in the seal.
steps.mistake: Crowding them so they stick together while steaming.
steps.fix: Leave space; steam the rest in a second batch.

steps.do: Set the steamer over a hard rolling boil, put the lid on and steam the dumplings for exactly 6 minutes.
steps.look: The wrappers turn from white to clear, so the pink prawns show through; the prawns read 145°F (63°C) and the dumplings look taut and glossy.
steps.mistake: Oversteaming, which makes the wrappers slump and go gummy.
steps.fix: Set a timer and pull them at 6 minutes.

steps.do: Serve within 1 minute of lifting the lid, in the bamboo basket, with small dishes of soy sauce and chilli oil.
steps.look: Glistening, translucent dumplings with pink filling and fine pleats.
steps.mistake: Leaving them in the steamer off the heat, where they turn sticky.
steps.fix: Bring the basket straight to the table.

science: Wheat starch is wheat flour with the gluten washed out, so the wrapper has no stretchy protein network; its structure comes only from starch granules that swell and gelatinise in boiling water. That is why the water must be at a full boil: starch needs heat to gelatinise, and water that has cooled leaves raw granules that make the dough chalky and crumbly. Tapioca starch adds stretch and chew. Gelatinised starch is translucent because the swollen granules scatter less light, which gives the crystal look. In the filling, salt and vigorous stirring dissolve some of the prawn proteins into a sticky binder, while the chunks contract quickly when steamed, giving the characteristic snap.
plating: Steam and serve in the bamboo basket on a plate, the dumplings set in a circle with their pleats facing outward. Small dishes of soy and chilli oil beside, and a pot of tea.

pairing.drink: Hot jasmine or oolong tea, the dim sum tradition; or a crisp Blanc de Blancs Champagne whose fine bubbles suit the delicate prawn.

variations: Scallop har gow: replace a third of the prawns with diced scallop.
Chive dumplings: use the same dough and fill with garlic chives and prawn.
Rainbow har gow: colour portions of the dough with a little beetroot or spinach juice.
safety: Pour boiling water carefully away from your body and use chopsticks, not hands, for the first stir.
Cook prawns to 145°F (63°C), when they turn pink and opaque.
Keep the filling chilled below 40°F (4°C) until you use it.

title: Sheng Jian Bao
summary: Shanghai's breakfast bun: a half-risen yeast dough pleated around pork and cubes of set aspic, fried in a heavy pan until the bases are crisp, then steamed under a lid so the tops turn soft and the aspic melts into soup. It is in the course because it combines a pork skin stock set firm overnight, a dough proofed only halfway, and a two-stage cook in one pan that ends with a hiss.
skills: a pork aspic set from skin
pan-frying then steaming in the pan
equipment: Shallow dish or loaf tin for setting it
Rolling pin, small and thin if possible
Large heavy frying pan, 11 to 12 inches (28 to 30 cm), with a tight lid

ingredients.note: from a butcher; scraped of fat
made by soaking sliced ginger and spring onion in cold water 15 minutes, then straining

ingredients.item: Chinkiang black vinegar and ginger matchsticks

mise: The day before: blanch the pork skin, scrape it, and simmer the aspic.
Make the ginger and spring onion water and keep it cold.
On the day, dice the set aspic into 1/4 inch (5 mm) cubes and keep them in the fridge.
Weigh out the dough and filling ingredients.
Have a damp tea towel ready to cover the dough and finished buns.

timeline.do: Make the pork skin aspic and chill overnight.
Make the filling and chill it hard.
Mix the dough; rest 40 minutes only.
Roll, fill and pleat 20 buns.
Fry the bases, then steam in the same pan.
Rest the buns 2 minutes before eating.

steps.do: Make the aspic: put the pork skin in a pan of cold water, bring to the boil and boil 3 minutes. Drain, rinse, and scrape off any fat left on the inside with a knife. Return the skin to the pan with the 4 cups (950 ml) water, ginger, spring onions and wine.
steps.look: Clean, pale skin with no fat clinging to it; it smells of pork, not stale fat.
steps.mistake: Leaving fat on the skin, which makes a greasy, cloudy aspic.
steps.fix: Scrape firmly with the back of a knife until the inside looks smooth and white.

steps.do: Simmer the skin very gently, uncovered, for 2 1/2 to 3 hours, skimming the foam, until the liquid has reduced to about 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) and the skin is soft enough to tear. Strain into a shallow dish and refrigerate overnight.
steps.look: A sticky stock that coats your fingers; by morning it sets into a firm, clear jelly you can cut with clean edges.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, which clouds the stock, or not reducing enough, so it barely sets.
steps.fix: If it sets only softly, melt it, reduce by a third and chill again.

steps.do: Make the filling: put the pork in a bowl with the soy, wine, salt, sugar and pepper. Stir in one direction while adding the cold ginger water 1 tbsp (15 ml) at a time, stirring 3 to 4 minutes until the pork becomes sticky and absorbs all the liquid. Mix in the sesame oil and spring onions, then fold in 5 oz (150 g) of the diced aspic. Chill 30 minutes.
steps.look: A pale, sticky, cohesive paste that clings to the spoon, with jelly cubes scattered through it.
steps.mistake: Adding the water too fast, so it pools instead of being absorbed.
steps.fix: Add a spoonful at a time and keep stirring until each is absorbed before the next.

steps.do: Make the dough: mix the 2 1/2 cups (300 g) flour, yeast and sugar, add the 3/4 cup (180 ml) warm water and knead 8 minutes until smooth. Cover and rest 40 minutes only.
steps.look: Smooth, slightly springy dough that has puffed by about a third, not doubled; a finger dent fills back slowly.
steps.mistake: Letting it rise fully, so the buns are too weak to hold the soup.
steps.fix: Use it at 40 minutes. If it has doubled, knock it back and knead 1 minute.

steps.do: Roll the dough into a log and cut 20 pieces of about 0.9 oz (25 g). Keep them under the damp towel. Flatten each into a disc and roll the edge only, turning as you go, to a round 3 1/2 inches (9 cm) across, thicker in the centre than at the rim.
steps.look: Even discs with a thin frill at the edge and a raised centre like a shallow dome.
steps.mistake: Rolling the centre thin, so it tears under the filling and soup.
steps.fix: Press only the outer ring with the pin; leave the middle alone.

steps.do: Place a 1 oz (25 g) spoonful of filling in the centre. Pleat the edge around it, folding and pressing with your thumb and forefinger, rotating the bun until the top gathers into a small swirl. Pinch the top hard to weld it shut.
steps.look: A round bun with fine pleats spiralling to a closed knot; no filling showing.
steps.mistake: A seam left loose, which opens in the pan and leaks soup.
steps.fix: Twist and pinch the top firmly. The seam is a weld, not a decoration.

steps.do: Heat the 2 tbsp (30 ml) oil in the large pan over medium heat. Set the buns in seam side down, 1/2 inch (1 cm) apart, and fry 3 minutes until the bases are deep golden.
steps.look: A steady sizzle; when one is lifted, the base is a hard, golden disc and taps like a biscuit.
steps.mistake: Too much heat, which burns the bases before the steam stage.
steps.fix: Medium heat; lift one with tongs to check after 2 minutes.

steps.do: Pour the 2/3 cup (150 ml) water around the buns, not over them, and cover at once with the lid. Steam 8 to 9 minutes until almost all the water has gone and the pan begins to hiss again.
steps.look: A furious bubbling under the lid that slowly quietens to a crackle as the water disappears; the tops look matt and dry.
steps.mistake: Lifting the lid during the steam, which lets the steam out and leaves the tops raw.
steps.fix: Keep it closed until you hear the sizzling return. Open away from your face.

steps.do: Scatter the sesame seeds and extra spring onions over the buns and fry uncovered for 1 minute more to recrisp the bases. The filling should read 160°F (71°C).
steps.look: Crisp, golden, sesame-crusted bases and soft white tops.
steps.mistake: Serving straight away while the soup inside is boiling.
steps.fix: Rest them 2 minutes in the pan first.

steps.do: Serve with black vinegar and ginger matchsticks. Bite a small hole in the side, sip the soup, then dip and eat.
steps.look: Hot soup that runs out when the bun is opened; it smells of pork and ginger.
steps.mistake: Biting straight into the middle and burning your mouth.
steps.fix: Warn guests and show them the sip-first method.

science: The soup inside begins as gelatin. Long, gentle simmering converts the collagen in pork skin into gelatin, which dissolves in the stock and sets into a firm jelly when chilled. Cut into cubes, it can be folded into the filling as a solid, then melts above about 95°F (35°C) as the bun cooks. The dough is proofed only halfway: a fully risen dough has a weak, open structure that tears and lets the liquid escape, while a half-risen one is still strong. The two-stage cook uses conduction first, browning the base through the Maillard reaction in hot oil, then steam to cook the top and filling evenly; once the water evaporates, the base crisps again in the remaining fat.
plating: Bring the pan to the table, or lift the buns onto a warm plate crisp side up so the guest sees the golden base and sesame. Black vinegar in small dishes with ginger matchsticks, and a soup spoon for each person to catch the broth.

pairing.drink: Hot jasmine tea, or warm unsweetened soy milk as Shanghai drinks it at breakfast: both soothe the heat of the soup and clear the richness of the pork.

variations: Prawn and pork: replace a third of the pork with chopped prawns.
Freeze uncooked buns on a tray, then fry from frozen with 2 minutes more steaming.
Pan-fried dumplings (guotie) with the same filling and an unleavened wrapper.
safety: Cook the filling to 160°F (71°C).
The soup is at boiling point; rest buns 2 minutes and warn guests.
Add the steaming water around the edges and cover immediately; hot oil and water spatter.

title: Homemade Skyr with Bilberries
summary: Skimmed milk pasteurised at home, cultured and set with a trace of rennet at a steady warmth, then strained through cloth until thick enough to hold a spoon upright, served with a bilberry compote. It is in the course because it is fermentation by control: a held temperature, clean equipment and patience turn plain milk into a dense, tangy fresh cheese.
equipment: Heavy-based stainless steel saucepan, at least 3 quarts (3 litres)
Sink or large bowl of cold water for cooling
Somewhere to hold 97 to 100°F (36 to 38°C): an oven with the light on, a cool box with hot water bottles, or a yoghurt maker
Large sieve lined with muslin or a new cheesecloth
Bowl that holds the sieve in the fridge

ingredients.item: Live skyr or plain live yoghurt
ingredients.note: from a previous batch or bought, with live cultures
diluted in 1 tbsp (15 ml) cool, unchlorinated water

ingredients.item: Bilberries or wild blueberries, fresh or frozen

mise: Wash the pan, whisk, sieve, bowl and jars in very hot soapy water and rinse well; boil the muslin for 5 minutes.
Fill the sink with cold water and a tray of ice for cooling the milk.
Warm your incubating space to 97 to 100°F (36 to 38°C) and check it with the thermometer.
Dilute the rennet drop in the 1 tbsp (15 ml) water just before you need it.
Bring the starter skyr to room temperature.

timeline.do: Heat the milk to 190°F (88°C) and hold 10 minutes.
Cool to 100°F (38°C), add starter and rennet.
Incubate at 97 to 100°F (36 to 38°C) until set.
Chill the curd 1 hour, then strain in the fridge overnight.
Make the bilberry compote and cool it.
Beat the skyr smooth and serve with compote.

steps.do: Pour the 8 1/2 cups (2 litres) milk into the heavy pan and heat over medium heat, stirring the bottom often, until it reaches 190°F (88°C). Hold it between 185 and 190°F (85 and 88°C) for 10 minutes, stirring.
steps.look: Steam rises and small bubbles appear at the edge but it does not boil; a thin skin forms if you stop stirring. It smells sweet and cooked.
steps.mistake: Letting it catch on the base, which gives a scorched taste to the whole batch.
steps.fix: Stir constantly along the bottom. If it scorches, pour it into a clean pan without scraping and carry on.

steps.do: Set the pan in the sink of cold water and stir until the milk drops to 100°F (38°C), 10 to 15 minutes.
steps.look: The thermometer falls steadily; the milk feels warm, not hot, on your wrist.
steps.mistake: Adding culture while the milk is too hot, which kills it.
steps.fix: Wait for 100°F (38°C) or a little below. If you overshoot to 90°F (32°C), warm it gently.

steps.do: Whisk the 2 tbsp (30 g) starter with a ladle of the warm milk until smooth, then stir it back into the pan. Add the diluted rennet and stir gently for no more than 30 seconds.
steps.look: No streaks of starter left; the milk looks uniform.
steps.mistake: Stirring for minutes after adding rennet, which breaks the forming curd.
steps.fix: Thirty seconds, then stop and leave it completely still.

steps.do: Cover the pan and keep it at 97 to 100°F (36 to 38°C) for 4 to 6 hours without moving it.
steps.look: The milk sets into a soft custard that pulls cleanly away from the side when the pan is tilted; a spoon cuts a sharp edge and a little clear, yellow whey seeps in.
steps.mistake: Checking by stirring, which breaks the set.
steps.fix: Tilt to check. If it has not set after 6 hours, give it 2 more hours; the room may be cool.

steps.do: Chill the set curd in the fridge for 1 hour. Line the sieve with the boiled muslin and set it over a bowl. Ladle the curd gently into the cloth.
steps.look: Clean slabs of curd and yellow-green whey running through immediately.
steps.mistake: Pouring the curd in from a height, which smashes it into the whey.
steps.fix: Ladle it in gently; broken curd strains more slowly but still works.

steps.do: Cover and strain in the fridge for 8 to 12 hours, until it has lost about three quarters of its volume and holds the ridge of a spoon.
steps.look: Thick, dense, white skyr in the cloth and about 6 cups (1.4 litres) of whey in the bowl. It smells clean and tangy.
steps.mistake: Straining at room temperature, which sours it and invites spoilage.
steps.fix: Strain in the fridge. If too thick, beat some whey back in; too thin, strain longer.

steps.do: Make the compote: put the 2 cups (300 g) bilberries, 3 tbsp (40 g) sugar and 1 tsp (5 ml) lemon juice in the small pan and simmer 5 to 7 minutes until the berries burst and the juices thicken slightly. Cool.
steps.look: Deep purple, glossy, syrupy fruit with some whole berries left; it smells floral and sharp.
steps.mistake: Cooking it to jam, so it loses its fresh taste.
steps.fix: Stop as soon as the juice coats a spoon; it thickens as it cools.

steps.do: Scrape the skyr into a bowl and beat it with a spoon until smooth and glossy, loosening with a little whey or milk if needed. Spoon into bowls, top with compote, and drizzle with cream and a sprinkle of brown sugar.
steps.look: Smooth, dense, glossy skyr that holds its shape, with purple compote running down one side.
steps.mistake: Serving it grainy without beating.
steps.fix: Beat for 1 minute; it turns silky.

science: Skyr is closer to a fresh cheese than a yoghurt. Heating the milk to 190°F (88°C) and holding it denatures the whey proteins, which then bind to casein and trap more water in the curd, giving a firmer set and a smoother texture. Lactic acid bacteria from the starter eat lactose and make lactic acid, lowering the pH until casein proteins clump into a gel; a trace of rennet, an enzyme, helps them knit into a stronger curd. Incubating at about 99°F (37°C) favours these bacteria. Straining then removes whey, concentrating protein so that roughly four parts of milk make one part of skyr. Keeping everything clean and the temperature steady lets the friendly bacteria crowd out unwanted ones.
plating: Spoon the skyr into chilled glass bowls in a smooth mound, make a shallow well in the top with the back of the spoon, and fill it with compote so the purple spills over one side. A thin thread of cream around the edge and a few raw berries on top.

pairing.drink: Strong black coffee or a cold glass of buttermilk: the coffee's bitterness frames the tang and sweet berries, as an Icelandic breakfast would.

variations: Rhubarb compote in spring: 2 cups (250 g) chopped rhubarb simmered with sugar until soft.
Use the leftover whey in bread dough or to soak oats overnight.
Skyr cake: fold sweetened skyr with whipped cream over a biscuit base.
safety: Heat the milk to 190°F (88°C) and hold 10 minutes; this pasteurises it at home as well as setting the texture.
Strain and store skyr in the fridge at 40°F (4°C) or below; eat within 1 week.
Discard any batch with pink, orange or fuzzy mould, or an off smell.

title: Sourdough Pancakes from Your Own Starter
summary: Light, tangy pancakes raised by a sourdough starter you have grown from flour and water over ten days, fed on schedule, and turned into an overnight sponge. It is in the course because keeping a starter alive is a daily discipline, a study in fermentation you can watch and smell, and these pancakes are its first reward.
skills: raising a starter over ten days
equipment: Clear glass jar, about 1 quart (1 litre), with a loose lid
Rubber band to mark the level
Large mixing bowl and cling film
Heavy frying pan, cast iron or a griddle
Oven set low to keep pancakes warm

ingredients.item: Wholemeal rye or wholemeal wheat flour, for the starter

ingredients.note: filtered, or tap water left out overnight

ingredients.item: Maple syrup or cane syrup, butter and berries

mise: Day 1: clean the jar well with hot soapy water and rinse it.
Keep a note of each feeding time on the jar or a card.
Choose a spot at about 75°F (24°C), out of direct sun.
The night before the pancakes: give the starter its larger feed in the morning (step 5) so it is at its peak in the evening.
On pancake morning: melt the butter, set out the eggs, and heat the oven to 200°F (95°C) for keeping warm.

timeline.do: Mix flour and water; stir once a day.
Discard and feed once a day; expect a false start then a quiet spell.
Discard and feed twice a day until the starter doubles reliably within 6 hours.
Give the starter a larger feed, keeping 2 oz (60 g) and adding 1 1/2 cups (180 g) plain flour and 3/4 cup (180 ml) water, so there is enough at its peak in the evening.
Mix the sponge of starter, flour and milk; leave covered overnight.
Beat in eggs, sugar, salt and butter; fold in soda and cook at once.

steps.do: Day 1: mix 1/2 cup (60 g) wholemeal flour with 1/4 cup (60 ml) lukewarm water in the jar to a thick paste. Cover loosely and leave at about 75°F (24°C). On day 2, stir it once.
steps.look: A stiff, beige paste; by day 2 a few small bubbles and an earthy, cereal smell.
steps.mistake: Sealing the jar tight, so gas cannot escape.
steps.fix: Rest the lid on loosely or use a cloth and band.

steps.do: Days 3 to 5: once a day, discard all but 2 oz (60 g) of the starter, then add 1/4 cup (30 g) wholemeal flour, 1/4 cup (30 g) plain flour and 1/4 cup (60 ml) lukewarm water. Stir well, scrape down the sides and mark the level with a rubber band.
steps.look: Day 3 may bring a sudden burst of bubbles and a sour, cheesy or even unpleasant smell; by day 4 or 5 it often goes quiet. Both are normal.
steps.mistake: Giving up on a quiet day 5 or panicking at the smell.
steps.fix: Keep feeding. The early bubbles are bacteria that die off as the mixture sours; the yeast you want takes over later.

steps.do: Days 6 to 10: feed twice a day, about 12 hours apart: keep 2 oz (60 g), add 1/2 cup (60 g) plain flour and 1/4 cup (60 ml) water. Watch how fast it rises after each feed.
steps.look: The starter rises to double within 4 to 8 hours, domes, then falls; it smells pleasantly sour, like yoghurt and green apple, with a web of bubbles inside.
steps.mistake: A layer of grey liquid on top (hooch), which means it is hungry, mistaken for spoilage.
steps.fix: Pour off or stir in the hooch and feed more often. Discard the whole batch only if you see pink, orange or fuzzy mould.

steps.do: Test it: the starter is ready when it doubles within 6 hours of feeding at room temperature on three days running. A spoonful dropped in water should float.
steps.look: A domed, bubbly, sticky starter that floats; it smells tangy, not like nail varnish.
steps.mistake: Using it too early, when it cannot raise anything.
steps.fix: Give it more days; some starters take two weeks.

steps.do: The night before the pancakes, about 6 hours after a larger morning feed (keep 2 oz (60 g), add 1 1/2 cups (180 g) plain flour and 3/4 cup (180 ml) water, which gives about 15 oz (420 g)), mix 1 1/4 cups (300 g) of the active starter with the 2 cups (250 g) plain flour and 1 1/4 cups (300 ml) milk in the large bowl. Cover and leave at room temperature 8 to 12 hours. Feed what remains in the jar as usual.
steps.look: A thick batter that by morning has risen, is full of bubbles and smells clearly tangy.
steps.mistake: Using all the starter so none is left to keep.
steps.fix: Always keep some back and feed it.

steps.do: In the morning, beat the 2 eggs, sugar, salt and the 3 tbsp (40 g) melted butter into the sponge.
steps.look: A smooth, thick batter, still full of bubbles, that smells tangy and buttery.
steps.mistake: Overbeating, which knocks out the bubbles.
steps.fix: Beat only until no streaks of egg remain.

steps.do: Heat the pan over medium heat until a drop of water dances, and brush with butter. Sprinkle the 1 tsp (5 g) bicarbonate over the batter and fold it in gently with a spatula.
steps.look: The batter foams, rises and lightens as the soda meets the acid in the sponge; you can hear faint fizzing.
steps.mistake: Adding the soda and then waiting, so the foam collapses before cooking.
steps.fix: Cook immediately after folding in the soda.

steps.do: Ladle 1/4 cup (60 ml) of batter per pancake into the pan, leaving room to spread. Cook 2 to 3 minutes until bubbles rise and burst across the surface and the edges look set and dry, then flip and cook 1 to 2 minutes more.
steps.look: Open bubbles that stay open on top, matt edges, and an even golden brown on the cooked side. It smells of toasted bread and tang.
steps.mistake: Flipping too early, so the raw batter splatters, or flipping twice.
steps.fix: Wait for the bubbles to stay open. Flip once.

steps.do: Keep cooked pancakes warm in a single layer on a tray in the 200°F (95°C) oven while you cook the rest, brushing the pan with butter between batches.
steps.look: Fluffy, tender pancakes with a fine, open crumb.
steps.mistake: Stacking them in a pile while hot, so they steam and go soggy.
steps.fix: Spread them out on the tray; stack only to serve.

steps.do: Serve in stacks of three with butter, syrup and berries. Feed the starter and keep it in the fridge if you bake only weekly, feeding once a week.
steps.look: Golden stacks glistening with syrup; a healthy jar of starter ready for next time.
steps.mistake: Forgetting the starter in a warm kitchen for days.
steps.fix: Refrigerate it; a cold starter needs only a weekly feed.

science: A starter is a stable community of wild yeasts and lactic acid bacteria that live on flour. In the first days other bacteria grow fast, causing the early burst and odd smells, but as lactic and acetic acids build up the mixture becomes too sour for them, and acid-tolerant yeasts and lactobacilli take over. Regular feeding supplies fresh starch and keeps the population in balance. Yeast makes carbon dioxide and alcohol; the bacteria make the acids that give the tang. In the pancakes, the overnight sponge develops flavour and acidity, and bicarbonate of soda is an alkali that reacts instantly with those acids to release carbon dioxide, giving a quick, strong lift that must be cooked straight away.
plating: Warm plates, three pancakes stacked slightly off centre so their edges show, a pat of butter melting on top, syrup poured from a jug at the table and a small heap of berries to one side.

pairing.drink: New Orleans coffee with chicory, black or with hot milk: its roasted bitterness balances the syrup and the gentle sourness of the pancakes.
pairing.brennans: New Orleans-Style Coffee with Chicory: the coffee Brennan's pours at breakfast, the natural cup beside a stack of pancakes.

variations: Sourdough waffles: the same batter cooked in a waffle iron.
Add 1 cup (150 g) blueberries to the pancakes as they cook, pressing a few into each.
Use discarded starter in crackers or flatbreads so nothing is wasted.
safety: Discard the whole starter if you see pink, orange or red streaks or fuzzy mould; grey liquid alone is harmless.
Keep the jar clean and wash your hands before handling it.
