title: Weisswurst with Laugenbrezeln and Sweet Mustard
summary: Bavaria's second breakfast: pale veal sausages emulsified with ice, poached gently below the simmer, served with lye-dipped pretzels and sweet mustard. It is in the course because both halves are exact and both are about safety: an emulsified sausage kept ice cold through grinding, and a lye bath handled with gloves and goggles that gives the pretzel its deep, shining crust.
skills: an emulsified veal sausage kept ice cold
a lye bath handled with gloves and goggles
equipment: Meat grinder with a fine plate (3 mm), chilled in the freezer
Food processor, bowl and blade chilled
Rubber or nitrile gloves and safety goggles
Glass or stainless steel bowl for the lye (never aluminium)
Two baking trays lined with baking paper (not foil)
Stand mixer or worktop for the dough

ingredients.note: or 1/2 cup (80 g) baked bicarbonate of soda; see step 9

ingredients.item: Cold water, for the lye bath

mise: Put the grinder parts, food processor bowl and blade in the freezer for 1 hour.
Cube the veal and back fat, spread on a tray and freeze 30 to 45 minutes until firm at the edges but not solid.
Soak the casings in warm water 30 minutes, then run water through them.
Mix the salt and spices; chop the parsley; zest the lemon.
Clear a space for the lye away from food, children and pets; lay out gloves, goggles, the glass bowl and slotted spoon.
Line trays with baking paper, never foil: lye reacts with aluminium.

timeline.do: Chill equipment and partly freeze the meat and fat; soak casings.
Mix and knead the pretzel dough; rest.
Grind, emulsify and stuff the sausages; refrigerate.
Shape pretzels and chill them uncovered for 1 hour.
Lye bath, salt, slash and bake the pretzels.
Poach the sausages at 165°F (74°C) water temperature.
Serve the sausages in their hot water with pretzels and mustard.

steps.do: Make the pretzel dough: mix the 4 cups (500 g) flour, salt, yeast, butter and the 1 cup plus 3 tbsp (280 ml) cold water and knead 10 minutes to a stiff, smooth dough. Cover and rest 30 minutes.
steps.look: A firm, smooth, slightly dry dough that holds a fingerprint.
steps.mistake: Adding water to make it soft; pretzel dough should be stiff.
steps.fix: Knead through the stiffness; it smooths out. Rest 10 minutes if it fights you.

steps.do: Grind the chilled veal and fat together through the frozen fine plate into a chilled bowl. Grind a second time.
steps.look: Distinct, clean strands of pink meat and white fat, cold to the touch.
steps.mistake: Warm meat, so the fat smears into a greasy paste.
steps.fix: If the mix rises above 40°F (4°C), return everything to the freezer for 15 minutes.

steps.do: Put the ground meat, salt and spices in the chilled food processor. Process, adding the crushed ice a handful at a time, for 3 to 4 minutes until it becomes a smooth, pale, sticky paste. Check with the probe: it must stay below 54°F (12°C).
steps.look: A glossy, pale pink paste like thick mousse; it clings to a spatula and has no visible fat particles.
steps.mistake: Processing past 54°F (12°C), when the emulsion breaks and the sausage turns grainy and greasy.
steps.fix: Stop and chill the bowl as soon as it nears 50°F (10°C). Add more ice if needed.

steps.do: Pulse in the parsley and lemon zest. Fry a teaspoon of paste in a small pan, taste, and adjust the salt.
steps.look: Green flecks evenly through the pale paste; the test patty is springy and well seasoned.
steps.mistake: Skipping the test fry and finding the batch bland after stuffing.
steps.fix: Always fry a test piece. Adjust now; you cannot later.

steps.do: Stuff the paste into the casings, filling firmly but not tightly. Twist into links 4 inches (10 cm) long, alternating the direction of each twist. Refrigerate while you shape the pretzels.
steps.look: Plump, even links with no large air pockets.
steps.mistake: Overfilling, so the casings burst when twisted or poached.
steps.fix: Leave a little slack. Prick visible air bubbles with a clean pin.

steps.do: Divide the dough into 8 pieces of about 3 1/2 oz (100 g). Roll each into a rope 24 inches (60 cm) long, thick in the middle and tapering to thin ends.
steps.look: A rope with a fat belly and thin arms, about 1 inch (2.5 cm) thick in the centre.
steps.mistake: An even rope, so the classic shape and contrast in texture is lost.
steps.fix: Roll the centre less and the ends more.

steps.do: Shape each: form a U, cross the arms, twist them once, then fold the ends down and press them onto the belly at about 4 and 8 o'clock. Place on the lined trays and refrigerate uncovered for 1 hour.
steps.look: Classic pretzels with a fat lower curve and thin crossed arms; after chilling, a dry, slightly leathery skin.
steps.mistake: Covering them, so the skin stays sticky and takes the lye unevenly.
steps.fix: Chill uncovered; a dry skin gives an even, glossy crust.

steps.do: Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C). Put on gloves and goggles. Pour the 4 1/4 cups (1 litre) cold water into the glass bowl first, then add the 2 tbsp (30 g) lye to the water slowly, stirring with the stainless spoon until dissolved.
steps.look: The solution warms slightly and turns clear. No splashes.
steps.mistake: Pouring water onto lye, which can boil and spatter caustic liquid.
steps.fix: Always add lye to water, never water to lye. If it touches skin, rinse with plenty of cold running water for 15 minutes.

steps.do: Dip each chilled pretzel into the lye for 10 to 15 seconds using the slotted spoon, lift, drain and return it to the tray. If using baked bicarbonate instead, dissolve the 1/2 cup (80 g) in 4 1/4 cups (1 litre) simmering water and dip each pretzel 30 seconds.
steps.look: A slick, slightly slippery surface; the dough looks pale yellow before baking.
steps.mistake: Touching the dipped pretzels with bare hands.
steps.fix: Keep gloves on until every dipped pretzel is in the oven.

steps.do: Sprinkle with coarse salt and cut a slash about 1/4 inch (5 mm) deep along the thick belly with the knife. Bake 14 to 16 minutes until deep mahogany.
steps.look: The slash opens into a pale, rough ear against a glossy, near-black brown crust; the kitchen smells like a German bakery.
steps.mistake: Pulling them out light brown.
steps.fix: Bake until truly dark; the crumb stays white and soft inside.

steps.do: Poach the sausages: bring a large pan of water to 165°F (74°C), never simmering, and lower in the sausages. Hold the water at 160 to 170°F (71 to 77°C) for 20 minutes until the centre of a sausage reads 160°F (71°C).
steps.look: The sausages firm, plump and turn bright white; the water barely moves.
steps.mistake: Boiling water, which bursts the casings and makes the texture crumbly.
steps.fix: Keep the thermometer in the water and adjust the heat. Add cold water if it creeps up.

steps.do: Serve the sausages in a bowl of their hot water at the table, with warm pretzels and sweet mustard. To eat, cut a sausage lengthways and peel the meat from the skin.
steps.look: Steaming white sausages, glossy dark pretzels and amber mustard: the whole Bavarian table.
steps.mistake: Eating the casing, which is tough on these sausages.
steps.fix: Show guests the peel: cut lengthways and roll the meat out, or suck it out as Bavarians do.

science: Weisswurst is an emulsion: salt dissolves muscle proteins such as myosin, and processing coats tiny fat droplets with them, trapping fat and water in a stable paste that sets when heated, like a savoury custard. Above about 54°F (12°C) the fat softens and the proteins can no longer hold it, so the emulsion breaks and the cooked sausage turns greasy and grainy; the ice keeps it cold and supplies the water. Poaching below a simmer sets the proteins gently. Lye is a strong alkali that breaks down proteins and starches on the pretzel surface; in the oven the alkaline surface undergoes very fast Maillard browning, giving the dark, glossy, slightly mineral crust that baking soda only partly copies.
plating: Bring the sausages to the table in a lidded tureen or deep bowl of their warm water, two per person. Pretzels on a board or hung on a pretzel stand, sweet mustard in a small pot with a wooden spoon. Serve on wooden boards with a knife for peeling.

pairing.drink: A Bavarian Weissbier (wheat beer): its banana and clove notes, soft carbonation and creamy body are the traditional partner to Weisswurst and sweet mustard.

variations: Butterbrezel: split a cooled pretzel and spread it thickly with cold salted butter.
Pretzel rolls: shape the dough into 8 small rolls, dip and slash with a cross.
Make sausage patties from the same paste if you have no stuffer, poached in a buttered pan of hot water or steamed.
safety: Lye causes severe burns. Wear gloves and goggles, add lye to water never the reverse, use glass or stainless steel, keep children and pets away, and rinse any splash with running water for 15 minutes.
Never use foil or aluminium with lye; it reacts and gives off hydrogen gas.
Keep the meat and fat below 40°F (4°C) while grinding and the paste below 54°F (12°C) in the processor, and poach until 160°F (71°C) in the centre.
Weisswurst is a fresh, uncured sausage: refrigerate and cook within 2 days.

title: Msemen and Baghrir with Amlou
summary: Two Moroccan breakfast breads made side by side: msemen, a square flatbread folded with butter and semolina into flaky layers and cooked on a griddle, and baghrir, the semolina pancake that bubbles into a thousand holes on one side only, served with amlou, a paste of toasted almonds, argan oil and honey. It is in the course because the two breads demand opposite batters and a calm hand on the griddle.
skills: a folded square flatbread laminated with butter and semolina
a semolina yeast batter of a thousand holes
equipment: Two heavy frying pans or a griddle and a non-stick pan
Clean, smooth worktop or a large tray, oiled
Small bowl for melted butter and a pastry brush

ingredients.item: Fine semolina, for the msemen dough

ingredients.note: plus a little more if needed

ingredients.item: Unsalted butter and honey, for the baghrir syrup

mise: Toast the almonds at 350°F (175°C) for 10 to 12 minutes until golden inside; cool.
Melt the butter for laminating and keep it warm; mix the sprinkling semolina in a small bowl.
Oil the worktop or a large tray generously.
Melt the butter and honey together for the baghrir syrup.
Lay out clean tea towels for stacking the cooked baghrir.

timeline.do: Toast almonds; make the amlou.
Make the msemen dough and rest it; blend the baghrir batter and leave to rise.
Shape and fold the msemen squares; rest 15 minutes.
Cook the baghrir one at a time, holes up.
Griddle the msemen.
Serve both breads warm with amlou and honey butter.

steps.do: Make the amlou: grind the toasted almonds in the food processor for 4 to 6 minutes, scraping down often, until they release their oil and form a runny paste. With the motor running, add the 1/3 cup (80 ml) argan oil and 3 tbsp (60 g) honey and a pinch of salt.
steps.look: First crumbs, then a clumped ball, then a smooth, pourable paste the colour of peanut butter, smelling of toasted nuts.
steps.mistake: Stopping at the crumb stage, so it is dry and gritty.
steps.fix: Keep processing; the oils release suddenly. Let the motor rest if it gets hot.

steps.do: Make the msemen dough: mix the 2 cups (250 g) flour, 1/2 cup (85 g) semolina, salt and sugar, add the 3/4 cup (180 ml) warm water and knead 10 minutes until very smooth and elastic.
steps.look: A soft, smooth dough that stretches without tearing.
steps.mistake: Under-kneading, so the dough tears when stretched thin.
steps.fix: Knead the full 10 minutes; rest 10 if it resists.

steps.do: Divide into 8 balls the size of a small egg, coat them in oil, and rest 20 minutes under a cloth.
steps.look: Smooth, glossy balls that feel relaxed and soft.
steps.mistake: Skipping the rest, so the dough springs back.
steps.fix: Rest longer; it cannot be rushed.

steps.do: Blend the baghrir batter: put the 1 1/2 cups (250 g) semolina, 1/2 cup (60 g) flour, yeast, salt, sugar and the 2 1/2 cups (600 ml) warm water in the blender and blend 2 minutes. Add the baking powder and blend 10 seconds. Leave 30 to 45 minutes.
steps.look: A thin batter like single cream that becomes foamy and bubbly on top.
steps.mistake: A thick batter, which makes heavy pancakes with few holes.
steps.fix: Add water 1 tbsp (15 ml) at a time until it pours like single cream.

steps.do: Shape the msemen: on the oiled surface, flatten a ball with oiled hands and spread it outward with your palms into a very thin, rough square about 10 inches (25 cm) across.
steps.look: A sheet so thin you can see the worktop through it, with a few small tears that do not matter.
steps.mistake: Using a rolling pin, which cannot stretch it thin enough.
steps.fix: Spread with flat, oiled palms; oil is what lets it stretch.

steps.do: Brush with melted butter and sprinkle with semolina. Fold the top third down and the bottom third up, like a letter, brush and sprinkle again, then fold the sides in to make a square about 3 inches (8 cm). Rest the squares 15 minutes.
steps.look: Neat, plump squares with layers you can see at the edges.
steps.mistake: Too little fat or semolina between the folds, so the layers fuse.
steps.fix: Brush every surface before each fold; the semolina keeps the layers apart.

steps.do: Cook the baghrir: heat the non-stick pan over medium heat with no oil. Stir the batter, ladle about 1/3 cup (80 ml) into the pan and let it spread to a round 6 inches (15 cm) across. Cook on one side only for 2 to 3 minutes.
steps.look: Holes appear across the whole surface as bubbles rise and burst, and the top changes from wet and shiny to dry and matt. The base is pale gold.
steps.mistake: Heat too high, so the base browns before the holes open.
steps.fix: Medium heat. If no holes form, the batter needs more rest or more water.

steps.do: Lift each baghrir out and lay it holes up on a tea towel in a single layer to cool. Do not stack until cool. Repeat with all the batter.
steps.look: Spongy, pale pancakes covered in holes, like a honeycomb.
steps.mistake: Flipping them or stacking them hot, so they stick together.
steps.fix: Never flip. Stack only when cool.

steps.do: Cook the msemen: heat the heavy pan over medium heat. Press each square to about 6 inches (15 cm) with oiled hands and cook 2 to 3 minutes a side, pressing with a spatula, until golden and crisp in spots.
steps.look: The square puffs slightly between layers, browns in patches and smells buttery; you hear a gentle sizzle.
steps.mistake: Too high heat, so the outside burns before the layers cook through.
steps.fix: Medium heat and patience. Press to help the layers cook.

steps.do: Serve both breads warm. Pour the honey butter over the baghrir holes, and offer the amlou and more honey with the msemen.
steps.look: Glossy honey filling the holes of the baghrir; flaky, golden msemen; a bowl of amlou.
steps.mistake: Serving the msemen cold and leathery.
steps.fix: Keep msemen warm wrapped in a towel; reheat for 1 minute in a dry pan.

science: The two breads succeed for opposite reasons. Msemen is laminated by hand: thin sheets of dough are separated by butter and semolina, and when the square hits the griddle, water in the dough turns to steam and pushes the layers apart, while the semolina grains keep them from fusing, so it flakes. Baghrir is a very wet, yeasted batter with baking powder added for a second lift. On a hot, ungreased pan, bubbles of carbon dioxide and steam rise from the base and burst through a top that sets slowly, leaving open channels; it is cooked on one side only so that those holes stay open. In the amlou, long processing breaks the cell walls of the almonds until their own oil turns the crumbs into a paste.
plating: Stack the msemen in a warm cloth-lined basket. Overlap the baghrir on a platter holes up and pour the warm honey butter over them so it pools in every hole. Amlou in a small bowl with a spoon, and mint tea in glasses.

pairing.drink: Moroccan mint tea, green gunpowder tea brewed with fresh spearmint and sugar, poured from a height: sweet and cooling beside the honey and almond.

variations: Stuffed msemen: spread spiced minced beef or onion and herbs inside before folding.
Baghrir with amlou: spread the warm pancakes with amlou instead of honey butter.
Harcha: a quick semolina griddle bread to add a third bread to the table.
safety: Toast almonds until golden but not dark; burnt nuts taste bitter and smoke.
Amlou is made from almonds and argan oil: ask your guests about allergies before serving.

title: Gaufres de Liège
summary: Liège waffles are not batter but a rich brioche dough, studded at the last moment with pearl sugar and pressed in a heavy iron until the sugar melts into glassy caramel pockets and a lacquered crust. It is in the course because it brings together enriched dough, a slow cold proof that builds flavour, and the control of caramel in a hot iron without burning it.
skills: a brioche dough with pearl sugar folded in last
equipment: Stand mixer with dough hook (strongly recommended)
Large bowl with lid or cling film
Heavy cast-iron or deep-pocket Belgian waffle iron
Silicone brush and a wooden skewer for cleaning the iron
Damp cloth for wiping the iron while hot

ingredients.item: Vanilla sugar, or sugar with 1 tsp (5 ml) vanilla extract

ingredients.note: not crushed sugar cubes if you can help it

mise: Warm the milk to about 95°F (35°C).
Let the eggs and butter come to room temperature; the butter should be soft as face cream.
Weigh the pearl sugar and keep it to one side; it goes in last.
Find the waffle iron and its manual, and lay a wire rack nearby.

timeline.do: Mix the dough, knead in the butter, rise 1 hour.
Knock back, cover and refrigerate overnight.
Fold in pearl sugar, divide into 10 balls, rest 15 to 30 minutes.
Heat the iron fully.
Bake the waffles one or two at a time.
Cool 2 minutes on a rack and serve warm.

steps.do: Mix the 3 cups (375 g) flour, yeast, salt and vanilla sugar in the mixer bowl. Add the warm milk and eggs and knead on low for 5 minutes to a smooth, firm dough.
steps.look: A smooth, slightly sticky dough that clears the sides of the bowl.
steps.mistake: Adding the butter now, before the gluten has formed.
steps.fix: Develop the dough first; butter coats the flour and slows gluten.

steps.do: With the mixer on medium-low, add the 14 tbsp (200 g) soft butter a piece at a time, waiting until each is absorbed before the next. Knead 8 to 10 minutes until glossy and elastic.
steps.look: The dough breaks up and looks greasy at first, then comes back together as a satiny, stretchy dough that pulls from the sides.
steps.mistake: Cold butter, which stays in lumps.
steps.fix: Use butter soft enough to dent easily. If lumps remain, keep kneading; they will work in.

steps.do: Cover and let the dough rise at room temperature for 1 hour until puffed by about half. Press it down, cover tightly and refrigerate overnight, 10 to 14 hours.
steps.look: A domed, soft dough that smells yeasty and buttery; after chilling it is firm and easy to handle.
steps.mistake: Skipping the chill and working with warm, greasy dough.
steps.fix: Chilling firms the butter and deepens flavour; at least 2 hours if you are in a hurry.

steps.do: Tip the cold dough onto a board and knead in the 1 1/4 cups (250 g) pearl sugar and cinnamon by hand, folding and pressing for 1 to 2 minutes until evenly spread.
steps.look: White nuggets scattered through the whole dough, still whole and sharp edged.
steps.mistake: Adding pearl sugar to the mixer earlier, where it dissolves or grinds.
steps.fix: Pearl sugar always goes in by hand, last.

steps.do: Divide into 10 balls of about 4 oz (110 g). Rest under a cloth for 15 to 30 minutes while the iron heats.
steps.look: Soft, slightly puffed balls studded with white sugar, cool rather than cold to the touch.
steps.mistake: Baking straight from the fridge, so the centres stay doughy.
steps.fix: Let them lose their chill; they should feel cool, not cold.

steps.do: Heat the iron to medium, around 350 to 375°F (175 to 190°C) if it has a dial. Place one ball in the centre of each grid, close the lid gently and bake 3 to 4 minutes.
steps.look: Steam pours out at first, then slows; the waffle smells of caramel and butter, and when opened it is deep golden with amber, glassy spots.
steps.mistake: An iron too hot, which burns the sugar black before the dough is cooked.
steps.fix: Turn the heat down a notch. If the first waffle is pale but cooked, bake the next a minute longer.

steps.do: Lift the waffle out with tongs onto the rack and cool 2 minutes before eating.
steps.look: A crisp, shiny crust with caramel pools that harden as they cool; inside, a soft, brioche crumb.
steps.mistake: Biting at once: molten caramel is extremely hot.
steps.fix: Wait 2 minutes. The crust crisps as it cools.

steps.do: Between waffles, scrape any burnt sugar from the grids with a wooden skewer and wipe with a damp cloth held in tongs. Clean the iron while still warm when you finish.
steps.look: Clean grids with no black crust building up.
steps.mistake: Leaving caramel to harden on the iron.
steps.fix: Clean warm; if it sets, heat the iron again and wipe.

science: The dough is a brioche: eggs and a lot of butter make it rich and tender, and the butter goes in only after kneading has built a gluten network strong enough to hold it. A long, cold proof slows the yeast but lets enzymes break down starch and protein into flavour compounds, while firming the butter so the dough is easy to shape. Pearl sugar is compressed sucrose that does not dissolve in the dough. In the hot iron the sugar on the surface melts, and above about 320°F (160°C) sucrose begins to caramelise, breaking down into hundreds of compounds that taste of toffee and give the glassy amber crust, while the Maillard reaction browns the dough around it.
plating: Serve on a small plate or a square of paper, just as they are, warm, the caramelised side up. If you want more, a few berries and a spoonful of whipped cream to the side, never on top, so the crust stays crisp.

pairing.drink: A café au lait or a Belgian strong golden ale: the coffee's roast meets the caramel, while the ale's dry finish cuts the butter.

variations: Speculoos Liège: add 1 tsp (2 g) speculoos spice to the dough.
Chocolate: fold 1/2 cup (85 g) chopped dark chocolate in with the pearl sugar.
Freeze cooled waffles and reheat in a 350°F (175°C) oven for 6 minutes.
safety: Caramel in the iron reaches over 300°F (150°C): use tongs and let waffles cool 2 minutes.
Unplug the iron before cleaning and keep fingers clear of the hinged lid.

title: Bougatsa with Hand-Stretched Phyllo
summary: Thessaloniki's breakfast pie: a warm semolina custard wrapped in many layers of phyllo you stretch by hand until it is thin enough to read through, baked until shattering and dusted with icing sugar and cinnamon. It is in the course because it takes the strudel lesson further, making the phyllo yourself, and joins it to a custard tempered with eggs.
skills: dusting with icing sugar and cinnamon
equipment: Kitchen table at least 3 by 2 feet (90 by 60 cm), covered with a clean, smooth cotton cloth
Medium heavy saucepan for the custard
Rimmed baking tray, about 12 by 16 inches (30 by 40 cm), lined with baking paper

ingredients.item: Vanilla extract and finely grated lemon zest

mise: Make the phyllo dough at least 2 hours ahead so it can rest.
Clear the table, cover it with the cloth and rub cornflour lightly over the whole cloth.
Take off rings and watches; they snag the dough.
Melt the butter and keep it warm; line the baking tray.
Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C) once the custard is cooling.

timeline.do: Mix and knead the phyllo dough; rest 2 hours.
Make the semolina custard and let it cool to warm.
Stretch the first sheet of phyllo, butter and fold; stretch the second.
Assemble the parcel and bake 35 to 40 minutes.
Rest the bougatsa 15 minutes.
Dust with icing sugar and cinnamon, cut and serve warm.

steps.do: Make the phyllo dough: mix the 3 cups (375 g) flour and salt, add the 1 cup (240 ml) water, 3 tbsp (45 ml) oil and 1 tbsp (15 ml) vinegar, and knead 10 minutes until very smooth and elastic. Divide in two, coat lightly with oil, wrap and rest at room temperature for 2 hours.
steps.look: A soft, silky dough that stretches far before tearing; after resting, it relaxes and slumps a little.
steps.mistake: Resting it too briefly, so it springs back and tears when stretched.
steps.fix: Rest the full 2 hours; the gluten must relax completely.

steps.do: Make the custard: heat the 4 cups (950 ml) milk with half the sugar until steaming. Whisk in the 2/3 cup (115 g) semolina in a thin stream and cook over medium-low heat, whisking, for 5 minutes until thick.
steps.look: The milk thickens to the consistency of loose porridge and bubbles slowly in big, lazy blips.
steps.mistake: Dumping the semolina in at once, which makes lumps.
steps.fix: Pour slowly while whisking. Whisk out any lumps or pass through a sieve.

steps.do: Whisk the eggs with the remaining sugar. Ladle a cup of the hot semolina into the eggs, whisking hard, then pour the eggs back into the pan. Cook, stirring constantly, 2 to 3 minutes until it reaches 175°F (80°C) and is thick. Off the heat, stir in the 2 tbsp (30 g) butter, vanilla and zest. Cover the surface with cling film and cool until just warm.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy, yellow custard thick enough to hold a ridge, smelling of lemon and vanilla.
steps.mistake: Adding eggs straight to the hot pan, which scrambles them.
steps.fix: Always temper with hot custard first. Specks of scrambled egg can be sieved out.

steps.do: Stretch the first piece: roll it out on the cloth into a rectangle about 12 by 8 inches (30 by 20 cm). Slip your floured hands, backs up and knuckles curled, under the centre and gently pull your hands apart, stretching the dough outwards from the middle, walking round the table.
steps.look: The dough thins and becomes translucent; you can see the pattern of the cloth through it.
steps.mistake: Stretching with fingertips, which poke holes.
steps.fix: Use the backs of your hands. Small holes do not matter; the layers cover them.

steps.do: Keep stretching until the sheet is about 36 by 28 inches (90 by 70 cm) and paper thin all over, letting the edges hang over the table. Trim off the thick edges with scissors.
steps.look: A huge, even, almost transparent sheet; you could read a recipe through it.
steps.mistake: Thick patches left in the middle.
steps.fix: Work from the thickest areas outwards; pull gently on thick parts with your fingers.

steps.do: Brush the whole sheet with melted butter. Fold the sheet in half to make a double layer, then brush again, and fold in half once more to a rectangle about 18 by 14 inches (45 by 35 cm), tucking any overhang under so it fits the tray. Lift it onto the lined tray. Stretch the second piece of dough the same way, butter and fold it, and set it aside on the cloth.
steps.look: Glossy, buttered layers of dough, four thick, on the tray.
steps.mistake: Letting the sheet dry before buttering, so it cracks.
steps.fix: Work quickly and brush at once; cover with a damp cloth if interrupted.

steps.do: Spread the warm custard over the centre of the dough on the tray, leaving a 2 inch (5 cm) border. Lay the second folded sheet over the custard. Fold the borders of the lower sheet up and over the edges to seal, then brush the top well with butter. Score the top lightly into 8 squares with a sharp knife.
steps.look: A neat parcel about 1 1/2 inches (4 cm) thick with the custard sealed inside; the top glistens with butter.
steps.mistake: Custard spilling out at the edges.
steps.fix: Tuck the borders firmly and leave room around the custard.

steps.do: Bake at 375°F (190°C) for 35 to 40 minutes until deep golden and crisp all over.
steps.look: The top puffs in layers and turns golden brown; you hear crackling as you open the oven, and it smells of butter and vanilla.
steps.mistake: Pulling it out pale, when the base is still soft.
steps.fix: Bake until the colour is clearly deep. Lift a corner to check the base is crisp.

steps.do: Rest 15 minutes, then dust heavily with icing sugar and cinnamon through the sieve. Cut along the scored lines with a sharp knife, pressing straight down, and serve warm.
steps.look: Clean squares with shattering layers of pastry and a soft, wobbling custard centre.
steps.mistake: Cutting it straight from the oven, so the custard runs out.
steps.fix: Fifteen minutes lets the custard set enough to slice.

science: Phyllo can be stretched paper thin because of gluten, a network of proteins formed when wheat flour is kneaded with water. Kneading builds it; resting lets the proteins relax so the sheet stretches without springing back. Oil coats the gluten strands, making them more extensible, and the small amount of acid in the vinegar loosens the network further. In the oven, water in each buttered layer turns to steam and separates the layers, while the butter fries them crisp. The custard is thickened twice: semolina starch swells in hot milk, and eggs set as their proteins unfold and bond between about 160 and 180°F (71 and 82°C). Tempering raises the eggs' temperature slowly so they thicken instead of curdling.
plating: Serve on warm plates in squares, cut side forward to show the layers and the custard. Dust icing sugar generously over the top and add a fine line of cinnamon across each square. Serve with coffee, nothing else.

pairing.drink: A Greek coffee, thick and unfiltered, or a cold glass of milk: bitter or cool, either balances the sweet custard and buttery pastry.

variations: Savoury bougatsa: fill with crumbled feta mixed with an egg and black pepper, finished without sugar.
Bought phyllo: use 1 lb (450 g) of commercial sheets, buttering every sheet, when time is short.
Mince bougatsa: spiced minced lamb filling for a savoury lunch.
safety: Cook the custard until it reaches 175°F (80°C) to cook the eggs fully.
Cool leftovers and refrigerate within 2 hours; reheat in a 350°F (175°C) oven to recrisp.

title: Pastelitos de Guayaba y Queso
summary: Havana's café pastry: squares of homemade puff pastry filled with guava paste and sweetened cream cheese, baked until risen in hundreds of layers and brushed with sugar syrup while hot. It is in the course because it puts full puff pastry, made with six turns, to work, and teaches cutting, sealing and baking so the layers rise straight.
equipment: Two sheets of baking paper for the butter block
Two baking trays lined with baking paper

ingredients.note: plus 1 to 2 tbsp (15 to 30 ml) if needed

ingredients.item: Unsalted butter, melted and cooled, for the dough
Unsalted butter, cold, for the block

ingredients.note: cut in slices 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick

mise: Chill the water with ice cubes in it.
Shape the butter block: put the cold butter between two sheets of baking paper, beat it flat with the rolling pin and shape it into a 5 inch (13 cm) square, then chill 20 minutes.
Beat the cream cheese with 2 tbsp (25 g) sugar until smooth; chill.
Slice the guava paste.
Make the syrup: boil sugar and water 2 minutes; cool.

timeline.do: Make the dough and butter block; chill 30 minutes.
Enclose the butter and give two turns; chill 30 minutes.
Two more turns; chill 30 minutes.
The last two turns; chill at least 1 hour.
Roll out, cut, fill and seal; chill 20 minutes.
Egg wash and bake 20 to 25 minutes.
Brush with syrup and cool slightly before serving.

steps.do: Make the dough: mix the 2 cups (250 g) flour and salt, add the 2 tbsp (30 g) melted butter and 1/2 cup (120 ml) ice water and mix to a shaggy dough, adding a little more water only if dry patches remain. Knead 1 minute, shape into a flat square, wrap and chill 30 minutes.
steps.look: A firm, slightly rough dough that just holds together.
steps.mistake: Kneading it smooth and elastic, which makes the pastry shrink and toughen.
steps.fix: Mix only until it holds. Rest longer if it springs back.

steps.do: Roll the dough into a square 8 inches (20 cm) across. Set the butter square on it at 45 degrees, like a diamond, and fold the corners of the dough over to meet in the middle, pinching the seams to enclose the butter completely.
steps.look: A neat parcel with no butter showing; the dough and butter feel equally firm and cool.
steps.mistake: Butter much harder or softer than the dough, so it breaks or squeezes out.
steps.fix: Both should bend without cracking. Chill or rest briefly to match them.

steps.do: Roll the parcel away from you into a rectangle about 18 by 6 inches (45 by 15 cm), keeping the edges straight. Fold it in three like a letter: bottom third up, top third down. Turn it 90 degrees so the open side faces you. That is one turn. Repeat once more, then wrap and chill 30 minutes.
steps.look: Clean, even layers visible at the edges; the dough stays cool and smooth.
steps.mistake: Butter breaking through the dough, or the dough sticking to the worktop.
steps.fix: Dust lightly with flour and keep the pastry cold. Patch a breakthrough with a pinch of flour and chill at once.

steps.do: Give two more turns the same way, mark the dough with four fingertip dents to remember, and chill 30 minutes. Give the last two turns for six in all, and chill at least 1 hour.
steps.look: A smooth, pale block with no streaks of butter visible on the surface.
steps.mistake: Losing count of the turns.
steps.fix: Mark the dough with dents equal to the turns given.

steps.do: Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C). Roll the pastry into a square about 16 by 16 inches (40 by 40 cm) and 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick. Trim the edges with a sharp knife and cut 16 squares of 4 inches (10 cm), pressing straight down without dragging.
steps.look: Clean, crisp edges where the layers are visible as fine lines.
steps.mistake: Dragging a blunt knife, which seals the layers together so they do not rise.
steps.fix: Use a sharp knife or pizza wheel and cut in one firm stroke.

steps.do: Lay 8 squares on the lined trays. Put a slice of guava and 2 tbsp (25 g) cream cheese in the centre of each, leaving a 1/2 inch (1 cm) border. Brush the borders with water, top with the remaining squares and press the edges firmly with your fingers. Chill 20 minutes.
steps.look: Neat, plump parcels with the filling sealed inside.
steps.mistake: Overfilling, so the filling leaks and burns.
steps.fix: Use the amounts given; the pastry needs room to rise.

steps.do: Brush the tops with egg wash, keeping it off the cut edges. Cut two small slits in each top with the knife tip. Bake 20 to 25 minutes until puffed and deep golden.
steps.look: The pastries rise in visible layers to about three times their height and turn golden; the kitchen smells of butter and guava.
steps.mistake: Egg wash dripping down the sides, gluing the layers shut.
steps.fix: Brush only the flat top. Wipe any drips.

steps.do: As soon as they come out, brush generously with the cooled syrup. Cool 10 minutes on the rack.
steps.look: A glossy, sticky shine across the tops; the syrup sizzles faintly as it meets the hot pastry.
steps.mistake: Brushing syrup on cold pastries, where it soaks in and turns them soggy.
steps.fix: Brush hot, so the syrup sets into a glaze.

science: Puff pastry rises without yeast. Each turn multiplies the layers: six letter folds give 729 layers of butter separated by dough. In a hot oven the water in the dough and butter turns to steam, which expands and pushes the layers apart, while the fat fries each layer crisp; the starch and protein set around the gaps. Everything depends on keeping butter and dough the same firmness and cold: soft butter smears into the dough and the layers merge, while hard butter shatters. Resting between turns lets the gluten relax so the pastry does not shrink. The syrup glaze is a solution of sugar in water that sets on the hot pastry as the water evaporates, giving shine and a sticky sweetness.
plating: Serve warm on a small plate or wrapped in paper as in a Cuban bakery window, two per person, one cut in half to show the layers and the pink and white filling.

pairing.drink: A café cubano or cortadito: a sweet, strong espresso whose bitterness cuts through guava and butter, as it is taken at a Havana counter.

variations: Pastelitos de carne: fill with seasoned picadillo for a savoury version.
Guava only (pastelitos de guayaba): skip the cheese and double the guava.
Rough puff: for speed, rub chunks of cold butter into the flour and give four turns.
safety: Hot guava filling stays very hot; let pastries cool 10 minutes before biting.
Refrigerate leftover pastries with cream cheese within 2 hours.

title: Wienerbrød (Danish Pastries)
summary: Wienerbrød: a yeasted dough laminated with butter, shaped into spandauer with custard, cinnamon snails and almond combs, filled with remonce and crème pâtissière, then glazed. It is in the course as a full morning's bake that builds on the croissant: yeasted lamination with several shapes and fillings, each asking for its own fold, proof and finish.
equipment: Long heavy rolling pin and ruler
Baking paper for the butter block
Sharp knife and a pizza wheel
Two baking trays lined with baking paper
Medium saucepan and whisk for the custard
Somewhere to proof at 75 to 78°F (24 to 26°C)

ingredients.item: Unsalted butter, soft, for the remonce
Light brown sugar, for the remonce

ingredients.note: beaten with a pinch of salt

ingredients.item: Icing sugar and water, for the glaze
ingredients.us: 1 cup icing sugar and about 2 tbsp water
ingredients.metric: 120 g icing sugar and about 30 ml water

mise: The day before: make the dough and the butter block, and give the turns.
Make the crème pâtissière the day before too, and chill it.
Mix the remonce: beat the soft butter, brown sugar and cinnamon until creamy. Divide in two and beat the grated almond paste into one half.
Line the trays and clear the fridge shelf.
On the day, set up a warm proofing spot: an oven with the light on and a tray of warm water, checked with a thermometer.

timeline.do: Mix the dough; chill 1 hour. Shape the butter block.
Enclose the butter; give three letter folds with 30 minutes chilling between; chill overnight.
Make the crème pâtissière and the remonce.
Roll out and shape spandauer, snails and combs.
Proof at 75 to 78°F (24 to 26°C) for about 90 minutes.
Egg wash and bake at 400°F (200°C) for 15 to 18 minutes.
Glaze while warm and serve.

steps.do: Mix the dough: combine the 3 1/4 cups (400 g) flour, sugar, yeast, salt and cardamom, add the 2/3 cup (160 ml) cold milk and the egg and knead 4 to 5 minutes to a smooth, fairly firm dough. Flatten into a rectangle, wrap and chill 1 hour.
steps.look: A smooth, cool dough that is not sticky and smells faintly of cardamom.
steps.mistake: Over-kneading to a very elastic dough, which fights the rolling pin.
steps.fix: Knead only until smooth; the folds develop the rest.

steps.do: Make the butter block: beat the 1 cup plus 2 tbsp (250 g) cold butter between baking paper and shape it into a square 7 inches (18 cm) across. Chill until firm but bendable.
steps.look: A smooth, even slab of butter that bends without cracking.
steps.mistake: Butter too warm and greasy, or so cold it snaps.
steps.fix: Rest it at room temperature for a few minutes or chill briefly until it bends like cold plasticine.

steps.do: Roll the dough to a square 10 inches (25 cm) across, set the butter on it as a diamond, fold the corners over to enclose it and pinch the seams. Roll into a rectangle 20 by 8 inches (50 by 20 cm) and fold like a letter. Wrap and chill 30 minutes. Repeat twice more for three folds, then chill overnight.
steps.look: Clean, distinct layers at the edges; no butter breaking through.
steps.mistake: Letting the dough warm up, so butter smears into it.
steps.fix: If butter shows or the dough feels soft, stop and chill 20 minutes.

steps.do: Make the crème pâtissière: heat the 1 cup (240 ml) milk with the vanilla. Whisk the yolks, sugar and cornflour, pour on the hot milk while whisking, return to the pan and whisk over medium heat until it boils and thickens, then cook 1 minute more. Cover the surface and chill.
steps.look: A thick, glossy, pale yellow custard that holds its shape and no longer tastes of starch.
steps.mistake: Stopping before it boils, so the starch does not thicken fully and the custard turns runny.
steps.fix: Let it bubble for a full minute while whisking hard.

steps.do: On the morning, roll the dough into a rectangle 16 by 12 inches (40 by 30 cm) and 1/4 inch (5 mm) thick. Cut it in three strips of 16 by 4 inches (40 by 10 cm).
steps.look: An even sheet with sharp edges, the layers visible when cut.
steps.mistake: Rolling unevenly, so pastries bake at different speeds.
steps.fix: Use a ruler and roll from the middle outward.

steps.do: Spandauer: cut the first strip into four 4 inch (10 cm) squares. Put a teaspoon of the cinnamon remonce in the centre of each, fold the four corners to the centre and press down firmly. Top with a heaped teaspoon of crème pâtissière.
steps.look: Neat squares with corners meeting in the middle under a dab of custard.
steps.mistake: Corners that open in the oven.
steps.fix: Press the corners down hard into the remonce, which glues them.

steps.do: Snails: spread the second strip with the cinnamon remonce, leaving a 1/2 inch (1 cm) border at one short end. Roll it up tightly from the other short end into a log about 4 inches (10 cm) long and cut 4 slices 1 inch (2.5 cm) thick. Lay them flat, tucking the tail underneath.
steps.look: Tight, even spirals of pale dough and dark cinnamon butter, each slice the same thickness.
steps.mistake: Rolling loosely, so the snails unravel.
steps.fix: Roll tightly and lay each tail under itself.

steps.do: Combs: spread the almond remonce down the middle of the third strip, fold it in half lengthways and press the edges. Cut into 4 pieces 4 inches (10 cm) long. Make 5 cuts halfway into the folded edge of each and curve it so the teeth fan open. Sprinkle with flaked almonds after the egg wash.
steps.look: Curved pastries with fanned teeth like a cockscomb.
steps.mistake: Cutting through the sealed edge, so the filling spills.
steps.fix: Cut only into the folded side, never the seam side.

steps.do: Proof all the pastries on the trays, loosely covered, at 75 to 78°F (24 to 26°C) for 75 to 90 minutes.
steps.look: They grow by about half and wobble slightly when the tray is shaken; the layers look puffy.
steps.mistake: Proofing above 80°F (27°C), where butter melts and leaks out, leaving flat, greasy pastries.
steps.fix: Keep the temperature down and give more time instead.

steps.do: Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C). Brush the pastries gently with egg wash, keeping it off the cut edges. Sprinkle flaked almonds on the combs. Bake 15 to 18 minutes, turning the trays once.
steps.look: Deep golden pastries with visible flaky layers; a few bubbles of butter around the base; the kitchen smells of butter and cardamom.
steps.mistake: Underbaking, which leaves the insides doughy.
steps.fix: Bake until deep golden; pale Danish taste raw.

steps.do: Brush the snails and combs with the warm apricot jam while hot. Mix the icing sugar with water to a thick drizzle and drizzle it over the snails and spandauer once they have cooled for 10 minutes.
steps.look: Shiny, jam-glazed tops and fine white threads of icing.
steps.mistake: Icing hot pastries, so it melts into a sticky film.
steps.fix: Jam glaze hot, icing on cool.

science: Danish dough combines two raising systems. Lamination traps thin sheets of butter between layers of dough; in the oven, water turns to steam and puffs those layers apart, giving flakiness. Yeast produces carbon dioxide during proofing, which opens the crumb inside each layer and makes it tender and bready rather than brittle like puff pastry. The two pull against each other: yeast needs warmth, but butter melts at around 90°F (32°C) and softens well before that, so proofing is kept below about 80°F (27°C). Crème pâtissière is thickened by starch, which needs to reach the boil to swell fully and to inactivate an enzyme in egg yolks that would otherwise thin the custard later.
plating: Arrange a mixed platter: snails in a row, spandauer in a square, combs curved along one edge, so each shape reads clearly. On a plate, one of each shape, the custard of the spandauer facing the guest.

pairing.drink: A strong filter coffee, black, in the Danish way: its bitterness and clean finish balance butter, almond and cardamom.

variations: Fruit spandauer: top the custard with a few raspberries or a poached apricot half before baking.
Kringle: a long strip filled with remonce and raisins, shaped into a pretzel and glazed.
Freeze shaped, unproofed pastries; thaw overnight in the fridge, then proof and bake.
safety: Bring the crème pâtissière to a full boil and chill it within 2 hours.
Refrigerate custard-filled pastries if not eaten the same day.

title: Sfogliatelle Ricce
summary: Naples' shell pastry: a stiff dough stretched into a long, thin sheet, rolled with lard into a tight log, sliced, pushed into cones and filled with a semolina and ricotta cream scented with orange and cinnamon, then baked until the hundreds of leaves fan out and shatter. It is in the course because it is among the hardest pastries in the world: patience, strength and an even hand in every stage.
skills: a stiff dough stretched into a long sheet
rolling a tight log with lard
equipment: Long work surface, at least 4 feet (1.2 m)
Small bowl of softened lard and a pastry brush or your hands
Two baking trays lined with baking paper

ingredients.note: butter gives a less crisp result

mise: The day before: drain the ricotta in a sieve in the fridge overnight.
Soften the lard to the texture of soft butter.
Clear the longest surface you have and set up the pasta machine at one end.
Mix the filling ahead if you like; it keeps 2 days in the fridge.
On baking day, heat the oven to 400°F (200°C).

timeline.do: Drain the ricotta; mix and knead the very stiff dough; rest 1 hour.
Roll the dough into a long thin sheet, brush with lard and roll into a tight log.
Wrap the log and refrigerate overnight.
Make the semolina filling and cool it.
Slice the log, shape cones and fill.
Bake 20 to 25 minutes.
Dust with icing sugar and serve warm.

steps.do: Mix the 2 1/2 cups (300 g) flour, 1/2 cup (120 ml) water, honey and salt in the mixer on low for 10 minutes. It will be very stiff and dry. Wrap and rest 1 hour.
steps.look: A hard, crumbly mass at first, then a stiff, smooth dough that is difficult to press with a finger.
steps.mistake: Adding water because it seems too dry; the dough must be stiff.
steps.fix: If it will not come together at all, add water 1 tsp (5 ml) at a time only.

steps.do: Cut the dough into 4 pieces. Flatten one and pass it through the pasta machine on the widest setting, fold it in half and pass again, 6 to 8 times, until smooth. Then roll it through progressively thinner settings to the second thinnest.
steps.look: A long, smooth, silky ribbon about 5 inches (13 cm) wide that you can almost see through.
steps.mistake: Tearing because you jumped settings.
steps.fix: Go one setting at a time. Patch small tears by overlapping.

steps.do: Lay the sheet on the long surface and gently stretch it wider with your fingertips, pulling from the centre outward, to about 8 inches (20 cm) wide. Brush or rub it evenly with softened lard.
steps.look: A translucent, greasy sheet with an even film of fat across it.
steps.mistake: Leaving dry patches without lard, so the layers fuse.
steps.fix: Cover every centimetre; the fat separates each leaf.

steps.do: Starting at one short end, roll the sheet into a tight log, stretching it as you roll by pulling it slightly towards you. When you reach the end, overlap the next sheet by 1 inch (2.5 cm), stretch, lard and keep rolling, until all four sheets make one log about 2 1/2 inches (6 cm) thick.
steps.look: A dense, tight log with fine visible spirals at each end; it feels firm.
steps.mistake: Rolling loosely, which gives few, thick layers.
steps.fix: Keep tension on the sheet with each turn. Tight rolling is what makes many leaves.

steps.do: Rub the outside of the log with more lard, wrap tightly in cling film and refrigerate overnight.
steps.look: A firm, cold log that feels solid when pressed and shows fine spirals at each end.
steps.mistake: Slicing it warm, when the layers smear.
steps.fix: It must be cold and firm to cut cleanly.

steps.do: Make the filling: bring the 1 cup (240 ml) water and sugar to the boil, whisk in the 1/3 cup (60 g) semolina and cook, stirring, 3 to 4 minutes until very thick. Cool completely. Push the drained ricotta through a sieve and beat it with the semolina, egg yolk, candied peel, cinnamon and vanilla.
steps.look: A thick, smooth, creamy filling flecked with orange that holds its shape on a spoon.
steps.mistake: Warm semolina that thins the ricotta.
steps.fix: Cool fully; chill if it seems loose.

steps.do: Trim the ends of the log and cut 12 slices about 1/2 inch (1 cm) thick with the sharp knife.
steps.look: Rounds showing a tight spiral of many fine lines.
steps.mistake: Pressing down with a blunt knife, which squashes the spiral.
steps.fix: Use a sharp knife with a gentle sawing stroke.

steps.do: Shape each slice: hold it with both thumbs in the centre and fingers behind. Push the centre outward with your thumbs while pressing the layers forward, rotating and sliding them so the slice becomes a cone about 3 inches (8 cm) long, like a shell.
steps.look: The rings slide over each other like a telescope; the cone has fine ridges on the outside.
steps.mistake: Pulling the layers apart so the cone tears.
steps.fix: Grease your fingers with lard and push gently; the layers should slide, not separate.

steps.do: Fill each cone with 1 1/2 tbsp (25 g) of filling and press the open edge lightly to close it a little. Set on the lined trays.
steps.look: Plump shells with the filling peeking out at the wide end.
steps.mistake: Overfilling, so the filling bursts out in the oven.
steps.fix: Fill to just below the rim.

steps.do: Bake at 400°F (200°C) for 20 to 25 minutes until deep golden and the ridges stand out crisp and separated.
steps.look: The leaves fan apart and turn amber; you hear the pastry crackling and the kitchen smells of orange and baked lard.
steps.mistake: Underbaking, when the leaves are pale and chewy.
steps.fix: Leave them until deep golden all over.

steps.do: Cool the sfogliatelle on the tray for 10 minutes, dust them heavily with icing sugar through a fine sieve and serve warm.
steps.look: Shattering leaves under a snowy dusting and a warm, soft filling.
steps.mistake: Serving cold, when the leaves lose their crunch.
steps.fix: Reheat leftovers at 350°F (175°C) for 5 minutes.

science: Sfogliatelle get their leaves from fat, not yeast or steam alone. The stiff, low-water dough develops a strong gluten network that can be stretched almost transparent without tearing. Each turn of the log traps a film of lard between dough layers. In the oven, water in the thin dough turns to steam and the fat fries each leaf, so the layers separate and crisp into a fan of thin shells. Lard works especially well because its crystals stay solid over a wide range of temperatures and it contains no water, giving crisper layers than butter. Shaping the cone slides the layers over each other, opening gaps that the heat can reach. The filling sets as the semolina starch and the egg yolk firm in the heat.
plating: Serve on a small white plate, two shells per person laid side by side with their ridged backs up, dusted generously with icing sugar. An espresso beside.

pairing.drink: A short Neapolitan espresso or a small glass of limoncello: the coffee's bitterness or the liqueur's lemon cut through lard and sweet ricotta.

variations: Sfogliatella frolla: a smooth shortcrust shell with the same filling, far easier.
Santa Rosa: add a swirl of crème pâtissière and black cherries on top.
Lobster tail (aragosta): fill baked shells with whipped cream and custard instead.
safety: Ricotta filling contains raw egg yolk until baked; bake until the filling is hot right through.
Keep fingers out of the pasta machine rollers; feed the dough with flat palms.

title: Tiradito Nikkei
summary: Raw white fish sliced like sashimi, laid flat on a chilled plate and dressed at the last second with a cold sauce of ají amarillo, lime, soy and dashi, the Japanese Peruvian refinement of ceviche. It is in the course because it is a composed cold starter where precision is everything: the angle of the knife, the thickness of the slice, and the timing of an acid sauce that would turn the fish chalky if it sat for a minute.
skills: slicing raw fish as for sashimi
an ají amarillo and citrus sauce
equipment: Long, very sharp slicing knife (yanagiba or the sharpest you own)
Fish-only chopping board on a damp cloth
Four flat plates, chilled in the freezer
Small saucepan or bowl for the dashi
Small spoon or squeeze bottle for saucing

ingredients.item: Sashimi-grade fluke, sole, sea bass or corvina loin, skinned
ingredients.note: previously frozen, sold for raw eating

ingredients.item: Key lime or lime juice, freshly squeezed
ingredients.note: about 8 limes, squeezed gently so the pith does not turn it bitter

ingredients.item: Ají amarillo, fresh and deseeded, or ají amarillo paste

ingredients.note: from a 2 inch (5 cm) square of kombu soaked 1 hour in 1/2 cup (120 ml) water, or instant dashi

ingredients.item: Ají limo or a small red chilli
ingredients.note: deseeded, cut in very fine strips
sliced paper thin on the diagonal

mise: Chill the plates in the freezer for at least 20 minutes.
Make the dashi by soaking the kombu in cold water for 1 hour; remove the kombu.
Deseed the ají amarillo; slice the ají limo and spring onion; pick the coriander.
Squeeze the limes no more than 20 minutes before serving, squeezing gently.
Put the fish loin on a plate in the freezer for 15 minutes to firm it.

timeline.do: Soak kombu for dashi; chill plates.
Make the sauce and chill it; prepare garnishes.
Firm the fish in the freezer for 15 minutes.
Slice the fish and lay it on the cold plates; refrigerate.
Sauce, garnish and serve at once.

steps.do: Blend the ají amarillo, garlic, ginger, salt, ice cubes and half the lime juice for 1 minute to a smooth, loose sauce. Strain through the sieve into a jug, pressing on the solids.
steps.look: A bright yellow-orange, silky sauce, cold to the touch, with a fruity, warm smell from the ají.
steps.mistake: Blending without ice, so friction warms the sauce and dulls the lime.
steps.fix: Always add ice; it chills and thins the sauce at once.

steps.do: Stir in the remaining lime juice, the 2 tbsp (30 ml) soy sauce and the 2 tbsp (30 ml) dashi. Taste: it should hit sour first, then salty, then a slow warmth. Chill in the fridge.
steps.look: A balanced sauce that makes your mouth water; salt behind the lime, gentle heat at the end.
steps.mistake: Too much soy, which turns the sauce brown and muddy.
steps.fix: Adjust with lime and a pinch of salt rather than more soy.

steps.do: Take the firmed loin from the freezer. Look at the direction of the muscle lines and set the knife across them at about 45 degrees.
steps.look: Fine white lines running along the fillet; the fish feels cold and firm but not frozen.
steps.mistake: Cutting along the grain, which makes stringy slices that fall apart.
steps.fix: Turn the fillet until the lines run away from you, then angle the blade across them.

steps.do: Slice the fish in one long pulling stroke per slice, starting at the heel of the blade, into slices 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick. Lay them flat and slightly overlapping in a single row or fan across each chilled plate.
steps.look: Glossy, even, translucent slices with clean edges; the knife glides through without sound.
steps.mistake: Sawing back and forth, which tears the fibres and makes the fish weep and look dull.
steps.fix: One pull per slice using the whole length of the blade; wipe it with a damp cloth between cuts.

steps.do: Cover the plates loosely with cling film and return them to the fridge until the moment of serving, no more than 10 minutes.
steps.look: The slices stay glossy, translucent and cold, with no dull or dry edges.
steps.mistake: Leaving the plated fish at room temperature.
steps.fix: Plate and chill straight away; serve within 10 minutes.

steps.do: At the pass, spoon the cold sauce over and around the fish, about 2 tbsp (30 ml) per plate, so it pools beneath and coats the slices lightly.
steps.look: The edges of the slices begin to turn opaque white within seconds while the centres stay translucent.
steps.mistake: Saucing in advance, so the lime denatures the fish all the way through and it turns chalky.
steps.fix: Sauce only as you carry it to the table.

steps.do: Scatter the ají limo strips, coriander, spring onion and sesame seeds over the fish and finish with a few flakes of salt. Serve at once.
steps.look: A clean plate: pale fish, a yellow pool, flecks of green and red.
steps.mistake: Heaping garnishes that hide the cutting.
steps.fix: Use a light hand; the knife work is what the guest should see.

science: Lime juice does not cook fish with heat; its acid denatures the proteins, unwinding their tightly folded structures so they bond into a firmer, opaque network, much as heat would. Thin slices cut across the grain go opaque at the surface in under a minute while staying juicy inside, which is why tiradito is sauced at the last moment. Let it sit and the acid works all the way through, the fibres tighten and squeeze out water and the fish turns chalky. Firming the fish in the freezer makes the muscle easier to cut cleanly. Dashi and soy add glutamate and other savoury compounds that round out the sharp acid, and ice in the blender keeps the sauce cold so the fish is not warmed when sauced.
plating: Use chilled, flat, white or dark plates. Lay the slices in a single straight line or a gentle crescent, each overlapping the last by a third. Spoon the sauce into a shallow pool beneath and a thin stripe over the top, then place the garnishes in a line along the slices, a coriander leaf on every second slice.

pairing.drink: A Pisco Sour or a crisp Sauvignon Blanc: both share the lime's sharpness and the green, herbal notes of coriander and ají, and stay fresh beside raw fish.
pairing.brennans: Famille Durand Val de Loire Sauvignon Blanc 2024: a bright, citrusy Loire white on the Brennan's list that matches the lime and coriander.

variations: Tiradito with leche de tigre: a classic Peruvian sauce of lime, fish trimmings, celery, ginger and chilli blended and strained.
Salmon tiradito with passion fruit in place of some of the lime.
Scallop tiradito: slice raw sashimi-grade scallops thinly and dress the same way.
safety: Use only fish sold for raw eating; wild fish should have been frozen to -4°F (-20°C) for 7 days. Lime juice does not kill parasites or bacteria.
Keep the fish at 40°F (4°C) or below until it is served and discard any leftovers.
Raw fish is not advised for pregnant guests, young children, the elderly or anyone with a weakened immune system.
Slice with the blade moving away from your other hand and keep the board steady on a damp cloth.

title: Pickled Herring Three Ways
summary: Fresh herring filleted at home, frozen for safety, cured in brine and a sweet vinegar pickle, then finished three ways: with onion and dill, in a creamy mustard sauce, and spiced with allspice and cloves. It is in the course because preserving one batch three ways is Nordic cooking at the level of a smörgåsbord, and it teaches filleting small oily fish and controlling salt, acid and sugar.
skills: a salt cure then three pickles: mustard, onion and dill, and spiced
equipment: Fish scaler or the back of a knife
Large glass or ceramic dish for brining
Three clean glass jars with lids, about 1 pint (500 ml) each
Whisk and small bowl for the mustard sauce

ingredients.note: very fresh, bright eyed, firm; or 16 fresh fillets
thinly sliced, for onion and dill

ingredients.item: Sweet, coarse Swedish mustard or honey mustard
New potatoes, sour cream, chives, hard-boiled eggs and crispbread

mise: Make sure the fish will be frozen for 7 days before curing; plan the timeline from that.
Clean all jars and lids with hot soapy water and rinse well.
Make the brine by dissolving the salt in the cold water.
Make the pickle: bring the vinegar, sugar and water to the boil, stir until dissolved, then cool completely.
Slice the onion and carrot; pick and chop the dill.

timeline.do: Fillet the herring and freeze the fillets at -4°F (-20°C) or colder for 7 days.
Thaw the fillets overnight in the fridge, or in cold water in sealed bags for 1 hour.
Brine the fillets 12 hours in the fridge.
Rinse, cut in pieces and cover with the sweet pickle for 24 hours.
Divide into three jars with three flavourings; chill at least 24 hours more.
Serve with new potatoes, sour cream, eggs and crispbread.

steps.do: Scale each herring under cold running water, scraping from tail to head; the scales come off easily. Cut off the head just behind the gills, slit the belly and remove the guts. Rinse well and scrape out the dark bloodline along the spine.
steps.look: Shining silver fish with a clean, pale cavity; they smell of fresh sea air, never of ammonia.
steps.mistake: Using fish that smells strong or has dull eyes; herring spoils fast.
steps.fix: Buy from a busy fishmonger and fillet the same day.

steps.do: Fillet: lay the fish on its side, run the knife along the backbone from head end to tail, keeping the blade against the bones, and lift off the fillet. Turn and repeat. Trim the belly edge and pull any obvious pin bones with tweezers. Pat dry.
steps.look: Two neat fillets with skin on and very little flesh left on the frame.
steps.mistake: Fretting over every fine bone; herring has many tiny bones that the pickle softens.
steps.fix: Remove the large belly bones and the obvious pins; the small ones dissolve in the acid.

steps.do: Lay the fillets flat in freezer bags and freeze at -4°F (-20°C) or colder for 7 days. Thaw overnight in the fridge.
steps.look: Firm, frozen flat sheets; after thawing, fillets still firm and glossy.
steps.mistake: Skipping the freeze because the fish will be pickled.
steps.fix: Vinegar and salt do not kill the parasites herring often carry; freezing does.

steps.do: Submerge the thawed fillets in the cold brine in the glass dish, cover and refrigerate for 12 hours.
steps.look: The flesh firms and turns slightly paler; it tastes seasoned but not harsh when you try a sliver.
steps.mistake: Brining much longer, which makes the fish too salty.
steps.fix: If it tastes too salty, soak 30 minutes in fresh cold water before pickling.

steps.do: Rinse the fillets, pat dry and cut them on a slight diagonal into pieces about 1 inch (2.5 cm) wide. Put them in a bowl, pour over the cooled pickle to cover, cover and refrigerate 24 hours.
steps.look: The flesh turns white and firm throughout as the acid works, and the skin turns a little silvery.
steps.mistake: Pouring on warm pickle, which cooks the outside and makes it mushy.
steps.fix: Always cool the pickle completely first.

steps.do: Onion and dill: drain a third of the herring, saving the pickle. Layer it in a jar with the red onion, carrot, a third of the allspice, a bay leaf and plenty of dill. Pour over enough of the saved pickle to cover.
steps.look: Pink onion rings and orange carrot between white pieces of fish, all covered by liquid.
steps.mistake: Leaving fish above the liquid, where it dries and spoils.
steps.fix: Press it down and top up with pickle so it is fully covered.

steps.do: Spiced: put the 6 cloves, cinnamon, ginger, peppercorns, the remaining allspice and a bay leaf in a small pan with 1 cup (240 ml) of the saved pickle and simmer 3 minutes, then cool completely. Pack another third of the herring into a jar and pour the spiced pickle over to cover.
steps.look: A golden pickle that smells of warm spices; fish covered in a second jar.
steps.mistake: Adding the spiced liquid hot.
steps.fix: Cool the spice liquid completely before pouring it on.

steps.do: Mustard: whisk the 3 tbsp (45 g) mustard, the sweet mustard, 1 tbsp (12 g) sugar and 1 tbsp (15 ml) vinegar in a bowl. Whisk in the 1/3 cup (80 ml) oil a few drops at a time, then in a thin stream, until thick and glossy. Fold in the crème fraîche and plenty of chopped dill.
steps.look: A thick, pale yellow, glossy sauce like a mustard mayonnaise.
steps.mistake: Adding the oil too fast, so the sauce separates.
steps.fix: Stop and whisk hard; if it splits, whisk it slowly into 1 tsp (5 g) fresh mustard in a clean bowl.

steps.do: Drain the last third of the herring well, pat dry and fold it into the mustard sauce. Spoon into the third jar. Refrigerate all three jars at least 24 hours before serving.
steps.look: Herring pieces coated in creamy yellow sauce, flecked with green dill.
steps.mistake: Wet herring, which thins the sauce.
steps.fix: Pat the pieces very dry first.

steps.do: Serve the three herrings in small dishes with boiled new potatoes tossed with dill, sour cream with chives, halved hard-boiled eggs and crispbread.
steps.look: Three contrasting herrings: sharp and sweet, warm and spiced, creamy and pungent.
steps.mistake: Serving them straight from cold jars with no accompaniments.
steps.fix: Let them stand 10 minutes out of the fridge; potatoes and sour cream are part of the dish.

science: Herring is an oily fish whose fat oxidises and spoils quickly, so it is preserved by stages. Salt draws water from the muscle by osmosis and moves into the flesh, firming it and making it less hospitable to bacteria. Vinegar then lowers the pH sharply, denaturing proteins so the flesh turns white and firm; the acid also softens the many fine bones. Sugar balances the sharpness and also draws water out. None of this kills the larvae of the parasite anisakis, which herring commonly carries; freezing at -4°F (-20°C) for seven days does. The mustard sauce is an emulsion: mustard contains compounds in its seed coat that coat oil droplets and keep them suspended.
plating: Serve the three herrings in small glass dishes or jars side by side on a board, each with a sprig of dill, so their colours read: pink and white, golden, yellow. Potatoes in a warm bowl, sour cream in a small dish with chives on top, eggs halved yolk side up, crispbread standing in a glass.

pairing.drink: Ice-cold aquavit sipped in small measures with a pale lager chaser, the Swedish way: caraway and dill in the spirit echo the herring, and the beer refreshes.

variations: Matjes style: brine longer and serve the fillets whole with sour cream, onions and potatoes.
Beetroot herring: add 1/2 cup (75 g) diced pickled beetroot and its juice to the onion jar.
Sherry herring: replace a quarter of the pickle water with medium sherry and add orange zest.
safety: Freeze herring at -4°F (-20°C) or colder for 7 days before pickling; salt and vinegar do not kill parasites.
Keep the jars in the fridge at 40°F (4°C) or below. Eat the mustard herring within 5 days and the pickled ones within 2 weeks.
Use only clean jars and utensils, and keep the fish covered by liquid.

title: Maryland Crab Cakes
summary: Crab cakes that are almost all jumbo lump blue crab, held together by the least possible binder, chilled until firm, then fried in butter until bronzed and served with a rémoulade. It is in the course because it teaches restraint: picking crab for shell without breaking the lumps, binding to the minimum, and letting the fridge do the work that filler does in a lesser cake.
skills: binding with as little as possible
equipment: Large rimmed tray, dark if possible, for picking crab
Baking tray lined with baking paper
Large heavy frying pan, cast iron or stainless

ingredients.note: fresh or pasteurised; the best you can find
zest finely grated; juice for the sauce and to serve

ingredients.us: a few dashes and a pinch
ingredients.metric: a few dashes and a pinch

mise: Make the rémoulade: stir together the mayonnaise, cornichons, capers, mustard, herbs, a squeeze of lemon, hot sauce and paprika; chill.
Crush the crackers to fine crumbs in a bag with a rolling pin.
Zest the lemon; chop the parsley.
Line a baking tray with baking paper.
Clear space in the fridge for the tray.

timeline.do: Make the rémoulade; pick the crab.
Mix the binder, fold in the crab, shape four cakes.
Chill the cakes 1 hour.
Heat the pan; fry the cakes 4 minutes a side.
Serve with rémoulade and lemon.

steps.do: Pick the crab: spread the crab meat in a thin layer on the tray. Run your fingertips lightly over it, feeling for hard, sharp pieces of shell and cartilage, and remove every one. Turn the lumps gently, never squeezing.
steps.look: Large, white lumps left intact; any shell clicks against the tray when dropped. The crab smells sweet and clean.
steps.mistake: Breaking up the lumps by picking roughly.
steps.fix: Touch lightly and lift shell out with fingertips; lumps are what you are paying for.

steps.do: Whisk the egg, 3 tbsp (45 g) mayonnaise, Dijon, Worcestershire, Old Bay, lemon zest and parsley in a large bowl. Sprinkle the crushed crackers over and stir to combine.
steps.look: A smooth, pale orange binder, flecked with green.
steps.mistake: Adding extra crumbs to make it feel firmer.
steps.fix: The binder should be loose; the chill firms it.

steps.do: Add the crab and fold it in with a spatula, turning the bowl and lifting from underneath, about six folds, until just coated.
steps.look: Large lumps of crab glistening with binder, still whole and distinct, with no dry crab left.
steps.mistake: Stirring vigorously, which shreds the crab into paste.
steps.fix: Fold gently and stop as soon as no dry crab remains.

steps.do: Divide into 4 portions of about 5 oz (140 g). Gently cup each in your hands into a thick puck about 3 inches (8 cm) across and 1 1/4 inches (3 cm) tall, without pressing hard. Set on the lined tray.
steps.look: Loose, craggy cakes that barely hold together, with lumps visible on the surface.
steps.mistake: Packing the mixture tightly, which makes a dense cake.
steps.fix: Cup, do not squeeze. Fragile is correct.

steps.do: Cover the tray loosely with cling film and chill the cakes in the fridge for at least 1 hour, ideally 2.
steps.look: The cakes firm up and hold their shape when the tray is tilted.
steps.mistake: Frying straight away, so they collapse in the pan.
steps.fix: The chill sets the mayonnaise and egg; give it the full hour.

steps.do: Heat the 2 tbsp (30 g) butter and 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil in the heavy pan over medium heat until the butter foams. Lay in the cakes with the fish slice, spaced apart.
steps.look: A steady, gentle sizzle and a nutty smell of butter.
steps.mistake: A pan too hot, which burns the butter before the cakes heat through.
steps.fix: Medium heat. If the butter browns fast, lower the heat.

steps.do: Fry 4 minutes without moving, until a deep golden crust forms, then turn carefully with the fish slice and fry 3 to 4 minutes more, until the centre reads 160°F (71°C).
steps.look: A bronze crust that holds when turned; steam rising from the edges; the cake feels springy.
steps.mistake: Turning too early, before the crust has set, so the cake breaks.
steps.fix: Wait until it releases easily. If one breaks, press it back together; it will still taste perfect.

steps.do: Drain the cakes for 30 seconds on kitchen paper and serve at once with the rémoulade and lemon wedges.
steps.look: Golden cakes, crisp outside and moist inside, falling into big lumps of crab under a fork.
steps.mistake: Covering them, so steam softens the crust.
steps.fix: Serve straight away and never cover them.

science: The crab cake is held together by protein and fat, not starch. Egg proteins and the egg yolk in mayonnaise coat the crab and set when heated, while the mayonnaise's fat and the small amount of cracker crumb absorb moisture. Chilling solidifies the fat in the mayonnaise and lets the crumbs absorb liquid, so the cake holds its shape in the pan; that is why the fridge replaces the extra filler that would mute the crab. Crab meat is already cooked, so frying only heats it through and browns the outside through the Maillard reaction. The cake must reach 160°F (71°C) to cook the raw egg. The rémoulade's acidity from cornichons, capers and lemon cuts through the butter and sweet crab.
plating: Warm plates. Set one cake slightly off centre, crust side up, and spoon the rémoulade in a neat quenelle beside it, not over it. A lemon wedge and a small salad of dressed leaves or a spoonful of corn relish on the other side.

pairing.drink: A crisp Muscadet or an ice-cold lager: both have the clean acidity and freshness to cut through butter and lift the sweet crab.
pairing.brennans: Domaine de l’Écu ‘Orthogneiss’ Muscadet Sèvre-et-Maine 2022: a mineral, saline Muscadet on the Brennan's list, a classic partner for crab.

variations: Grilled crab cakes: brush with melted butter and cook under the overhead grill (broiler) on high 10 to 12 minutes without turning.
Crab cake Benedict: a smaller cake under a poached egg and hollandaise.
Lighter sauce: lemon aioli or a simple tartare sauce in place of the rémoulade.
safety: Cook crab cakes until the centre reaches 160°F (71°C), because they contain raw egg.
Keep crab meat at 40°F (4°C) or below and use fresh crab within 2 days of opening.
