title: Melton Mowbray Pork Pie
summary: A raised pork pie in the Melton Mowbray manner: a hot water crust shaped by hand around a jar, filled with hand-chopped seasoned pork, baked free-standing and filled through the lid with stock that sets to jelly. It is in the course because it is a British art of pastry and charcuterie together: a pastry worked while warm, a filling seasoned only with salt and pepper, and a jelly that seals the meat.
skills: a hot water crust raised by hand
filling with stock that sets to jelly
equipment: Straight-sided jar or a pie dolly, about 5 inches (13 cm) across
Large mixing bowl and wooden spoon
Sharp knife and board for hand-chopping
Small funnel or a piping nozzle

ingredients.item: Egg yolk and milk, for the wash
Pork or chicken stock, well flavoured

mise: Wrap the outside of the jar in cling film and dust it lightly with flour.
Cut the chilled pork shoulder and belly into 1/4 inch (6 mm) dice by hand, keeping a third of the belly slightly coarser.
Cut a strip of baking paper about 4 inches (10 cm) wide and long enough to wrap the pie, and a length of string.
Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C).
Soak the gelatine in cold water just before making the jelly.

timeline.do: Chop and season the filling; chill.
Make the hot water crust and raise the case around the jar.
Fill, lid and crimp the pie; collar it with paper.
Bake 30 minutes at 400°F (200°C), then about 75 minutes at 350°F (175°C).
Cool 1 hour; pour in the cool jelly through the hole.
Chill overnight to set.
Serve cold in wedges with pickle and mustard.

steps.do: Make the filling: put the diced shoulder and belly in a bowl with the salt, white and black pepper and mace and mix well with your hands for 1 minute until slightly sticky. Fry a small piece to taste for seasoning. Chill.
steps.look: A coarse, pink, well-seasoned mixture that just holds together when pressed.
steps.mistake: Mincing it fine, which makes a dense, sausage-like filling.
steps.fix: Chop by hand for the classic open texture.

steps.do: Make the hot water crust: mix the 3 cups (375 g) flour and salt in the bowl. Heat the lard and 2/3 cup (150 ml) water in the saucepan until the lard melts and the water just boils. Pour it into the flour and stir with the wooden spoon, then knead briefly when cool enough to handle, to a smooth, warm dough.
steps.look: A smooth, soft, pliable dough, warm to the touch and slightly glossy.
steps.mistake: Letting the dough go cold, when it cracks and cannot be shaped.
steps.fix: Work it warm. Keep the portion you are not using covered and warm in the bowl.

steps.do: Cut off a quarter of the dough for the lid and keep it warm and covered. Flatten the rest into a thick disc, set the floured jar in the centre, and push and coax the pastry up its sides with your hands, turning the jar, until the walls are an even 3/8 inch (1 cm) thick and about 3 inches (8 cm) high.
steps.look: An even, smooth-walled case standing around the jar.
steps.mistake: Thin patches near the base, which leak during baking.
steps.fix: Press the base and lower walls a little thicker. Patch thin spots with dough while warm.

steps.do: Let the case cool and firm for 10 minutes, then twist and lift the jar out gently, peeling away the cling film.
steps.look: A free-standing pastry case that holds its shape.
steps.mistake: Pulling the jar out while the pastry is still soft, so it collapses.
steps.fix: Wait until the walls feel firm and cool.

steps.do: Pack the filling into the case, pressing it into the edges and doming it slightly in the middle. Roll the reserved dough into a lid, brush the rim of the case with egg wash, set the lid on, and pinch and crimp the edges together firmly. Cut a 1/2 inch (1 cm) hole in the centre.
steps.look: A full, slightly domed pie with a crimped edge and a neat steam hole.
steps.mistake: Leaving air gaps, which leave holes in the slice.
steps.fix: Press the meat down firmly as you fill.

steps.do: Wrap the paper strip around the pie and tie it loosely with string to support the walls. Brush the lid with egg wash.
steps.look: A neat paper collar holding the pie walls straight and upright, tied without denting them.
steps.mistake: Tying too tightly, which dents the soft pastry.
steps.fix: Snug but loose; it only stops the walls bowing.

steps.do: Bake on the tray at 400°F (200°C) for 30 minutes, then lower to 350°F (175°C) for 60 to 75 minutes. Remove the collar for the last 20 minutes, brush the sides with egg wash and return until golden all over. The centre should read 160°F (71°C).
steps.look: A deep golden, glossy crust; juices bubbling up through the hole; it smells of baked pork and pepper.
steps.mistake: Pale sides, or pulling it before the centre is cooked.
steps.fix: Use the probe through the hole; bake until golden and 160°F (71°C).

steps.do: Cool the pie 1 hour. Make the jelly: squeeze the soaked gelatine and dissolve it in the warm stock, then cool until it is just pourable, the thickness of egg white. Pour it slowly through the hole with the funnel, a little at a time, letting it soak in, until the pie will take no more.
steps.look: The jelly disappears into the gap between meat and pastry, then rises to the hole.
steps.mistake: Pouring hot jelly, which softens the crust and leaks out.
steps.fix: Use cool, syrupy jelly and pour in stages.

steps.do: Refrigerate overnight so the jelly sets. Serve cold, cut into wedges with a sharp knife, with English mustard and pickle or piccalilli.
steps.look: A clean slice: golden crust, a layer of clear jelly, then pale grey pork with a coarse texture.
steps.mistake: Slicing warm, when the jelly runs.
steps.fix: Chill thoroughly; slice straight from the fridge.

science: Hot water crust works differently from other pastry. Pouring boiling water and melted lard into flour partly gelatinises the starch and coats the flour in fat, so very little gluten forms; the warm dough is soft and mouldable like clay and sets firm as it cools, which is why the case can stand on its own. In the oven the lard keeps it crisp and sturdy rather than flaky. The meat shrinks as its proteins contract and release juices, leaving a gap under the crust. Jelly fills that gap: gelatin from the stock sets when cold, sealing the meat from air, keeping it moist and helping the pie keep. A Melton Mowbray pie uses uncured pork, which is why the meat is grey, not pink.
plating: Serve on a wooden board, the whole pie with one wedge cut and pulled slightly away to show the layers of crust, jelly and meat. Mustard and piccalilli in small pots, pickled onions and a few watercress sprigs beside.

pairing.drink: A pint of English bitter or a crisp cider: malt and gentle bitterness, or apple acidity, both cut through lard pastry and rich pork.

variations: Gala pie: add a line of hard-boiled eggs through the middle of the filling in a loaf-shaped pie.
Pork and apple: add 1 diced apple and a little sage to the filling.
Small pies: make six individual pies around a small jar, baking 45 to 55 minutes.
safety: Bake until the centre reaches 160°F (71°C).
Add the jelly only once the pie has cooled for 1 hour, then refrigerate promptly; keep the pie at 40°F (4°C) or below and eat within 4 days.
Hot lard and water burn: pour carefully and stir with a wooden spoon before touching the dough.

title: Pâté en Croûte
summary: The summit of French charcuterie: a cured forcemeat of pork, liver and ham with pistachios, baked in a pastry-lined hinged mould to a precise internal temperature, filled with aspic through chimneys, chilled for a day and sliced clean. It is in the course because it brings together curing, forcemeat, pastry and aspic, and is judged by one thing: a slice with no gaps.
skills: a pastry lining a hinged mould
equipment: Hinged pâté en croûte mould, about 12 by 3 inches (30 by 8 cm), or a loaf tin
Digital scale reading to 0.01 g for the curing salt
Meat grinder with a 1/4 inch (6 mm) plate, chilled
Two small tubes of rolled foil or card for chimneys
Long thin knife or electric knife for slicing

ingredients.item: Chicken livers, trimmed of green spots and sinew
Curing salt number 1 (pink salt, 6.25% sodium nitrite)
ingredients.note: weigh exactly: 0.25 percent of the meat

ingredients.item: Egg yolk and water, for the wash
Cornichons, Dijon mustard and dressed leaves

mise: Weigh the meat and calculate the salts from that weight; weigh the curing salt on the precise scale and label it.
Chill the grinder parts and bowls in the freezer for 1 hour.
Grease the mould lightly with butter.
Roll two tubes of foil about 2 inches (5 cm) long for the chimneys.
Soak the gelatine in cold water just before making the aspic.

timeline.do: Cure the diced meats with salts, Madeira and spices for 12 hours in the fridge.
Make the pastry and chill it at least 1 hour.
Grind, mix and test the forcemeat; line the mould; fill and lid.
Bake 20 minutes at 400°F (200°C), then at 325°F (160°C) until the centre reads 165°F (74°C).
Cool 1 hour, then chill overnight.
Pour in the cool aspic in stages; chill 24 hours more.
Unmould, slice with a thin knife and serve with cornichons and mustard.

steps.do: Toss the pork, back fat, livers and ham with the 1 tbsp (18 g) fine salt, the 1/2 tsp (3 g) curing salt, Madeira, white pepper and quatre épices. Cover and refrigerate 12 hours.
steps.look: The cubes turn deep pink and feel tacky, clinging to each other.
steps.mistake: Guessing the curing salt by volume; too much is dangerous.
steps.fix: Weigh it on a scale that reads to 0.01 g and mix it evenly through the fine salt first.

steps.do: Make the pastry: rub the 14 tbsp (200 g) cold butter into the 4 cups (500 g) flour and salt until it looks like coarse gravel. Add the 1/2 cup (120 ml) iced water and bring it together into a firm dough with no dry patches. Wrap and chill at least 1 hour.
steps.look: A firm, smooth dough with small flecks of butter.
steps.mistake: Overworking, which makes the pastry tough and shrink.
steps.fix: Mix only until it holds.

steps.do: Grind the cured meats through the chilled 1/4 inch (6 mm) plate into a chilled bowl. Beat in the 2 eggs and the pistachios with a wooden spoon for 1 minute until sticky. Fry a teaspoon and taste for salt and spice.
steps.look: A coarse, pink forcemeat studded with green pistachios, cold and sticky; the test piece is well seasoned and springy.
steps.mistake: Letting the mixture warm, so the fat smears and it turns greasy.
steps.fix: Keep everything cold. If it warms, chill 20 minutes.

steps.do: Roll two thirds of the pastry to 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick and line the mould, pressing it into the corners and leaving 3/4 inch (2 cm) hanging over the top. Patch any thin spots.
steps.look: Pastry lining every surface evenly with no cracks or holes.
steps.mistake: Holes or thin spots, where the juices and later the aspic will leak.
steps.fix: Press patches on firmly and seal with egg wash.

steps.do: Pack the forcemeat into the lined mould in layers, pressing into the corners to remove air, and level the top slightly domed.
steps.look: A tightly packed, level filling with no air pockets.
steps.mistake: Loose filling, which leaves gaps in the slice.
steps.fix: Press firmly in layers and tap the mould on the worktop.

steps.do: Brush the overhang with egg wash, fold it over the filling, and lay the rolled-out lid on top, pressing the edges to seal. Cut two holes about 5/8 inch (15 mm) across in the lid and insert the foil chimneys. Decorate with pastry trimmings and brush all over with egg wash.
steps.look: A neat, sealed top with two chimneys standing up.
steps.mistake: Forgetting the chimneys, so steam bursts the crust.
steps.fix: Insert them firmly; they let steam out and the aspic in later.

steps.do: Bake at 400°F (200°C) for 20 minutes, then lower to 325°F (160°C) and bake about 1 hour 15 minutes, until a probe through a chimney reads 165°F (74°C) in the centre.
steps.look: A deep golden crust; juices bubbling up the chimneys; it smells of roast pork, Madeira and butter.
steps.mistake: Taking it out by time alone.
steps.fix: Trust the probe, not the clock; cover with foil if it browns too fast.

steps.do: Cool the pâté in its mould for 1 hour at room temperature, then refrigerate overnight.
steps.look: The filling shrinks slightly, leaving a gap under the crust.
steps.mistake: Adding the aspic while the pâté is hot.
steps.fix: Chill it fully overnight first.

steps.do: Make the aspic: squeeze the gelatine and dissolve it in the warm stock. Cool it until syrupy, the thickness of egg white. Pour through the chimneys with the funnel in three or four stages, letting each soak in, until the gap is full. Chill 24 hours.
steps.look: The aspic disappears into the gaps, then rises to the top of the chimneys.
steps.mistake: Pouring hot aspic, which melts the fat and runs out of the seams.
steps.fix: Pour it cool and syrupy, a little at a time.

steps.do: Unmould the pâté and slice it with a long, thin knife dipped in hot water and wiped between slices, about 1/2 inch (1 cm) thick. Serve with cornichons, mustard and dressed leaves.
steps.look: Clean slices: a golden crust, a thin line of clear aspic, then a pink forcemeat with green pistachios and ham.
steps.mistake: Sawing with a blunt knife, which crumbles the crust.
steps.fix: A hot, sharp knife and long, single strokes.

science: Curing does three jobs. Salt dissolves muscle proteins so the forcemeat binds; sodium nitrite in curing salt keeps the meat pink, adds the cured flavour and inhibits the bacterium that causes botulism, which is why it is weighed to the hundredth of a gram, because too much is toxic. As the pâté bakes its proteins contract and shed liquid and fat, so the forcemeat shrinks away from the crust that has already set. Aspic fills that gap: gelatin dissolved in stock sets when cold, sealing the meat from air so it stays moist and keeps longer. Baking to a measured 165°F (74°C) cooks the pork and liver safely without overshooting, which would dry the forcemeat.
plating: Use a long, cold plate. Lay one slice flat in the centre so the cross-section faces up, two cornichons fanned beside it, a small spoonful of Dijon mustard and a little heap of dressed bitter leaves. A slice of toasted bread on the side.

pairing.drink: A Beaujolais cru, served slightly cool: bright red fruit and gentle tannin cut the fat of the forcemeat and pastry, the classic bistro partner.
pairing.brennans: Marcel Lapierre Morgon 2023: a Beaujolais cru on the Brennan's list, the textbook wine for charcuterie and pâté.

variations: Game pâté en croûte: replace half the pork shoulder with venison or duck, and the ham with diced duck breast.
Add a central garnish of seared duck breast or foie gras laid along the middle of the forcemeat.
Terrine: bake the same forcemeat without pastry in a bain-marie to 165°F (74°C).
safety: Curing salt is toxic in excess: weigh it precisely, label it clearly and store it out of reach of children.
Bake until the centre reaches 165°F (74°C), the poultry standard, because the forcemeat holds chicken liver.
Keep the finished pâté refrigerated at 40°F (4°C) or below and eat within 1 week.
Keep the forcemeat below 40°F (4°C) while grinding and mixing.
